event_model_payload.headline: Engineering AI Discover
event_model_payload.summary:
The challenges and decisions behind AI Discover’s intelligence layer

By Varun Khaitan, Peng Ren, Gary Tang, Itay Teller, Atif Faheem, Nipun Kumar, Donnie DeBoer, Eduardo Lundgren, Matteo Rinaldi, Raghav Bakshi

We recently introduced AI Discover, a new tab in our TV app where a small group of members can try new ways to find something to watch. For years, our recommendations have worked in the background, inferring what a member might enjoy from their viewing history. AI Discover moves from that silent ranking toward steerable discovery. A member picks a theme, say “Quick Watches,” and gets a row of matching titles, a short note on why they fit and a few narrower themes to try next. From there, they can keep narrowing, head somewhere new or tune what they see.

Building AI Discover raised a question many teams will recognize: how do you deliver a better member experience with generative AI on TV without sacrificing speed, reliability or safety? Our answer is a new intelligence layer, the agent harness behind AI Discover. For each request, it decides how to combine LLMs with our recommendation systems. It builds on years of work understanding what members enjoy, and on our recent work applying LLMs to recommendations and generative experiences. The layer itself plans each request, runs it across those systems, serves the result and evaluates it offline.

This post covers the challenges we designed for and the key decisions we made along the way.

Why an intelligence layer?

Every Netflix page combines recommendations with rules. We pick titles a member may enjoy, and eligibility, maturity and safety rules decide what can appear. An experience built on LLMs needs the same rules, plus code that decides when to call an LLM and how to handle its output. That code is called an agent harness, and it’s the core of our intelligence layer.

The simplest implementation hands the entire request to an LLM and lets it pick the titles, write the labels and decide what happens next. However, that leaves us relying on probabilistic output where we need governed results, because every turn in AI Discover ends on a screen in someone’s living room. At our scale, even rare failures happen many times a day. A member sees every slow call, unavailable title or off-brand line. Seven challenges shaped our design:

  1. Fitting LLMs into a product and architecture designed without them. Traditional recommenders rank titles based on past behavior. LLMs can do more: understand what a member is asking for and plan how to respond. Our existing experience would leave most of that unused.
  2. Keeping recommendations grounded. Every pick must be a real, available title from our changing catalog. Retrieval and rankers work in tandem with LLMs to choose titles that fit the member’s taste and intent.
  3. Working with slow, unpredictable LLMs. LLM calls are the slowest and most expensive part of the system. Tail latencies can spike, and the output may not be what you asked for. So we use LLMs selectively, treat what they return as untrusted input and test performance and quality before anything ships.
  4. Adapting to fast-changing models, tools and prompts. Modeling and engineering solutions keep evolving, so the product can’t depend on any single model, tool or prompt.
  5. Building for TV. Typing on a TV is hard, so members rely on the remote, and the app should respond to every press right away on widely varying hardware. TV apps also update slowly, so changes have to ship without an app release. A typical TV request returns in moments, while multi-step generation can take several seconds.
  6. Holding a safety and reliability bar at scale. Members always get a page, even when an LLM call fails or yields poor results. Their choices and our content standards hold on every request, and when something breaks, structured records show why.
  7. Learning from what members say alongside what we already know. Recommendations have always learned from viewing behavior. AI Discover also lets members tell us what they want, and that has to shape what they see next.

System Architecture

When a member picks a theme, the TV app sends the request to the Page Server, which builds pages for all Netflix apps and hands the request asynchronously to the intelligence layer. At a high level, this new layer has two components: a controller and an executor.

The controller decides what to run. It gathers the context needed for each request, including real-time signals such as the time of day. It then settles on a plan, either an established one or a new one drafted by its planner, validates it and retrieves only the member details that this plan requires from Memory Hub, our per-member memory store. These details may include member taste summaries generated by MemberLLM, our in-house language model for personalized recommendations, or feedback shared by the member. We talk more about Memory Hub and member taste summaries later.

A plan is a graph of approved steps, each running a capability. A capability is a named unit of work that can have multiple versions and belongs to a family such as retrieval, ranking, generation or packaging. It declares its inputs and outputs, the context it may see and what happens if it fails.

Capability declarations make a plan verifiable. Before execution, the controller validates the graph: every step is approved, every input has a producer, nothing loops and the plan ends in exactly one page. Afterward, the controller checks the result before it’s served.

The executor runs the plan. Steps pass typed outputs to each other through the declared contracts, so each receives exactly what it asked for. Independent steps run in parallel, each with its own deadline and appropriate fallback behaviors. Some steps are optimized LLM calls with one task each, such as writing row titles or suggesting next themes, and they act only within the validated plan. Checks before the run and contracts during it give us governed execution, where every action stays within limits set in code.

Both parts write to the request records, the traces we use offline to evaluate and improve the system.

Key Decisions

Each challenge led to one decision. Here’s what we chose and what it bought us.

1. Design the product and architecture around LLMs

We reimagined the experience around LLMs. The easier path would have been to drop them in as rankers, keep today’s latency budgets and precompute where necessary. AI Discover is built on a back-and-forth around themes a member can steer, which gives LLMs work only they can do: generating themes, explaining rows, summarizing taste and helping choose the titles that fit the member and the moment. Members pick themes with the remote, so they never have to type. On the TV, those themes and explanations get their own native UI elements. Behind the screen, LLMs can draft plans, and asynchronous serving gives multi-step agentic orchestration the time it needs.

This opens up experiences our traditional stack couldn’t support on its own.

2. Make existing systems composable

Keeping recommendations grounded meant building on the systems that already know our catalog and members. Most capabilities wrap complex, proven Netflix systems such as search, large-scale ranking and catalog metadata access. Some of them may run their own agents in the future.

Reshaping them took careful work, because agentic orchestration challenges many long-standing assumptions of distributed systems. A capability now has to work in combinations no one designed, for a caller that chooses to call it at runtime. Each one needs a clear purpose and a semantic interface, and shaping it means deciding how much to combine into a single step and how much to leave to the planner. Too fine, and the planner has more ways to go wrong; too coarse, and it loses room to compose richer plans.

In return, the planner gets building blocks it can mix in new ways, and connecting services takes far less manual wiring. Because plans can only use these blocks, even one drafted on the fly stays grounded in our catalog and member taste.

3. Plan first, then execute

To contain LLM latency and errors, we plan every request before anything runs. The familiar way to let an agent use tools is a loop: reason, call a tool, read the result, reason again. It’s flexible, but you can’t tell up front how many steps it will take or whether it has gone down a wrong path. In agent terms, ours is a plan-and-execute agent: an LLM can propose the path, but code decides whether it runs.

Plans come from two places: established plans we’ve already tested, and plans an LLM drafts on the fly. A router we control decides which one is served. Either way, the plan passes the same checks before it runs. If the planner is slow or its plan fails a check, we fall back to a tested plan.

This allows for adaptive planning. The planner can find new ways to serve a request, and we can balance cost, latency and quality for each task, from a lean single-call plan to a richer multi-step one.

4. Stay model and capability agnostic

The best model or capability for a task today may be second-best, or overkill, in a few months, so we built the system to switch between them. We assign each task to the model or capability version that fits it. Today that’s a per-task setting we can override live. Only some steps in a request use an LLM.

That only works if switching is easy. All the LLMs we use sit behind one common interface. Before we switch, each candidate is scored on the same tasks by automated checks and LLM judges, so every swap is a measured change.

Much of the system’s behavior lives in server-side prompts and configuration, so we can swap models, tools and capabilities without new code or a TV app release.

Upgrades get cheap and experiments get easy. Moving to a better model, ranker or retrieval system is a plan or setting change, not a migration, so each component can keep improving without a large investment.

5. Make page generation asynchronous

Inference keeps getting faster, but member expectations rise just as quickly: richer responses, more context and more of the page shaped by LLMs. The line between what feels instant and what’s worth waiting for will keep shifting, so we built the asynchronous path as a first-class way of serving.

Most of a TV app is synchronous: press a button, get a page. Generative work breaks that pattern. Holding one request open for many seconds across services would tie up too many threads. So requests that involve generation are asynchronous. The press returns right away with an acknowledgement, and the TV switches to a thinking state that explains what’s being prepared. Meanwhile, the executor runs the plan in the background. When the result is ready, the server notifies the TV, which then fetches it.

Slow generation no longer slows anything else. The serving path stays healthy however long a turn takes, and every press still gets immediate feedback on screen.

6. Enforce safety in code

Some rules must hold no matter what an LLM writes: content and maturity standards, what each step can access, and what a member has asked us not to show them. Putting those rules in a prompt makes them probabilistic, so we enforce them in code. Generated text is cleaned up before it reaches the screen. The planner sees a stripped-down request, and member details are limited to what the validated plan needs.

For example, the planner decides which inputs each step needs, such as the profile’s maturity rating for retrieval. Instead of writing parameter values directly, it uses placeholders. After the plan passes validation, the controller fills them with values from the request, matched by declared type. This also protects against prompt injection.

Each request also leaves a structured record: the plan, each step and its outcome, and which rules applied. When a page misses, we can tell whether the plan, the data, a rule or the model was at fault. The same records feed our offline evaluation and replay.

Together, these rules and records let an experiment ship at the same safety and privacy bar as the rest of the product.

7. Remember what members tell us

A taste summary is a short profile of what a member enjoys, such as favorite genres, tone and recurring themes. MemberLLM generates it ahead of time from the member’s viewing history, which keeps that LLM work off the request path. It helps us further personalize their page, and steps that write themes and explanations receive it as context, so their wording reflects the member. We’ll cover MemberLLM in more detail in an upcoming post.

In AI Discover, members can also tune their recommendations and tell us directly what they want. Those choices apply right away and carry across visits, and they give us a new signal alongside what we already know about their taste. This is a first step toward remembering more about each member, from their preferences to the habits that show up over time and the corners of the catalog they like to explore. We keep it all in Memory Hub, our persistent, low-latency memory store, next to their taste summaries, and we can add new kinds of memory as we need them. We apply these memories to later requests where they’re relevant, together with real-time context.

The member holds the remote

In this version, members interact by selecting themes and using tuning options such as “don’t recommend.” There’s no free-text input or open-ended chat. That keeps the LLM’s job narrow by design.

  • The usual protections still apply. Profile settings and our safety and privacy policies hold here as everywhere else.
  • Generated text was tested before launch. We ran safety evaluations on theme labels, row titles and explanations to make sure they meet our standards.

What’s next

It would have been faster to let an LLM do everything and stop there. The intelligence layer gave us an AI-native product, grounded building blocks, adaptive planning, quicker experimentation, asynchronous generation, governed execution and agent memory for tunable personalization. While AI Discover is its first experience, we designed it with more in mind.

We’ve organized our efforts to answer two questions:

  • How much do members want to shape their recommendations? Whether they’d rather steer or lean back, and how much, which kinds of themes help, and how we should blend what members tell us with our existing personalization systems.
  • What tradeoffs does this technology bring? How cost and latency hold up in production as we ramp traffic, how long members will wait for generated results, and whether errors came from the model, the harness or our existing systems. Multi-turn sessions also need different evaluation and observability than single requests.

Longer term, our goal is a system that improves itself, starting from the record each request leaves behind. Today we replay past requests against a new prompt, model or rule to see what changes, and we judge each change with automated checks, LLM judges and human evaluations. Eventually, we want the system to propose improvements, test them safely and keep only what proves better, within our privacy and data-use policies. As LLMs improve, more of the work may move into them, and the intelligence layer lets us move that line deliberately.

This is part of a bigger shift. Recommendation systems have long learned quietly from what members watch and answered with ranked rows. LLMs let them listen and respond, and members may increasingly expect that. We’ll keep exploring what that means for discovery on Netflix.

event_model_payload.headline: Updated B2B location access in the Customer Account API
event_model_payload.summary:
We've changed what B2B customers can read on all versions of the Customer Account API. Customers now read only the company data and the orders for companies that they belong to.

Company location access

The schema doesn't change. Some fields now return null, an empty list, or fewer results.

CompanyContact.locations returns an empty list unless the contact belongs to the current customer. The current customer reads the locations that they have a role in from their contact's locations field, from Company.locations, and from companyLocation(id:).

On a CompanyLocation where the current customer has no role, the following fields return null or an empty list:

  • Tax field: taxIdentifier.
  • Contact fields: contacts and roleAssignments.

Orders after a customer is removed from a company

When a merchant removes a customer from a company, order(id:) and draftOrder(id:) refuse that company's orders and draft orders. customer.orders and customer.draftOrders exclude the orders and draft orders for that company. The customer's personal orders are still listed.

What you need to do

If your app reads a location's tax or contact data through another contact's locations or through an order's purchasingEntity, then expect null or an empty list for locations where the customer has no role. If your app shows a customer's order history, then the history omits the orders that the customer placed for a company that they no longer belong to. You don't need to change your queries.

event_model_payload.headline: Amazon EventBridge webhook payload size limit increased to 1 MB
event_model_payload.summary:
You can now receive webhook and Events payloads up to 1 MB (1,000,000 bytes) through Amazon EventBridge, up from 256 KB. This increase applies automatically across all API versions, and you don't need to update your existing subscriptions.

What changed

Previously, Amazon EventBridge deliveries capped payloads at 256 KB:

  • Classic webhook payloads over 256 KB fell back to a minimal {"id": ...} body, requiring a follow-up Admin API request to fetch the full resource.
  • Events payloads over 256 KB used large-payload overflow and delivered a temporary payload_url download link instead of the inline payload.

Shopify now sends raw UTF-8 payloads up to 1,000,000 bytes directly to your Amazon EventBridge partner event source, leaving headroom under EventBridge's 1 MiB entry cap for the source, detail-type, and detail envelope. Large resources such as products with many variants or orders with many line items now arrive inline, reducing follow-up Admin API requests and payload_url downloads in your app.

Payloads over 1,000,000 bytes keep the existing fallback behavior: classic webhooks send {"id": ...}, and Events deliveries send a stub payload with payload_url, payload_size_bytes, and expires_at.

What to do

No action is required. Existing EventBridge subscriptions configured in shopify.app.toml or through the GraphQL Admin API (eventBridgeWebhookSubscriptionCreate and webhookSubscriptionCreate) automatically receive inline payloads up to 1 MB across all API versions.

To review how your app handles large deliveries:

  • Keep fallback handling in place for payloads that exceed 1 MB ({"id": ...} for classic webhooks and payload_url for Events), or narrow payloads with include_fields and targeted Events [events.subscription] query selections.
  • Verify that the downstream AWS targets attached to your EventBridge rules accept events up to 1 MB, or configure an EventBridge input transformer if a target enforces a smaller quota.

event_model_payload.headline: Find the log line that matters faster with full-text search in Grafana Cloud Logs
event_model_payload.summary:
A support ticket comes in with one clue: a transaction ID. The answer is somewhere in your logs, but you don't know which service logged it, which pod handled it, or which day it happened. So you write the query you always write, {service="payments"} |= "txn-123456", widen the time range to the last two weeks, and wait. Then the query times out.

Loki was originally built around a simple idea: index labels, not log content, and store compressed logs cheaply in object storage. That design keeps storage costs low and operations light, and it's why teams keep choosing Loki and Grafana Cloud Logs, the fully managed log aggregation system powered by Loki, as their log volumes grow. For most queries, this model works very well. But when you search for a highly unique value, like a request ID, job ID, user ID, or device ID, labels can only narrow the search so far. Loki still has to read a lot of raw log data to find a handful of matching lines. At terabyte and petabyte scale, that process can be slow and costly.

To fix that, we built full-text search for Grafana Cloud Logs, a capability based on the Logline technology Grafana Labs acquired in April 2026. Full-text search, now generally available in Grafana Cloud Logs, adds a purpose-built secondary index to Loki, so you can find specific log lines across weeks of logs in seconds without a full scan. You go straight to the one transaction ID, user ID, or error that matters and cut time to resolution. 

“When I ran our first query on newly submitted logs after enabling Logline, the improvement was clear,” said Timo Kirzdörfer, OpenTelemetry & Grafana Cloud Admin, DATEV eG. “We went from processing nearly a terabyte of logs in three minutes to around 100 gigabytes in under three seconds. That represents an 80-90% reduction in the volume of logs searched for newly submitted logs, and we saw the results immediately.”

In this post, we’ll explore how full-text search speeds up log investigations. You can also learn more in the ObservabilityCON 2026 talk below.

Why labels alone only get you so far

Historically, Loki only indexed labels, then scanned every line in the selected streams. That is fast when the selector and the time range are already narrow. Searching a wide selector over a long window for one request ID means reading all of those lines. If you've run Loki at scale, you've probably reached for one of these techniques to avoid that scan:

  • Put the whole or partial ID in a label. This is an obvious fix, but it creates high cardinality. Request IDs and user IDs make so many unique streams that ingestion and query performance suffer and eventually hit configured limits. Loki's cardinality guidance warns against this for good reason.

  • Shrink the time range and guess. This works if you already know roughly when something happened. During an incident, or with a ticket that came in days later, you usually don't.

  • Send some logs to a separate full-text index. That means running a second system, paying to index every field, and making engineers switch tools mid-investigation.

Full-text search removes that tradeoff. The secondary index tells Loki which data can contain a literal string, so Loki reads only that data and skips the rest. That makes a big difference in how much data a query scans and how fast it returns.

And it does this without the overhead of a traditional inverted index. The Logline technology behind it adds approximately 10% to compute costs and 10% to storage at Grafana Cloud scale with the current capabilities. Much of that cost is offset by the query compute Loki saves by reading less data.

Loki also stays schemaless. You keep your labels and your ingestion pipelines, whether that's Alloy, the OpenTelemetry Collector, or another supported client, and you keep writing LogQL. For supported queries, searches that used to time out can now return in seconds or less.

Find answers faster with full-text search 

Full-text search accelerates several LogQL patterns used for needle-in-a-haystack lookups:

  • Exact string matches, using |=.

  • Literal regex searches, using |~, including case-sensitive searches and case-insensitive searches with (?i).

  • Label filter expressions over structured metadata and label attributes, such as | transaction_id="12345".

  • Post-parser literal expressions over extracted attributes, such as | json | transaction_id="12345".

Some advanced regex constructions are not supported; see the full-text search documentation for details.

These patterns above support investigations ranging from following a transaction ID to tracking down an intermittent error. Here’s how faster lookups help engineers and AI agents follow those leads.

Trace one ID across weeks of logs

Most needle-in-a-haystack searches start from a single identifier: a customer ID from a support ticket, a failing transaction from a payment alert, or a trace ID copied from a slow span.

With full-text search, the line filter you already use is the fast path:

{service="payments"} |= "txn-123456"

Loki no longer has to read every chunk in the stream selector across the whole time range. The index sends it to the data that can contain txn-123456. You can search a wider time range with a broader stream selector and still get results fast enough to stay focused.

Anyone on the on-call rotation can paste an ID, set a long time range, and get an answer. You no longer need a Loki expert to make that query efficient.

Hunt down rare and intermittent errors

Some of the hardest incidents to investigate never show up on a dashboard. An error shows up a few times a day on a few hosts, and the only evidence is a specific string buried in the logs.

Full-text search speeds up literal and case-insensitive searches, so you can look across services for rare errors without knowing in advance where they'll appear:

{service="api"} |~ "(?i)webhook signature mismatch"

You can also combine literals to narrow results while staying on the fast path:

{service="api"} |= "txn-123456" |~ "(?i)webhook signature mismatch"

You find the first occurrence of an intermittent failure faster, which makes it easier to tie that failure to a deploy, a dependency, or a specific customer.

Speed up AI-driven investigations 

Fast lookups matter even more as AI agents take on more of the investigation work. AI-driven investigations often run many queries in a row: an agent checks a hypothesis, searches for an ID, follows it into another service, and searches again. 

Faster needle-in-a-haystack queries mean each of those steps returns sooner, so the investigation keeps moving.

Get started

If you use Grafana Cloud Logs, full-text search is available now at no additional cost. You don't need to change ingestion, redesign labels, or learn a new query language.

Try full-text search in your stack, or create a free Grafana Cloud account to get started today.  

To run your first search:

  1. Open Explore in your Grafana Cloud stack and choose your Grafana Cloud Logs data source.

  2. Pick a stream selector and add a line filter for a value you'd normally search for, such as a request ID, customer ID, or error string.

  3. Set a longer time range than you'd usually risk, such as the last few days or weeks, and run the query.

For supported query patterns and best practices, see the full-text search documentation.

Faster search is one way we’re helping teams get more value from their logs. At ObservabilityCON 2026, we also announced Adaptive Logs updates to give you more control over storage costs. To learn more, check out this on-demand talk from the event.

event_model_payload.headline: AI Demand is Constant, Unpredictable, and Extreme. MongoDB is Built for It.
event_model_payload.summary:
When a huge surge in demand meets limited resources, an awful experience usually isn’t far behind. Fans feel it when trying to compete for concert tickets with bots and scalpers. Diners feel it when they try to get a reservation at a trendy restaurant that’s fully booked for months. Websites and applications feel it when they go viral and get an accidental DDoS from a “Reddit Hug of Death.”

Unpredictable spikes in demand are only becoming more common, and scaling resources to meet them is hard. In my lifetime, I’ve seen big shifts in the amount of demand systems need to handle. First, the internet era, then the cloud era, we saw increased demand that was often predictable. Think of an annual flash sale or regular seasonality. Things might speed up, with more frequent spikes, but they were still spikes you could plan around.

Then AI happened. And this is where we live now: demand that’s constant, unpredictable, and extreme, increasing in frequency and intensity at the same time. If the internet era taught customers to expect an instant response, then the AI era is teaching them to expect something else: instant value. You can snap a photo of something you want, and an agent can identify it, buy it, and have it on your doorstep tomorrow. Those capabilities cut both ways. Change now hits every layer underneath faster and harder than before. The user isn't only human anymore. Agents are in the product too.

Agents don’t ease in. The second they’re on, they hit your system with massive, simultaneous reads and writes. They also take in and act on more information at once than any team of people ever could. Enterprises need a data layer built for that reality, where the only predictable thing is how unpredictable the load will be. Teams that can scale into those spikes will be the ones that last.

Introducing Atlas Infinite

Today, we're announcing Atlas Infinite, the largest architectural innovation for MongoDB Atlas ever. Atlas Infinite is purpose-built to handle the speed of development and unpredictable demand of applications that customers expect, with independent scaling of compute and storage to absorb sudden bursts of traffic.

Atlas Infinite is not a new database. It's a new deployment option within Atlas. Same document model, same drivers and APIs, no code changes required. Also, the current deployment option you know and love as MongoDB Atlas is not going anywhere. It just has a new name, MongoDB Atlas Core. Atlas Core and Atlas Infinite are the two database deployment options within the Atlas platform. You pick the right one for each workload.

How does Atlas Infinite deal with four key scaling and future-proofing problems organizations are dealing with today?

  1. Scaling delay: Gone. Atlas Infinite cuts read scaling time by more than 96% compared to Atlas Core. Compute and storage automatically scale independently within minutes, not hours.

  2. Storage ceiling: 10x higher. Atlas Infinite grows with you, from prototype to a petabyte, on the same foundation. You scale on your terms, when you need more performance, not when you run out of room. Atlas Infinite supports replica sets that hold 10x the data of replica sets in Atlas Core. 

  3. Capacity planning: No more guesswork. Atlas Infinite meets your needs in real time as you scale up and down. Atlas Infinite also runs more efficiently on the same hardware compared to Atlas Core, so you get nearly triple the performance per dollar.

  4. Re-architecture: Not required. Zero application changes required. Enjoy more elasticity and scalability on literally the same database.

This isn't only a scalability story. It's a more capable, more performant engine. Internal tests* using MongoDB 9.0 have shown that Atlas Infinite provides 189% more throughput per dollar compared with Atlas Core. And customers like Icon Solutions are using it to drive more growth.

"Atlas Infinite let us process 55% more transactions per second than our equivalent previous setup on MongoDB 8.0, with zero application changes. In payments, that kind of headroom without a re-architecture means faster, more reliable experiences for the customers on the other end of every transaction," said Mike Wallis, Head of DevOps at Icon Solutions.

Atlas Infinite is available as a public preview, and I can’t wait for you to try out the next generation of MongoDB Atlas.

MongoDB 9.0: The best version of MongoDB ever

In addition, we just released the best version of MongoDB ever, MongoDB 9.0. We’ve hardened the core to ensure a rock-solid foundation for the most demanding enterprises, and we’re setting a new bar for security, durability, availability, and performance.

That bar was already high. MongoDB 8.0 was released just two years ago, and today, nearly 80% of our Atlas fleet has adopted it, with higher customer satisfaction and stronger retention among these customers.

We are proud of what 8.0 delivered, and 9.0 pushes further still. Here are some of my favorite enhancements in MongoDB 9.0.

Performance*: 

  • In our internal tests against MongoDB 8.0, MongoDB 9.0 delivers:

    • Up to 35% faster find-one queries

    • Up to 30% faster update-one queries

    • Up to 2x throughput on large instances

    • Up to 20% higher throughput for transactional workloads

Security:

  • Queryable Encryption now supports prefix, suffix, and substring searches, allowing organizations to query sensitive information without ever decrypting it. 

  • Expanded private networking capabilities make it easier to deploy MongoDB Atlas securely across complex enterprise environments.

Durability and Availability:

  • Intelligent Workload Management automatically protects clusters when they are overloaded with requests and ensures short-running operations continue when demand is unpredictable.

  • Enhanced backup, restore, and recovery capabilities help organizations to maintain application availability and speed recovery when disruptions occur.

Observability & Developer Productivity:

  • Expanded observability into application and database performance

  • New developer productivity features that make it easier to modernize applications with familiar tools and frameworks, without costly rewrites.

MongoDB 9.0 continues to give you the freedom to run anywhere. MongoDB 9.0 is available in MongoDB Atlas and in self-managed environments through MongoDB Enterprise Advanced and MongoDB Community Edition.

MongoDB 9.0 on Atlas Infinite changes the calculus on scale. It's not something you plan around anymore, it's just there when you need it. There's never been a better time to build on MongoDB.

*Performance results are based on internal MongoDB testing comparing MongoDB 9.0 and MongoDB 8.0 using public benchmark methodologies. Results may vary by workload, deployment, hardware, and configuration.

event_model_payload.headline: Build Once, Grow Freely: Search and Vector Search on Atlas Infinite
event_model_payload.summary:
Enterprise workloads are getting bigger, more variable, and harder to predict, especially as agentic applications introduce spiky, unpredictable demand. Most data platforms weren't built for this reality—to cope with demand, they bolt AI services onto aging architecture, leaving customers to manage, monitor, and pay for multiple systems to get the job done. That fragmentation slows your teams down and limits how fast and how far your agentic applications can run.

In a traditional database architecture, storage is tied to the machine that runs your queries. Scaling up, adding a replica, or restoring a backup comes down to copying data from one machine to another, and the bigger the database, the longer that takes. My colleague Abhishek Chauhan calls this “storage gravity.” “Data doesn’t want to move,” he wrote for the MongoDB Engineering Blog. The bigger the data gets, the harder it pulls.

MongoDB built Atlas Infinite precisely for this reality; purpose-built to absorb spikes in demand with flexible, elastic scaling. Whether you’re launching a first prototype or running at petabyte-scale in production, Atlas Infinite enables you to build on a foundation that scales with you and never forces re-architecture. With MongoDB Search and Vector Search supported on Atlas Infinite in public preview, your database and retrieval live in one platform, with nothing to stitch together.

How Atlas Infinite works

A new deployment option within MongoDB Atlas, Atlas Infinite separates compute from storage so each scales independently and rapidly. Storage moves into a fully managed layer that handles replication, durability, and backup across availability zones, so compute no longer has to carry the data with it.

The impact is dramatic. Read replicas come online in minutes because there's no data to copy. A single shard holds up to 128 TB, so you no longer shard just to add disk space. You only pay for the data you store, not capacity provisioned in advance, so a small team never has to buy a bigger compute tier just to get more disk. And it’s all driven by the same MongoDB API, drivers, and tooling, so your application doesn’t need to change.

The separation of storage and compute matters most where agentic applications grow fastest: the retrieval layer. Every answer an assistant gives and every step an agent takes starts with a search over your data, and the data behind that search, especially vector embeddings, can grow large quickly. With MongoDB Search and Vector Search running natively on Atlas Infinite, that data lives on the same foundation as the rest of your application and can grow without re-architecture. Build your agentic workload once and keep scaling it on the same foundation as demand grows.

Figure 1. Compute and storage as independent layers in Atlas Infinite.

Retrieval, built into the database

Many retrieval stacks are cobbled together from disconnected components—a database, a search engine, and a vector database—which means running all of those separate parts, plus managing the pipelines that keep everything in sync. On Atlas Infinite, retrieval is part of the platform, so there are fewer pieces to build, secure, and maintain. Here is what that looks like:

  • One platform, nothing to stitch together: On Atlas Infinite, your database and retrieval work together seamlessly, with no separate search engine or vector database to stand up, sync, or monitor. MongoDB Atlas keeps your indexes in sync with your data automatically, so there is no pipeline for your team to build or maintain, and no extra systems to copy sensitive data into or secure. With Atlas Infinite, retrieval is built in, alongside the ability to scale to absorb unpredictable demand with zero waste.
  • Start small, never outgrow your data platform: A team can start with a 5GB prototype that includes semantic search and keep building on the same foundation. Rather than sizing and maintaining two infrastructures, storage grows automatically with your data, billed only for what you store. The operational data behind your search has room to grow to petabyte scale on Atlas Infinite, with no re-platforming when the application takes off.
  • Agent memory and context retrieval: Give agents one place to store and retrieve context, history, and state alongside your operational data. Support thousands of agents hitting your retrieval layer while also persisting agent memory and context within a single, durable system that scales when they need it.

Figure 2. Search and Vector Search run alongside the database on Atlas Infinite, with indexes kept in sync automatically and data stored once in Atlas-managed storage.

How Atlas Infinite handles your largest text and vector workloads

Separating compute from storage in the database also changes the scaling behavior and economics of large retrieval workloads. Text and vector data lives in the database first, where it drives storage requirements. Because Atlas Infinite manages that storage separately from compute, the economics come down to one property of the data: how well it compresses.

Databases shrink data on disk with compression, which works by finding repetition. Text is full of repetition: common words, repeated field names, predictable structure. Text in MongoDB typically compresses to about 40% of its original size. An embedding is an array of decimal values with almost no repetition, so it shrinks by only about 13%. In practice, a vector takes up as much space on disk as it does in your application.

How each deployment option stores that data

Atlas Core uses attached storage volumes. Each node in a replica set keeps a full copy of the data on its own disk, provisioned ahead of time with room to grow, and compute and storage come in matched tiers. That gives every node complete isolation and predictable performance, and it's the right fit for many workloads, especially ones where data and query load grow together.

Vector workloads tend to be storage-driven because high-dimension embeddings are so large. A RAG knowledge base can hold hundreds of gigabytes of embeddings, which drives up storage needs relative to query volume. On Atlas Core, storage can drive scaling decisions: once you outgrow a tier’s maximum disk size, you have to move up a tier to get more storage, even if you don’t need more compute, and very large datasets eventually call for sharding.

On Atlas Infinite, compute and storage scale independently. Storage is billed per logical (uncompressed) GB of data you store, metered hourly. Replication across availability zones happens inside the storage layer and isn't billed separately. There's no headroom to provision, and because a shard holds up to 128 TB, a growing dataset doesn't push you to a larger compute tier or to more shards. Because embeddings barely compress, their logical size and their size on disk are nearly the same, so you pay only for the data you store and nothing for the copies and headroom underneath it. As vector collections grow to hundreds of millions of documents, that billing model becomes an advantage.

Here is an example. For a collection with 100 million documents, each with a 1,024-dimension float32 embedding and about 1 KB of other fields, storage is roughly 500 GB uncompressed.  Assuming moderate query traffic, an M30 cluster tier’s compute is sufficient.

On Atlas Core, since embeddings barely compress, the data shrinks to ~435GB on disk. Each node also needs space for the oplog and room for the collection to grow. At 1.3× headroom, that comes to about 565 GB per node, more than the 512 GB an M30 supports, so the cluster has to move up to an M40 for the disk. On Atlas Infinite, the cluster stays at the compute tier its queries need, and storage is billed once on the 500 GB it holds. With storage billed once and no tier-up for disk, the total monthly cost of this deployment, Search Nodes included, comes out about 25% lower than on Core. At 1 billion vectors (about 5 TB), it is about 30% lower, and the gap keeps widening as vector data grows. These figures are modeled on list prices in US East, with Search Nodes sized to the smallest tier that fits the index, so your results will vary.

Where the difference is smaller

Text-heavy search workloads also see a TCO benefit on Atlas Infinite, around 5% to 10% cost reduction at multi-terabyte scale. Text compresses well, so Core's storage cost per GB is already low. The advantage of Atlas Infinite comes from deferring early tier-ups and delaying sharding for disk. Under 500 GB, the two deployment options are roughly even on cost, so a smaller workload gets Atlas Infinite’s room to grow without paying more for it. Choose the deployment option based on the elasticity and growth you expect.

Get started with Search and Vector Search on Atlas Infinite

MongoDB Search and Vector Search are available on Atlas Infinite in public preview on AWS. Choose Atlas Infinite as the deployment option for your next workload, add a search index the way you would on Atlas Core, and keep building on the same foundation as your application grows. Whether you’re prototyping an AI feature or running a large production application, you can start small and keep going. Start with the Atlas Infinite documentation.

event_model_payload.headline: Agentic Treasury: How AI Agents Turn Cash Blind Spots Into Real-Time, Governed Action
event_model_payload.summary:
At 8 a.m., a $4 million payroll is due, but an expected customer payment hasn’t arrived. Leafy International’s treasury agent spots the gap in live payment data. It checks current balances and recommends a cash sweep from an overnight deposit. It’s enough to fund payroll while keeping Leafy’s $1 million minimum cash buffer intact.

Just as the treasurer reviews the proposal, an approved, time-stamped market feed flags a material EUR/USD move after a central bank announcement. The agent connects the signal to Leafy’s upcoming euro payment, refreshes the exposure, and flags it for review. A market alert is a reason to reassess, not permission to trade.

The treasurer views the rationale, data source, and update time, and then approves or delegates within the agreed mandate. If a balance, payment status, or foreign exchange (FX) rate changes before execution, the agent checks again. This is agentic treasury: Monitoring relevant conditions, recommending next steps, and helping carry them out only when authorized.

Leafy International is fictional, but the pressures and actions are real. Treasury teams are exploring how AI can improve decisions across payments, cash, working capital, and financial risk—and how to govern these systems.

Agentic treasury has two key requirements:

  • Context that stays current as balances, payments, and markets move

  • An independent check that confirms each action is authorized before it runs.

MongoDB provides the data layer for both, keeping the agent's context fresh as conditions change, and holding the controls and audit log that decide what the agent is allowed to do.

The industry shift to AI action

Cash and liquidity optimization remain persistent challenges for treasury teams. Nearly two-thirds of people surveyed by AFP cite cash management and forecasting as a top priority, while nearly 50% say they’re concerned about liquidity and cash planning. For the first time, AI and automation also ranked among the top five priorities, cited by 30% of respondents.

Similarly, Citi’s 2026 MEA treasury survey highlights that half of those surveyed point to cash visibility and forecasting and liquidity optimization as their biggest concerns.

Interest is already turning into practice. According to Strategic Treasurer's 2025 AI in Treasury & Finance Survey, 22% of companies already use agentic AI, with 18% reporting active use within their own treasury or finance department. Beyond current use, 25% are actively testing agentic tools, 32% have experimented with them, and 72% say they understand the technology.

Adoption is early, but agentic AI is no longer hypothetical. The opportunity lies in delivering timely, consolidated context that surfaces liquidity gaps earlier. This frees treasurers to focus on judgment and exceptions rather than monitoring out-of-date dashboards.

From batch snapshots to continuous operations

Traditional treasury workflows rely on batch processing of morning balance files and end-of-day reporting. This lag exposes teams to intraday liquidity risks and unhedged FX volatility. A continuous, real-time view of cash positioning and market data enables proactive liquidity management and dynamic risk mitigation.

Treasury agents need current, decision-ready context across authorized balances, payment and receipt status, deposit terms, FX rates, and relevant events. Not every signal update calls for action. The agents reassess only when a material signal could change a decision. Freshness should match urgency since payroll cutoffs need tighter checks than overnight-surplus reviews.

A continuous operating model runs on a repeatable loop:

  1. Sense: Gather the current context (e.g., authorized balances, payment and receipt status, market signals) with each source and update time visible.

  2. Plan: Compare the projected cash position with what must be funded, such as payroll and the required buffer. Identify any surplus available to deploy.

  3. Propose: Explain a specific action, its rationale, and its expected effect on cash or exposure.

  4. Check and act: Confirm that the action is authorized and the data is fresh enough for the decision’s urgency. Then execute, request approval, or stop.

The contextual layer: 4 data capabilities an agent needs

An agent is only as trustworthy as its context: balances, payments, market signals, policy, and memory, each with its source and age visible. Four data capabilities keep that context current and useful.

1. Detect relevant changes

Relevant events can include an overdue payment, a payment-status change, or an authorized FX or news feed. After the application ingests an external update into MongoDB, change streams can notify an agent of the change. The agent then refreshes its context and reassesses. Atlas Database Triggers build on change streams and automatically run a function when a matching change occurs, such as a payment-status update.

2. Absorb new shapes of information

Suppose an ISO 20022 feed adds a remittancePurpose field. Teams can validate and map it without reshaping historical payment information. MongoDB’s flexible document model lets new payments include the field while older ones retain their shape.

With schema validation, teams can require the remittancePurpose field on every new payment and block writes that break the rules at the database level. Validation levels and actions control how strictly those rules apply, so teams can roll out enforcement gradually without rewriting historical payments.

3. Retrieve by meaning, not just keywords

Explaining a recommendation may require market events, FX trends, invoice or remittance details, and the policy governing the decision. MongoDB Vector Search retrieves by semantic meaning and can rank candidates by relevance. Automated Embedding generates embeddings inside MongoDB, reducing the need for a separate pipeline. Keeping context alongside balances and payments helps connect relevant evidence to a decision.

4. Remember with agent memory

Short-term memory tracks the current payroll run, balances, and pending approvals. Long-term memory preserves reusable context, such as payroll calendars and target buffers. Time-sensitive details can expire while useful context carries forward. Proposed actions, checks, and outcomes remain in the audit log. These are among the approaches for managing agent memory with MongoDB.

Make delegation safe by design

Dependable agentic treasury requires decision-ready context and an independent, governed check before action. Timely data does not authorize action.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore’s Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime (SAFR) offers what law firm Ashurst Perkins Coie calls the first reference framework of its kind for governing AI agents in financial services at runtime. It is not a regulatory compliance checklist.

In this framework, the agent submits a governance envelope containing the proposed action, its action trace, and relevant context. Four components work through that envelope:

  • Agent identity: Verifies the registered agent.

  • Controls repository: Supplies the policy, regulatory, and delegated-authority controls that the disposition engine applies.

  • Disposition engine: Evaluates each proposal against those controls and decides the outcome.

  • Audit log: Keeps a tamper-evident, append-only record of the envelope, mandate, checks, and outcome.

In the cash sweep example, the agent first assembles the context it needs: its authority, the deposit terms, the current balance, pending payments, and the freshness of the data. If a material input is stale, the agent refreshes it or pauses before submitting the action for governance. The check returns one of four outcomes:

  • Auto-execute: The action is routine, within mandate, and passes all checks.

  • Observe: The action proceeds, but is flagged for monitoring and later review.

  • Escalate: The action may be appropriate, but needs an authorized approver.

  • Deny: The action conflicts with a hard limit, customer instruction, or restriction.

Governance data also varies in shape. Policies, delegated-authority limits, action traces, and check results differ by product, jurisdiction, and mandate. This variety suits MongoDB’s flexible document model.

An FX hedge and a cash sweep, for example, have different structures yet both belong in the same governance envelope. A document can take the shape each action needs and can change as execution unfolds. No rigid, predefined table design is required.

Figure 1. One collection, different document structures: An FX hedge and a cash sweep each carry the fields their action needs, side by side as part of the governance envelope.

Hosting the controls repository, governance envelopes, and audit log in MongoDB puts the controls alongside the data they govern. The disposition engine then decides each outcome on current data rather than a copy, and the audit log shows what the engine relied on.

Independence also matters. The agent can submit an envelope, but it should not be able to change the controls it is judged against or rewrite the audit log. An insert-only audit role is a practical baseline against changes by the application. For higher assurance, safeguards such as application-level hash chaining or replication to immutable storage add independent tamper evidence.

Figure 2. From real-time data to governed action: One data layer keeps the agent’s context current, and an independent check decides whether each proposal proceeds.

Governed agents across treasury

The same governed approach applies to other recurring decisions:

  • Invest surplus cash: Once obligations are covered, the agent can propose an overnight placement with an approved institution within concentration and maturity limits. The agent can compare options—such as dynamic discounting or supply-chain finance—on effective return, funding cost, supplier participation, and fees, and not just the headline rate.

  • Hedge a foreign-currency payable: Leafy owes €2 million in 60 days, but holds U.S. dollars. A material FX move or credible news-sentiment shift prompts a fresh exposure check rather than an automatic trade. If policy calls for hedging 60% to 90% of the exposure, the agent could propose buying €1.5 million through a forward contract (75% of the exposure). The proposal shows the source, time stamp, and rationale for the treasurer's review.

  • Pool cash across subsidiaries: Before proposing an intercompany transfer, the agent checks the authorized route, timing, local restrictions, and cutoffs. If the route is not permitted or the information is stale, the agent pauses or blocks the proposal and explains why.

Start small, build confidence

Agentic AI in treasury doesn’t have to begin with autonomous execution. Choose one recurring, measurable use case, such as monitoring liquidity ahead of payroll. Compare recommendations with outcomes, strengthen the data and controls, and learn from implementation. Expand to approval-based actions, then automate only routine decisions that stay within mandate.

The next 8 a.m. liquidity surprise is coming. Have your treasury’s answer ready before the surprise becomes a problem.

event_model_payload.headline: MongoDB Acquires Firebolt to Bring Lightning-Fast Real-Time Analytics Into Its Intelligent Data Platform
event_model_payload.summary:
Real-time analytics on live operational data, built so applications and AI agents can act on what’s happening now.

The most valuable analytics no longer live in a dashboard. They live inside the application. A logistics app reroutes a shipment around a delay. A retail system reorders inventory before the shelf goes empty. A payments platform flags unusual behavior before the transaction clears.

Each of these decisions requires comparing live operational data against historical patterns. Which routes are backing up, and is that normal? What’s selling faster than usual, and should we restock? Is this login typical for this account at this time of day? Enterprises that can answer these questions in the moment adapt as conditions change. Those that can’t are reacting to yesterday.

Data infrastructure has long been split into two worlds: operational databases that run applications, and data warehouses that analyze what already happened. That paradigm was built for humans looking at morning dashboards, where data a few hours or days old was fine. As analytics moved into applications, real-time analytics emerged as a category of its own, combining complex queries over massive datasets with the speed, freshness, and concurrency that live applications demand. Agents raise the bar on all three. They act continuously, can drive thousands of concurrent queries, and need sub-second answers on fresh data. As businesses rely more on agents, real-time analytics becomes a core part of their data infrastructure.

Eliminate the data-movement tax

Running analytics on operational data often means copying it into a separate system, forcing organizations to build and maintain data pipelines, keep systems in sync, and run yet another platform. Even once the data is flowing, the added complexity, operational overhead, infrastructure cost, and risk of stale answers remain. This is the data-movement tax, and it compounds as agents drive more decisions.

Systems that require customers to move and synchronize data across separate platforms often struggle to deliver fresh answers at the speed and scale that live applications need. For MongoDB customers, the operational data their applications and agents rely on is already in MongoDB, so analytics should be able to run there too, at the source. That's why MongoDB acquired Firebolt.

One platform for operational data and real-time analytics

By integrating Firebolt into MongoDB’s Intelligent Data Platform, we’re bringing a high-performance analytics engine to where your operational data already lives. Firebolt’s engine will run right alongside your database, and we’ll keep it in sync automatically, so there’s no pipeline to build or manage. You’ll get one platform for operational and real-time analytical workloads, so teams can ship faster, with fewer systems to operate and secure.

Our Intelligent Data Platform already brings together operational data, search and vector search, Voyage AI models, stream processing, and the ability to build and run agents in production. Real-time analytics will extend that foundation, enabling applications and agents to analyze live data and act on it in the moment. Over time, customers will also be able to analyze data from other sources and formats alongside their MongoDB data.

When analytics powers a live application, an outage no longer just delays a report. It breaks the customer experience or stalls an agent mid-decision. MongoDB operates in this mission-critical world: today, approximately 75% of the Fortune 100 trust MongoDB with applications that require the highest levels of security, durability, and availability. We’re bringing that same level of reliability and operational excellence to real-time analytics.

Why Firebolt, and what’s next

Firebolt’s analytics engine is proven in production. It was built from the start for the high concurrency required by live applications and agents, not just internal dashboards and reports. Similarweb, for example, uses Firebolt to power complex, customer-facing analytics over more than a trillion rows at petabyte scale, with dynamic queries delivering sub-second performance without extensive pre-aggregation.

Firebolt’s team has tackled some of the hardest problems in analytical engines. CEO Benjamin Wagner’s background is in analytical database research at the Technical University of Munich. He built the Munich engineering team behind Firebolt’s engine and led engineering before becoming CEO. CTO Mosha Pasumansky was an architect of Microsoft Analysis Services, co-invented the MDX query language, and led the technical development of Dremel and BigQuery at Google.

“Firebolt was designed for the cloud to do what many people believed was impossible: low-latency, high-QPS analytics with fast-changing data on object storage,” says Mosha Pasumansky, Firebolt’s CTO. “We also knew that today’s applications deal with complex and flexible schemas, the kind MongoDB’s document model supports natively. So we made sure to keep the benefits of columnar storage and vectorized processing on those schemas through smart automatic column shredding.”

“Firebolt and MongoDB share the same DNA,” says Benjamin Wagner, Firebolt’s CEO. “We both build mission-critical data infrastructure for engineers. We spent the last several years building an analytics engine for what live applications and agents demand: high-concurrency, sub-second answers on fresh data. Joining MongoDB puts our engine where millions of developers already build. We can’t wait to bring real-time analytics to MongoDB customers.”

We’re thrilled to welcome the Firebolt team to MongoDB, and our teams are already working together to bring Firebolt’s engine into MongoDB. In the coming months, customers will be able to turn on real-time analytics for their MongoDB data, so their applications and agents can act on what’s happening now.

More to come soon. Join the waitlist to be among the first to try real-time analytics on MongoDB.

FAQ

What is Firebolt?

Firebolt is a high-performance analytical database designed for low-latency queries and high-concurrency applications.

Do Firebolt and real-time analytics replace a data warehouse?

No. Traditional data warehouses and data lakes remain the right fit for internal BI, reporting, and data science. Real-time analytics is for application-facing analytics, which has a different set of requirements: complex queries over massive datasets, sub-second responses, high concurrency, and fresh data for live applications and AI agents.

What happens to existing Firebolt customers?

Nothing changes for existing Firebolt customers. They can continue using the product with the same support and service. Firebolt’s customers are a big reason we wanted to bring this team and engine into MongoDB. They’ve shown what the technology can do under real production load.

event_model_payload.headline: Speed Insights now measures soft navigations

Speed Insights now measures soft navigations: client-side route changes that update page content without a full reload. This means you can now track performance as users move through your app, not just on full-page loads.

Speed Insights captures LCP, FCP, INP, and CLS for soft navigations and includes these measurements in your Real Experience Score. TTFB is not captured because there is no new document request.

Soft-navigation tracking is enabled by default for all projects using Speed Insights, with no action required. It works with modern web frameworks such as Next.js, SvelteKit, and Nuxt, in Chromium-based browsers.

In your project's Speed Insights dashboard, use the new Navigation Type filter to view All, Hard, or Soft navigation data.

Soft-navigation events count toward Speed Insights Plus usage. Existing Plus customers will receive an email with details about when billing for these events begins. For projects that newly enable Plus, these events are billed from the start.

To disable soft-navigation tracking, set softNavs to false in your application code and redeploy. This option requires @vercel/speed-insights version 2.1.0 or later:

Learn more in the Speed Insights documentation.
