event_model_payload.headline: How to Scrape Google News Headlines and Real Article URLs
event_model_payload.summary:
How to Scrape Google News Headlines and Real Article URLs

Google News is still one of the fastest ways to see what is being written about a topic, a company or a person, across languages and countries. The painful part is the links: many scrapers leave you with Google redirect URLs instead of the publisher's article. This guide shows how to scrape Google News search results, topics and top stories, and keep the real article URL.

You will use the Google News Scraper on Apify. It covers keyword search, topic headlines and top stories in 47 country and language editions, and can resolve Google redirects to the publisher's own URL. You also get the title, publisher, date and related coverage.

By the end of this article you will have a CSV or JSON file on your machine, and a short Python snippet you can rerun or schedule. The same Actor is also callable from JavaScript and from AI agents through the Apify MCP server.

What you need

  • An Apify account. The Free plan is enough to try a small run.
  • A list of inputs for the Actor (URLs, IDs or search terms — details in the steps below).
  • Optional: Python 3 with the apify-client package if you want to automate the run.

No Google login and no proxy setup are required for normal use. Think of it as a small Google News API you do not have to maintain.

How to run it in the Apify Console

Step 1: Open the Actor

Open https://apify.com/veenkes/veenkes-google-news and click Try for free.

Step 2: Enter queries or topics

A search query such as artificial intelligence is enough. You can also add topic pages. Pick an edition such as US:en, GB:en, DE:de or JP:ja.

Step 3: Set a time range

Use a rolling window (for example the last 7 days) or explicit dates. Keep max items per query small on the first run, and leave URL resolution on if you want publisher links.

Step 4: Export

Start the run and download CSV or JSON. De-duplication can drop the same article if several queries return it.

Time range applies to search queries. URL resolution is the difference between a redirect and a link you can fetch or open directly.

How to run it from Python

Install the official client and call the Actor by its Store id veenkes/veenkes-google-news. Replace YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN with a token from Apify Console > Integrations. Do not commit the token to a public repository.

pip install apify-client

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("veenkes/veenkes-google-news").call(run_input={
    "queries": [
        "artificial intelligence"
    ],
    "region": "US:en",
    "timeRange": "7d",
    "maxItemsPerQuery": 50,
    "resolveUrls": True
})

# Write every dataset item, then export from the Console or keep going in code.
for item in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(item)

The JavaScript client (apify-client on npm) uses the same Actor id and the same input object. You can also start the run with a plain HTTP POST to the Apify API if you prefer.

Sample output

Here is a shortened example of one dataset record (field values are illustrative of the schema, taken from a real sample run shape):

  …
}

Once the run has finished, open the dataset in the Console and use Export > CSV if a spreadsheet is your destination. JSON is usually better for code and for language models.

What to use the data for

Media-monitoring teams watch brand and competitor names in several editions. Researchers build a headline corpus for a topic. AI briefing agents need a short list of recent stories with working URLs. A scheduled hourly or daily run is a simple news radar.

Pricing

Pay-per-result pricing starts at $2.00 per 1,000 articles on the Apify Free plan, with lower unit prices on paid Apify plans, plus a small per-run start fee. Always check the live pricing on the Actor page, because plans and unit prices can change. For a first test, keep the input tiny so you can inspect the schema before you scale up.

Scheduling and automations

In the Apify Console you can schedule the Actor (daily or hourly) and leave the same input in place. For incremental jobs, prefer a "since" or "posted after" style filter when the Actor offers one, so you are not paying to re-collect old rows. When a run finishes you can send a webhook, or connect the Actor in Zapier, Make or n8n. AI agents can discover and call veenkes/veenkes-google-news through Apify's MCP server using the same input.

Good practices and limits

This is not an official Google News API, and the Actor is not affiliated with Google. Headlines and snippets belong to their publishers; use them for monitoring and research rather than republishing a news site. Resolved URLs still point at the publisher, who may have their own access rules.

If a run returns fewer rows than you expected, check the input caps, language or country filters, and the Actor log. A zero-row run is usually a filter or an unavailable source, not a silent crash — read the log before you increase limits.

Next step

Open the Actor and run a small job: Google News Scraper: Search, Topics & Article URLs.

If you later want this on a schedule, save the input that worked, add a date filter where it applies, and export CSV automatically from the dataset or from the API snippet above.

event_model_payload.headline: What a data pipeline actually does, with 60 lines of Python you can run
event_model_payload.summary:
A data pipeline moves data from the place it is produced to the place it gets used, and changes its shape on the way. That is the whole idea. Most explanations stop at a diagram with three boxes labelled extract, transform, load, which tells you nothing about what the code looks like or why it breaks.

So here is a pipeline you can actually run. About 60 lines of Python, no framework, no cloud account. Then I will go through what it deliberately does not handle, because that gap is where most of the real work lives.

I build these for a living at Brickclay, mostly on client data platforms, so the failure list near the end is not theoretical. It is what has actually gone wrong on jobs I had to fix.

The input, which is messy on purpose

Save this as orders.csv. It has five rows and two of them are broken, which is roughly the ratio you get from a real export.

id,customer,amount_cents,placed_at
A-1001,Ada@Example.com ,124900,03/04/2026
A-1002,  Grace@example.com,8050,03/05/2026
A-1003,lin@example.com,not_a_number,03/05/2026
A-1004,hopper@example.com,45000,2026-03-06
A-1005,ken@example.com,99900,03/07/2026

Row A-1003 has a non-numeric amount. Row A-1004 has a date in a different format from the rest. The first two rows have whitespace and inconsistent email casing. Nobody writes a CSV like this on purpose. You get it when three different systems have written to the same file over two years.

The pipeline 

import csv
import logging
import sqlite3
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s %(message)s")

SCHEMA = """
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS orders (
    order_id   TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer   TEXT NOT NULL,
    amount_usd REAL NOT NULL,
    placed_at  TEXT NOT NULL,
    loaded_at  TEXT NOT NULL
)
"""

UPSERT = """
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (:order_id, :customer, :amount_usd, :placed_at, :loaded_at)
ON CONFLICT(order_id) DO UPDATE SET
    customer   = excluded.customer,
    amount_usd = excluded.amount_usd,
    placed_at  = excluded.placed_at,
    loaded_at  = excluded.loaded_at
"""


def extract(path):
    with open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        yield from csv.DictReader(fh)


def transform(row):
    return {
        "order_id": row["id"].strip(),
        "customer": row["customer"].strip().lower(),
        "amount_usd": int(row["amount_cents"]) / 100,
        "placed_at": datetime.strptime(row["placed_at"], "%m/%d/%Y").date().isoformat(),
        "loaded_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(timespec="seconds"),
    }


def run(csv_path, db_path):
    conn = sqlite3.connect(db_path)
    conn.execute(SCHEMA)
    clean, rejected = [], []
    for row in extract(csv_path):
        try:
            clean.append(transform(row))
        except (KeyError, ValueError) as exc:
            rejected.append((row.get("id", ""), str(exc)))
    conn.executemany(UPSERT, clean)
    conn.commit()
    logging.info("loaded %d rows, rejected %d", len(clean), len(rejected))
    for order_id, why in rejected:
        logging.warning("rejected %s: %s", order_id, why)
    conn.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run(Path("orders.csv"), Path("orders.db"))

Run it:

INFO loaded 3 rows, rejected 2
WARNING rejected A-1003: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'not_a_number'
WARNING rejected A-1004: time data '2026-03-06' does not match format '%m/%d/%Y'

Three rows landed. Two were rejected with the reason attached to the order id, so you can go and ask someone about A-1003 instead of guessing which row died.

Four things are happening in those 60 lines, and each one maps to a decision you will have to make again on a larger pipeline.

extract is a generator. It yields one row at a time instead of loading the file into memory. On a 4 GB export this is the difference between a job that runs and a job the kernel kills.

transform converts rather than repairs. Cents become dollars, the US date format becomes an ISO date, emails get lowercased and trimmed. It raises on anything it cannot convert instead of writing a zero or a null. A null that should have been 1249.00 will survive every test you write and surface three months later in a revenue report.

The rejection list is separate from the load. Bad rows do not stop good rows, and they do not disappear either. This single choice is the difference between a pipeline people trust and one people re-run by hand every morning.

The load is an upsert, keyed on order_id. That is what makes the job safe to run twice.

Run it twice, then count the rows

Still three rows after two runs. If UPSERT were a plain INSERT, the second run would either crash on the primary key or, with a table that has no key, quietly double your revenue.

This property has a name worth knowing: idempotency. Running the job twice produces the same end state as running it once. You want it because you will re-run jobs. The network drops, a credential expires, someone fixes the source file at 2am and asks you to load it again. A pipeline you cannot safely re-run becomes a pipeline somebody has to babysit.

What these 60 lines do not handle

This is the honest part. The script above is a pipeline, but it is the first ten percent of one.

Schema drift. Someone renames amount_cents to amount and every row rejects at once. The fix is to validate the header against an expected contract and fail the whole run with a clear message, rather than reporting 40,000 individual rejections.

Partial failure and retries. If the load dies halfway through a large batch, executemany inside one transaction rolls back and you are clean. Start writing in chunks and committing per chunk, which you will do for memory reasons, and you now need to track which chunks landed.

Incremental loads. This script reads the whole file every time. At real volume you need a watermark, usually the maximum placed_at or an updated timestamp from the source, so each run only picks up what is new. Then you need a way to force a full reload when the watermark logic itself is wrong.

Late-arriving and corrected data. An order placed on the 4th can arrive on the 9th with a different amount. The upsert handles the correction. Any report you already sent out does not.

Observability. Right now the only record that the job ran is a log line in a terminal. The minimum useful version is a run table: start time, end time, rows in, rows loaded, rows rejected. Without it you cannot answer whether today's numbers are low because sales were low or because the job failed.

Orchestration. Something has to decide when this runs, what runs after it, and who gets told when it fails. That is what Airflow, Dagster and Prefect exist for, and it is also why you should not reach for them on day one.

The three failures that actually show up

Across the data platform work I do at Brickclay, three problems come up far more often than any argument about tooling.

The silent partial load. The job reports success, loads 80 percent of the rows, and nobody notices for a week. Caused by swallowing exceptions in a loop. Fixed by counting rows in and rows out and failing when the difference is not explained by your rejection list.

The timezone that was never a timezone. A source writes local timestamps with no offset, the pipeline stores them as UTC, and every daily total is wrong by the number of hours in the shift. This one is expensive because the data looks completely reasonable.

The pipeline nobody can re-run. Usually a plain insert, or a transform that reads the current date, so re-running yesterday's job produces different output than it did yesterday. Notice that loaded_at in the script above has exactly this smell. It records when the row was written, which is fine for an audit trail, but it means the output bytes differ between runs. Keep that kind of field out of anything you compare run to run.

If you are starting one of these from scratch, build the rejection list and the run table before you add a scheduler. The scheduler makes the job automatic. Those two make it trustable, and on every project I have worked on, trust was the part that took longer.

If you have hit a failure mode I did not list, put it in the comments, I collect these.

event_model_payload.headline: Catch a stale opening caption with a small SRT test in Python
event_model_payload.summary:
The opening of a caption tutorial shows “glaze,” and so does the final playback. At least that’s what you want. If the ending still says “glass” after you fixed the opening, a quick search for “glaze” won’t catch it. And “glass” belongs in the middle of the file, where you demonstrate the original error.

Give the check two ranges, one for the opening and one for the ending. Ask for the corrected cue exactly once in each. Leave the demonstration outside both ranges so you can change that part of the tutorial without breaking the check.

Disclosure: AI assisted the drafting of this tutorial. The included script and fixture were run locally.

Set up the fixture

Use a plain UTF-8 SRT export. The following example is a small local fixture, independent of a video project. Save it as sample.srt.

1
00:00:00,300 --> 00:00:01,900
Glaze.

2
00:00:03,200 --> 00:00:05,100
Start with the raw clip.

3
00:00:19,200 --> 00:00:20,600
Glass.

4
00:00:42,400 --> 00:00:44,100
Glaze.

In this fixture the opening copy is entirely inside the first two seconds. The final segment starts at 42 seconds. Those are test values. On an actual job, use the times of the cut you are handing off. A source timecode from the raw recording will miss the shifted edit.

Compare the text inside the correct windows

This script is dependency-free and runs on Python 3.9 or newer. It uses ordinary SRT numbering, blank lines, and comma-separated timestamps. It reads a UTF-8 BOM and supports multiple text lines within a cue. The expected phrase is compared to the whole cue after normalizing case and punctuation, so a caption containing additional words will fail the test. That choice is useful for a one-line fixture and may be too strict for a longer subtitle.

import argparse
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path
import re
import sys

TIMESTAMP = r"[0-9]{2,}:[0-5][0-9]:[0-5][0-9],[0-9]{3}"
CUE_TIMES = re.compile(rf"({TIMESTAMP})\s+-->\s+({TIMESTAMP})")


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Cue:
    start: int
    end: int
    text: str


def milliseconds(timestamp):
    hrs, mins, secs, ms = map(int, re.split(r"[:,]", timestamp))
    return ((hrs * 60 + mins) * 60 + secs) * 1000 + ms


def read_cues(path):
    text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8-sig").strip()
    if not text:
        raise ValueError("empty subtitle file")

    cues = []
    for block in re.split(r"\n[ \t]*\n+", text):
        lines = block.splitlines()
        if len(lines) < 3 or not lines[0].strip().isdecimal():
            raise ValueError("expected cue number, time range and text")
        match = CUE_TIMES.fullmatch(lines[1].strip())
        if match is None:
            raise ValueError(f"invalid time range for cue {lines[0]}")
        start, end = map(milliseconds, match.groups())
        if end <= start:
            raise ValueError(f"nonpositive duration for cue {lines[0]}")
        cues.append(Cue(start, end, " ".join(lines[2:])))
    return cues


def normalized(line):
    return " ".join(re.findall(r"[\w']+", line.casefold()))


def review(cues, expected, opening_end, closing_start):
    expected = normalized(expected)
    if not expected:
        raise ValueError("expected text must contain words")
    if not 0 < opening_end < closing_start:
        raise ValueError("use nonoverlapping opening and closing ranges")

    opening = [cue for cue in cues if 0 <= cue.start < cue.end <= opening_end]
    closing = [cue for cue in cues if closing_start <= cue.start]
    for label, candidates in (("opening", opening), ("closing", closing)):
        exact = [cue for cue in candidates if normalized(cue.text) == expected]
        if len(exact) != 1:
            print(f"CHECK {label}: {len(exact)} exact matches for '{expected}'")
            return False
    print(f"PASS opening and closing each contain one cue for '{expected}'")
    return True


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("srt", type=Path)
    parser.add_argument("expected")
    parser.add_argument("--opening-end", type=int, required=True, help="milliseconds")
    parser.add_argument("--closing-start", type=int, required=True, help="milliseconds")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    try:
        ok = review(read_cues(args.srt), args.expected, args.opening_end, args.closing_start)
    except (OSError, ValueError) as exc:
        print(f"ERROR {exc}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    return 0 if ok else 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

Run a passing and a failing example 

python check_cues.py sample.srt "Glaze" --opening-end 2000 --closing-start 42000

The fixture prints:

PASS opening and closing each contain one cue for 'glaze'

Now duplicate the file as stale.srt and change only the last cue text to “Glass.” Repeat the command with stale.srt. It reports CHECK closing: 0 exact matches for 'glaze' and exits with code 1. The earlier wrong caption in the tutorial remains outside the checked ranges, so it never affects either test. A malformed cue exits with code 2. In a build script those codes can distinguish an expected review failure from a fixture that needs repair.

Check the export as well

After the script passes, open the actual export. It can still have the wrong SRT attached, the line can come in early, or the playback controls can cover the word. Play the opening and the end from the rendered media and listen across both boundaries. At phone size, inspect the lower area for any collision between sample captions, a tutorial label and the video player.

Some projects intentionally split the phrase across two cues. In that case set the expected text for each opening and closing cue or define a richer rule for adjacent cues. Avoid running a global substring search to compensate. It would hide the stale-copy failure this check exists to catch.

event_model_payload.headline: Scrape Property Finder Data with Python: What Furniture Adds to a Dubai Rent
event_model_payload.summary:
A furnished 1-bedroom apartment in Al Barsha listed on Property Finder this week asks a median AED 85,000 a year. An unfurnished one asks AED 65,000. That is 30.8% more for a sofa, a bed and a fridge, and it is the largest gap I found for 1-bedroom flats in ten Dubai areas.

Tenants moving to Dubai ask the same question every year: is it cheaper to rent unfurnished and buy the furniture? Landlords ask the mirror question: does furnishing a flat pay? Both start with one number, the premium a furnished flat commands over an unfurnished one in the same area. Property Finder has a furnishing filter, so I pulled both sides with Python and compared them. The median premium across the ten areas is 11.3% for 1-bedroom flats and 12.5% for 2-bedroom flats. The bigger lesson is in Dubai Hills Estate, where furnished flats look cheaper and are not.

The data

Every listing here was pulled through the Property Finder API. Its /search-rent endpoint takes a furnishing parameter (furnished, unfurnished or partly), so the split costs nothing extra: one call per area, bedroom count and furnishing state.

On 4 November 2026 I made 40 calls: ten areas, 1- and 2-bedroom apartments, furnished and unfurnished, the first page of yearly rentals sorted by newest. That returned 1,465 rows. After dropping project cards and a few broken rows (more on both below), 1,307 listings were left, about 33 per area, bedroom count and furnishing state. Each response also carries total_count, the number of matching listings on the site, which shows how much of each market is furnished: 15,800 furnished against 16,920 unfurnished listings in these twenty segments.

The ten areas fall into three groups: the waterfront (Dubai Marina, Emaar Beachfront, Palm Jumeirah), the central towers (Downtown Dubai, Business Bay, Jumeirah Lake Towers or JLT) and the suburbs (Jumeirah Village Circle or JVC, Dubai Hills Estate, Al Barsha, Dubai Silicon Oasis). /autocomplete-location turns each name into a location ID.

The code

This is the whole comparison for one area and bedroom count. Install requests, set the RAPIDAPI_KEY environment variable to your RapidAPI key, and run it.

import json
import os
import statistics

import requests

HOST = "uae-real-estate-property.p.rapidapi.com"  # Property Finder API on RapidAPI
BASE = os.environ.get("API_BASE", "https://" + HOST)


def headers():
    if "API_BASE" in os.environ:
        return json.loads(os.environ.get("API_HEADERS", "{}"))
    return {"x-rapidapi-host": HOST, "x-rapidapi-key": os.environ["RAPIDAPI_KEY"]}


def get(path, **params):
    r = requests.get(BASE + path, params=params, headers=headers(), timeout=120)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()


def location_id(name):
    found = get("/autocomplete-location", query=name)["data"]
    exact = [x for x in found if x["name"].lower() == name.lower()]
    return (exact or found)[0]["id"]


def rents(loc, bedrooms, furnishing):
    """Newest yearly rents for one furnishing state: (rent, size in sq ft) pairs, and the total count."""
    body = get("/search-rent", location_id=loc, property_type="apartment", bedrooms=bedrooms,
               rent_frequency="yearly", furnishing=furnishing, sort="newest", page=1)
    rows = []
    for x in body["data"]:
        price, size = x.get("price") or {}, (x.get("size") or {}).get("value")
        # Skip new-project cards (sale prices), non-yearly prices and rows with no size
        if (x.get("listing_type") != "property" or not price.get("value")
                or price.get("period") != "yearly" or not size):
            continue
        if price["value"] / size > 1000:  # a sale price, or a size typed in square metres
            continue
        rows.append((price["value"], size))
    return rows, body["total_count"]


area, beds = "Jumeirah Lake Towers", 1
loc = location_id(area)
furn, furn_total = rents(loc, beds, "furnished")
unfurn, unfurn_total = rents(loc, beds, "unfurnished")

for name, rows in (("furnished", furn), ("unfurnished", unfurn)):
    print("%-12s %2d listings, median AED %s a year, AED %.0f per sq ft" % (
        name, len(rows), format(statistics.median(r for r, s in rows), ",.0f"),
        statistics.median(r / s for r, s in rows)))

premium = statistics.median(r for r, s in furn) / statistics.median(r for r, s in unfurn) - 1
premium_psf = statistics.median(r / s for r, s in furn) / statistics.median(r / s for r, s in unfurn) - 1
print("furniture premium: %+.1f%% on the median rent, %+.1f%% per sq ft" % (premium * 100, premium_psf * 100))
print("furnished share of listings: %.0f%%" % (100 * furn_total / (furn_total + unfurn_total)))

For a 1-bedroom in JLT it printed:

furnished    33 listings, median AED 95,000 a year, AED 110 per sq ft
unfurnished  33 listings, median AED 79,999 a year, AED 101 per sq ft
furniture premium: +18.8% on the median rent, +8.9% per sq ft
furnished share of listings: 58%

The API_BASE switch is there so the same script can point at a test server; with only RAPIDAPI_KEY set it calls RapidAPI. The full version loops over the ten areas, caches every response and also compares listings building by building. Two numbers come out of every pair, and you need both: the premium on the median rent and the premium per square foot.

Furnished flats ask about 11% more

For 1-bedroom apartments, furnished listings ask more than unfurnished ones in 7 of the 10 areas. The median premium is 11.3%.

Al Barsha leads at 30.8%, then Downtown Dubai at 25.0% (AED 150,000 furnished against AED 119,999) and JLT at 18.8%. Business Bay shows no premium at all: both sides have a median of AED 90,000. Palm Jumeirah furnished 1-beds ask 3.1% less, and Dubai Hills Estate 12.7% less.

For 2-bedroom flats the median premium is 12.5%, and furnished asks more in 9 of 10 areas. Downtown Dubai stands out again at 33.3%: AED 220,000 against AED 165,000. Dubai Silicon Oasis shows 64.7%, but only 24 furnished 2-bedroom flats were listed there in total, and they are much bigger than the unfurnished ones (a median of 1,501 sq ft against 1,082). That is a sample to note, not a finding.

Area 1-bed unfurnished (AED) 1-bed furnished (AED) 1-bed premium 1-bed per sq ft 2-bed premium 2-bed per sq ft
Dubai Marina 85,000 95,000 +11.8% +17.5% +3.9% +6.8%
Downtown Dubai 119,999 150,000 +25.0% +47.8% +33.3% +51.6%
Palm Jumeirah 160,000 155,000 -3.1% +4.1% +13.6% +27.2%
Business Bay 90,000 90,000 0.0% +3.3% +6.3% +8.5%
JVC 72,000 80,000 +11.1% +5.5% +9.5% +5.9%
Dubai Hills Estate 106,500 93,000 -12.7% +16.2% -21.9% +14.7%
Emaar Beachfront 130,000 145,000 +11.5% +8.3% +11.4% +17.8%
Dubai Silicon Oasis 62,000 64,999 +4.8% +28.7% +64.7% +36.9%
Al Barsha 65,000 85,000 +30.8% +35.6% +26.3% +28.0%
JLT 79,999 95,000 +18.8% +8.9% +14.3% +16.0%

Medians of the newest yearly listings, about 33 per cell, collected on 4 November 2026. "Per sq ft" compares the median yearly rent per square foot.

In money, the premium is easy to read. A furnished 1-bed in JVC asks AED 8,000 a year more than an unfurnished one; in JLT the gap is AED 15,001, and in Downtown Dubai about AED 30,000. That Downtown figure compares different buildings, though: in the 6 Downtown buildings with both kinds of 1-bed listing, the median furnished flat asked 13.5% less than the unfurnished one. Whether that beats buying your own furniture depends on how long you stay, but it is a yearly cost, paid again at every renewal.

Divide by the size and every gap turns positive

Dubai Hills Estate was the result that made me look twice. On the median rent, furnished flats there are 12.7% cheaper for 1-bedrooms and 21.9% cheaper for 2-bedrooms. That would make it the one area where landlords pay you to take their furniture.

They don't. The furnished flats in Dubai Hills are smaller. The median furnished 1-bed is 645 sq ft against 743 sq ft unfurnished, and the median furnished 2-bed is 748 sq ft against 1,118. My reading is that the compact 2-bedroom units are the ones landlords furnish, while the large family layouts are let empty. Per square foot, furnished flats in Dubai Hills ask 16.2% more for 1-bedrooms and 14.7% more for 2-bedrooms.

The same thing happens on Palm Jumeirah, where furnished 1-beds look 3.1% cheaper and are 4.1% dearer per square foot. Measured per square foot, furnished flats ask more in all 20 area and bedroom pairs. The median premium per square foot is 12.6% for 1-bedrooms and 16.9% for 2-bedrooms.

Per square foot is still not a perfect control, because a furnished flat can sit in a newer or better building. So I also matched listings building by building. In 132 cases the same building had both furnished and unfurnished listings in my sample. Comparing the medians inside each building, furnished asked more in 91 of them (69%), and the median premium was 9.6%: 6.5% for 1-bedrooms and 13.6% for 2-bedrooms. That is the cleanest estimate here, and it is a little lower than the area figures, which suggests part of the area premium is the building, not the furniture.

How common furnished flats are does not set the premium

The total_count field gives the share of each market that is furnished, and it varies more than the premium does.

Downtown Dubai (67.9%), Palm Jumeirah (65.7%) and Emaar Beachfront (64.4%) list most 1-beds furnished. My guess is that they draw more short stays and new arrivals, though this data cannot show it. At the other end, only 19.9% of 1-bed rentals in Al Barsha and 12.6% in Dubai Silicon Oasis are furnished.

It would be neat if scarcity set the price, but the data does not say so. Al Barsha has one of the smallest furnished shares and the largest 1-bed premium, 30.8%. Dubai Hills Estate is mostly unfurnished too (23.7% furnished), and its furnished 1-beds ask 12.7% less, because they are smaller. Dubai Silicon Oasis, where furnished is rarest, asks only 4.8% more. And in Downtown, where furnished is the norm, the area median still shows 25.0% more for a 1-bed, perhaps because furnished Downtown flats are often serviced units in branded towers, even though the same-building comparison above points the other way. Across all twenty segments, 48.3% of the listings are furnished.

Pitfalls I hit in the listings

Project cards ignore the filter. 154 of the 1,465 rows were new-project cards (listing_type is project), with a "from" sale price instead of a yearly rent. 77 of them were identical in the furnished and unfurnished results for the same search, so the furnishing filter does not apply to them. Keep only listing_type == "property" with a price.value and price.period == "yearly".

Some rents are not rents. One unfurnished 1-bed in Dubai Hills Estate was listed at AED 4,000,000 a year for 757 sq ft, which is a sale price in the wrong box. Two others had sizes of 11 and 135 sq ft, most likely square metres typed as square feet. A ceiling of AED 1,000 per sq ft a year removes all three and nothing else. The median barely notices them; an average does.

The median rent hides the size mix. This is the Dubai Hills lesson. Before you report a furnished premium for an area, check the median size on both sides. If they differ by more than a few percent, report the rent per square foot too.

There is a third option. Property Finder also has furnishing=partly. I left it out, so the furnished share above is furnished against unfurnished only, not against the whole market.

"Newest" can reach back months. Where a segment is small, the first page of the newest listings is most of the segment. The oldest listing in my sample was posted on 20 May 2026. In Dubai Silicon Oasis the 24 furnished 2-beds are the whole furnished market for that size, not a sample of it.

Asking is not signed. All of these are asking rents. The registered lease records in /get-transactions do not say whether a flat was furnished, so this data cannot check the premium against signed rents. Treat the figures as what landlords ask for furniture, not what tenants end up paying for it.

Where I would take it next

I would repeat the building match with more pages per segment, so each building has five or more listings on each side, and add furnishing=partly as a middle group. I would also track the same buildings over a few months: if furnished listings stay on the market longer, the premium is partly wishful.

For the signed-rent side of these areas, the Al Barsha rent page and the Dubai Hills Estate rent page on UAEPropertyAPI show median lease rents by bedroom count, updated monthly. The parameters used here are documented in the Happy Endpoint reference for the Property Finder API, more Python and JavaScript examples sit in the GitHub repo, and a key is a sign-up away on RapidAPI. For every Property Finder listing with its price changes as one file, see the listings dataset, or contact us for something custom.

event_model_payload.headline: Web Scraping with Python and BeautifulSoup: A Practical Beginner's Guide
event_model_payload.summary:
The web is the largest data source in the world, but most of that data is locked inside HTML pages designed for humans, not programs. Web scraping is the technique of fetching those pages and pulling out the pieces you care about: product prices, article headlines, job listings, research data, and more.

In this guide, you'll learn how to scrape websites with Python and BeautifulSoup, one of the friendliest parsing libraries around. By the end, you'll have built a complete scraper that walks through multiple pages and saves its results to a CSV file.

What Is Web Scraping?

Web scraping is the automated process of requesting a web page, reading its HTML, and extracting structured data from it. A scraper typically does four things:

  1. Fetches a page over HTTP.

  2. Parses the HTML into a searchable structure.

  3. Extracts the elements it needs (text, links, attributes).

  4. Stores the results in a useful format such as CSV, JSON, or a database.

Python is a popular choice for this because of its readable syntax and an excellent ecosystem of libraries.

Why BeautifulSoup?

BeautifulSoup (package name beautifulsoup4) is a library for parsing HTML and XML. It doesn't download pages itself; it focuses on making the parsed document easy to navigate and search. Here's why it's a great starting point:

  • Forgiving: it handles messy, broken HTML that real websites are full of.

  • Intuitive: searching by tag, class, id, or CSS selector reads almost like English.

  • Lightweight: no browser, no heavy setup.

It pairs naturally with the requests library, which handles the HTTP side.

Before You Scrape: Be a Good Citizen

Scraping is powerful, so use it responsibly:

  • Read the site's Terms of Service. Some sites prohibit scraping.

  • Check robots.txt. Found at https://example.com/robots.txt, it tells crawlers which paths are off limits.

  • Prefer official APIs when they exist. They're more stable and often explicitly permitted.

  • Don't hammer servers. Add delays between requests.

  • Identify yourself with a descriptive User-Agent header.

  • Avoid personal or sensitive data, and respect copyright and privacy laws that apply to you.

Python can even check robots.txt for you:

from urllib.robotparser import RobotFileParser

rp = RobotFileParser()
rp.set_url("https://example.com/robots.txt")
rp.read()

print(rp.can_fetch("MyLearningScraper", "https://example.com/some/page"))

Setting Up

You'll need Python 3.9 or newer (the full scraper below uses built-in generic type hints like list[dict]). Create a virtual environment and install the two libraries:

python -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate        # On Windows: venv\Scripts\activate
pip install requests beautifulsoup4

Your First Scrape

Let's fetch a page and read its title. We'll use books.toscrape.com, a sandbox site built specifically for practicing scraping.

import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

url = "https://books.toscrape.com/"
response = requests.get(url, timeout=10)
response.raise_for_status()          # Raise an error for 4xx/5xx responses

soup = BeautifulSoup(response.content, "html.parser")

print(soup.title.get_text(strip=True))

A few notes on what happened:

  • requests.get() downloads the page. Always set a timeout so your script can't hang forever.

  • raise_for_status() turns bad HTTP responses into exceptions you can handle.

  • We pass response.content (raw bytes) so BeautifulSoup can detect the encoding from the page itself. Some servers don't declare a charset in their headers, and in that case requests falls back to ISO-8859-1 for response.text, which garbles characters like £ into £.

  • "html.parser" is Python's built-in parser. You can also install lxml for extra speed.

Understanding the Soup

Once parsed, the document is a tree of objects you can navigate. Here's a tiny example using an HTML string so you can see the basics without any network calls:

from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

html = """


  
Mechanical Keyboard

  $89.99
  View details




  
Wireless Mouse

  $24.50
  View details


"""

soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser")

Finding elements 

# First matching element
first = soup.find("div", class_="product")
print(first.h2.get_text(strip=True))        # Mechanical Keyboard

# All matching elements
for product in soup.find_all("div", class_="product"):
    name = product.find("h2").get_text(strip=True)
    price = product.find("span", class_="price").get_text(strip=True)
    print(name, price)

Note: class is a reserved word in Python, so BeautifulSoup uses class_ (with an underscore).

Using CSS selectors

If you know CSS, select() and select_one() are often cleaner:

# All prices
prices = [el.get_text(strip=True) for el in soup.select("div.product span.price")]
print(prices)                                # ['$89.99', '$24.50']

# One element by id
mouse = soup.select_one("#p2 h2")
print(mouse.get_text(strip=True))            # Wireless Mouse

Reading attributes

Elements behave like dictionaries for their attributes:

link = soup.select_one("a")
print(link["href"])                          # /products/keyboard
print(link.get("href"))                      # Same, but returns None if missing

Use .get() when an attribute might not exist, which prevents a KeyError.

Quick reference

Task Code
First match by tag/class soup.find("div", class_="x")
All matches soup.find_all("a")
CSS selector (one) soup.select_one("ul.menu > li")
CSS selector (many) soup.select("a[href]")
Text of an element el.get_text(strip=True)
Attribute value el["href"] or el.get("href")
Parent / siblings el.parent, el.find_next_sibling()

Building a Real Scraper

Now let's put it all together. Our goal: scrape every book on books.toscrape.com, collecting the title, price, rating, availability, and URL, then save everything to a CSV.

First, inspect the page using your browser's developer tools (right-click, then Inspect). You'll find each book lives inside an

, with the title in the link inside

, the price in p.price_color, and the rating encoded as a class name like star-rating Three.

import csv
import re
import time
from urllib.parse import urljoin

import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

BASE_URL = "https://books.toscrape.com/"
HEADERS = {"User-Agent": "MyLearningScraper/1.0 (educational project)"}
RATINGS = {"One": 1, "Two": 2, "Three": 3, "Four": 4, "Five": 5}

def fetch(url: str) -> BeautifulSoup:
    """Download a page and return it as a BeautifulSoup object."""
    response = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, timeout=10)
    response.raise_for_status()
    return BeautifulSoup(response.content, "html.parser")

def parse_book(card, page_url: str) -> dict:
    """Extract the fields we care about from one book card."""
    link = card.h3.a
    rating_word = card.select_one("p.star-rating")["class"][1]
    price_text = card.select_one("p.price_color").get_text(strip=True)
    availability = card.select_one("p.availability").get_text(strip=True)

    return {
        "title": link["title"],
        "price": float(re.sub(r"[^\d.]", "", price_text)),
        "rating": RATINGS.get(rating_word),
        "in_stock": "In stock" in availability,
        "url": urljoin(page_url, link["href"]),
    }

def scrape_all(start_url: str, max_pages: int = 50, delay: float = 1.0) -> list[dict]:
    """Follow the 'next' links page by page, collecting every book."""
    books = []
    url = start_url
    page = 0

    while url and page < max_pages:
        page += 1
        print(f"Scraping page {page}: {url}")

        soup = fetch(url)
        for card in soup.select("article.product_pod"):
            books.append(parse_book(card, url))

        next_link = soup.select_one("li.next a")
        url = urljoin(url, next_link["href"]) if next_link else None

        time.sleep(delay)            # Be polite: pause between requests

    return books

def save_to_csv(rows: list[dict], filename: str) -> None:
    """Write the scraped rows to a CSV file."""
    if not rows:
        print("Nothing to save.")
        return

    with open(filename, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=rows[0].keys())
        writer.writeheader()
        writer.writerows(rows)

    print(f"Saved {len(rows)} rows to {filename}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    books = scrape_all(BASE_URL)
    save_to_csv(books, "books.csv")

Save it as scraper.py and run python scraper.py. The site has 50 pages of 20 books each, and with a one-second pause between requests the crawl takes a minute or two, leaving you with a books.csv of about 1,000 books.

What's worth noticing

  • Small, focused functions. Fetching, parsing, crawling, and saving are separate, so each is easy to test and change.

  • urljoin for links. Pages often use relative links like catalogue/page-2.html. urljoin resolves them against the current URL correctly.

  • Pagination by following "next". Rather than guessing page numbers, the scraper follows the site's own li.next a link and stops when it disappears.

  • Politeness built in. A custom User-Agent, a timeout, and a delay between requests.

Making Your Scraper More Robust

Real-world scraping is messy. Here are the issues you'll most likely run into.

Handle network errors and retries 

import requests
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter
from urllib3.util.retry import Retry

session = requests.Session()
retries = Retry(total=3, backoff_factor=1, status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504])
session.mount("https://", HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retries))
session.headers.update({"User-Agent": "MyLearningScraper/1.0"})

response = session.get("https://books.toscrape.com/", timeout=10)

A Session reuses connections (faster) and shares headers across requests. The retry adapter automatically retries temporary failures with increasing delays.

Guard against missing elements

Pages are inconsistent. If select_one() finds nothing, it returns None, and calling .get_text() on None crashes your script. Defend against it:

price_el = card.select_one("p.price_color")
price = price_el.get_text(strip=True) if price_el else None

Watch for site changes

Scrapers break when a site's HTML changes. Prefer stable hooks (ids, semantic classes, data attributes) over fragile ones (deeply nested positions like "the third div inside the second div"), and log or alert when a page doesn't match your expectations.

When BeautifulSoup Isn't Enough

BeautifulSoup only sees the HTML the server sends. Many modern sites load content with JavaScript after the page opens, so the data you see in your browser isn't in the raw HTML. In that case you have a few options:

  1. Look for a hidden API. Open the Network tab in your browser's developer tools; the page may fetch JSON from an endpoint you can call directly with requests. This is often the cleanest solution.

  2. Use a browser automation tool like Playwright or Selenium to render the page, then hand the final HTML to BeautifulSoup.

  3. Use a full crawling framework like Scrapy when you need to crawl large sites with concurrency, pipelines, and built-in throttling.

Wrapping Up

You've now seen the complete scraping workflow: fetch a page with requests, parse it with BeautifulSoup, locate elements with find/select, extract text and attributes, follow pagination, and save the results. The same pattern scales from a ten-line script to a serious data pipeline.

A few next steps to practice:

  • Scrape another sandbox, such as quotes.toscrape.com, and try extracting authors and tags.

  • Save your data as JSON or load it into a pandas DataFrame for analysis.

  • Add logging and retries to make your scraper production-ready.

Happy scraping, and remember to scrape responsibly!

event_model_payload.headline: Using LLMs outside of reflection is an anti-pattern
event_model_payload.summary:
LLMs have a great deal of value in that they are the world's most advanced rubber duck.[1]

They contain all of the references[2] from Google + the ability to somewhat encourage self-evaluation and reflection. However in terms of patterns/anti-patterns, the use of LLMs to create code without human interaction is itself an emerging anti-pattern. Just like any bit of code that functions despite being a form of pasta[3], an anti-pattern doesn't mean things won't function... but you are guaranteed to bake-in a certain level of performance loss and general negative quirkiness; just like in cases of programming in regards to date & time-zones, the devil is in the details and often appears years down the line, not right away.

The fruit of the LLM tree is made more tempting by taking away part of what creates good code: the difficulty. Difficult games or experiences create people who are capable of handling deviations from standard running procedures and anticipate failure upstream. This isn't possible with a LLM structure because the whole aim is reducing the difficulty of production and increasing speed.

Consider the example of the Luddite[4], where the artisan weaver is replaced by a leap in industrialization: this isn't so much the case with a LLM. They work faster, but with far less accuracy. Imagine a rug weaved together in minutes with no discernible pattern. Certainly under the supervision of an expert this improves but imperfections emerge in the system that require a halt of the speed, rollbacks that eat away at production time and create vast effects in terms of customer opinion of the process and the product.

Not to use LLMs at all is likely folly. Knowing how to use them well will be the difference between the master and the apprentice.[5]

Hopefully more identification of LLM patterns and anti-patterns will begin to evolve along with what seems to be another new release from Pandora's Box.[6]

[1] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubber_duck_debugging

[2] https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/03/google-search-artificial-intelligence

[3] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaghetti_code#Pasta-related

[4] https://www.britannica.com/event/Who-were-the-Luddites-and-why-did-they-protest-machinery

[5] https://disney.fandom.com/wiki/ The_Sorcerer%27s_Apprentice

event_model_payload.headline: Market.metafields matches keys in any case as of Storefront API version 2027-01
event_model_payload.summary:
As of Storefront API version 2027-01, the metafields field on the Market object matches each requested key in any case, as Market.metafield already does. This is a breaking change for apps and custom storefronts that request a market metafield key in a different case from the stored key, or that read a key that the buyer's markets store that differ by letter case. If your app does either, review its Market.metafields queries before you move it to 2027-01.

What changed

In version 2027-01, Market.metafields returns a metafield when the requested key matches the stored key in any case. In earlier versions, Market.metafields returns a metafield only when the requested key and the stored key have the same case.

For example, a market stores a metafield with the namespace custom and the key colour:

  • In version 2026-10 and earlier, the entry for { namespace: "custom", key: "Colour" } is null.
  • In version 2027-01, the entry returns the stored metafield.

Who's affected

The change applies to apps and custom storefronts that query metafields on a Market object, from Localization.market or Country.market, with Storefront API version 2027-01 or later. Your app is affected only if one of these conditions is true:

  • It requests a key in a different case from the key that the market stores.
  • The buyer's markets store the same key in different cases.

Your app isn't affected if it requests each key in the case that the markets store it, or if it uses only Market.metafield, which already matches keys in any case. Versions 2026-10 and earlier don't change.

Why this matters

In earlier versions, Market.metafield and Market.metafields can return different results for the same key: Market.metafield finds the metafield, and Market.metafields returns null. In 2027-01, both fields return the same metafield, so your storefront shows the same value whichever field it queries.

What to do

Market.metafield already matches keys case-insensitively, and it returns the metafield from the buyer's most specific market. So on the version that you use today, Market.metafield returns the result that Market.metafields returns in 2027-01. You can compare the two fields to find out whether the change affects your app.

  1. For each market metafield that your app reads, query Market.metafield and Market.metafields with the same namespace and key, and compare the results.
  2. If the results are the same for every key, then you don't need to make changes.
  3. If a result is different, then check whether the difference has a material impact on your app or your storefront.
  4. If it does, then update your app and your metafields so that they don't depend on the case of keys. For example, request each key in the case that your markets store it, and use one case for each key on every market.
query CompareMarketMetafields @inContext(country: CA) {
  localization {
    market {
      metafield(namespace: "custom", key: "Colour") {
        key
        value
      }
      metafields(identifiers: [{ namespace: "custom", key: "Colour" }]) {
        key
        value
      }
    }
  }
}

Related docs

  • Market object in the Storefront API
  • Storefront API 2027-01 reference
  • Retrieve metafields with the Storefront API
  • About Shopify API versioning

event_model_payload.headline: How to Model an Insurance Policy Without Joining Dozens of Tables
event_model_payload.summary:
Ask an underwriter to describe a policy, and you’ll get a coherent answer: A contract, for a customer, covering a car or a house, with a handful of coverages, each with a limit and a deductible, plus a history of every change since it was issued. One policy—with parts. Many parts.

Now ask your database the same question. In most insurance core systems, that single policy is sliced across dozens of relational tables: one each for coverages, vehicles, named parties, endorsements, and billing schedules. Every time a screen loads, the system reassembles the policy by joining those tables back together. Every time a product changes, several of the tables need altering. When Manulife(1) rebuilt its policy servicing platform, its chief architect described replacing more than 500 core tables with one document per policy and reported that the new system won overwhelming approval from its developers.

That gap—between how the business thinks about a policy and how the database stores it—is the central problem a document database like MongoDB solves. This blog post explains the one design decision that matters most when you make that move and why it’s an insurance decision as much as a technical one.

One rule drives everything

A document database stores records as nested structures, closer to a folder than a spreadsheet row. A policy document can hold its coverages, its vehicles, its parties, and its event history all within itself. The temptation is to simply pour the old table diagram into this new shape. That’s the wrong instinct.

The core idea is to model the data around what the business does with it, not around how the entities look on a diagram. Concretely, that means designing for the policy lifecycle (quote, underwrite, issue, bill, endorse, renew, cancel, claim) and asking, at each step, what gets read and written together.

Once you ask that question, every design choice reduces to one decision: whether to embed or reference.

Embed or reference: The decision that matters

For any two related pieces of data, you have two options. Embed one inside the other, so they live in a single document. Or reference one from the other, storing just an identifier that points to a separate document, the way a relational foreign key does.

The test can be reduced to two very simple statements:

  • Embed data that is part of something and is always read alongside it.

  • Reference data that has its own lifecycle or is shared across many records.

Apply that to a policy and the answers fall out naturally. Coverages belong inside the policy. Nobody ever looks up collision coverage without the policy it sits within. The insured vehicle belongs inside the policy—as does the event history, because an endorsement or a cancellation is meaningless apart from the contract it changed. In document form, that looks like this:

Anyone in the business can read that. It looks like the policy.

The claim follows the same logic, with a payoff that finance teams will appreciate. A claim’s reserves and payments belong inside the claim document. Because a single document is always written atomically, posting a reserve and updating the claim’s total becomes one operation that either fully succeeds or doesn’t happen at all. There’s no window where the ledger and the claim disagree.

Now let’s look at the other side of the test. A customer’s policies should not be embedded inside the customer record. Policies are large, they change constantly, and they’re almost always looked up by policy number rather than through the customer record. Instead, store policies in their own collection and have each policy reference its customer by ID. Claims should not be embedded inside policies either, because a claim can outlive the policy that spawned it: a canceled policy can still have open claims. Store claims separately, with each claim referencing the policy it belongs to.

The agent who sold the policy and the product it was written on should also be referenced, not embedded, and here the reasoning is operational. Thousands of policies share one agent and one product. Embed the agent’s details, and a change to their license number becomes a write across every policy in their book. Keep the product catalog as the single, versioned source of truth, and let the policy store only a point-in-time snapshot of the coverage terms it was bound against.

Two storms that test the design

Insurance also stress-tests data models in a way few other industries do: catastrophes.

The hurricane claim

Most auto and property claims carry fewer than 10 supporting attachments (photos, estimates, or a police report, for example). Embedding them in the claim is fine. But a major-loss claim after a hurricane can accumulate 60 or more attachments. MongoDB has a hard 16 MB size limit per document, but even well below that, a bloated minority of claims slows down every screen that loads them.

The wrong fix is to move all claim documents into a separate collection “just in case,” penalizing the 99% for the 1%. The right fix is what MongoDB’s engineers call the outlier pattern: embed by default, and when a claim crosses a threshold, flip an overflow flag and store the excess in a side collection. The design serves the common case and handles the exception explicitly.

Here’s what that looks like for a hurricane claim. Once the claim crosses the threshold, the application sets the flag and moves the extra documents to the side collection, so the claim record stays small:

The wildfire intake surge

When a database outgrows one server, MongoDB splits it across several, and a field called the shard key decides which server each record lands on. It seems sensible to shard claims by catastrophe (CAT) event code, since the CAT dashboard queries by it. It’s a trap. During an active wildfire, nearly every new claim for days shares one CAT code, so every new claim routes to one server—precisely when intake throughput matters most. Use a hashed shard key on the claim number to spread new claims evenly, and keep the CAT code as an ordinary index for the dashboard.

Both examples carry the same lesson: The data model is where operational resilience is decided, long before the storm arrives.

Three patterns to adopt on day one

Beyond the embed-versus-reference rule, there are three more design patterns to adopt:

  1. Computed totals. Store “total incurred” and “total paid” on the claim rather than re-summing reserves and payments on every read. Claim detail is among the busiest screens in the company; don’t make it do math.

  2. Schema versioning. Stamp every policy and claim with a version number. Insurance records survive for decades under regulatory retention and litigation discovery, and your document shape will change over that time. Without a version marker, that drift becomes an audit problem, not just a technical one. Travelers Insurance(2) is reported to have eliminated a three-day wait for schema changes after moving off a rigid relational model; versioning is what makes that agility safe.

  3. Append-only history. Policy events, claim activity, and increasingly, the step-by-step decision trace of any automated underwriting or fraud-screening agent should only ever be added to, never edited or deleted. In most industries, that’s good hygiene. In insurance, it’s compliance. As regulators turn their attention to AI-driven decisions, an auditable trace of what an automated system decided and why will be the difference between a quick review and a drawn-out one.

What this means for you

None of this requires your engineers to abandon what they know. Multi-document transactions still exist for the moments that need them, such as binding a submission into a policy. The shift is in the starting question. Instead of “What are the entities and how do they relate?” it becomes, “What does the business read and write together, and what changes on its own?”

Keep what’s always read together, well, together. Separate what lives its own life. Plan explicitly for the outlier and the surge. Get those right, and the database finally describes a policy the way your underwriters do.

References: 1. Why Leading Insurer Manulife Ditched SQL For MongoDB 2. Travelers Insurance speeds up business ask-to-production process with MongoDB

event_model_payload.headline: Treating web animations as editable clips in a video timeline
event_model_payload.summary:
A web animation can play in a browser. But putting it in a video timeline requires more than a play button: you need to trim it, move it, duplicate it, and jump directly to a particular moment.

In Breatic, we represent each web-animation clip with a position on the timeline, an in-point in the original animation, and a duration. Trimming changes those values while leaving the animation’s source intact.

For example, take a 10-second animation and keep only seconds 3–6. Place that clip at second 20 of the timeline. When the playhead reaches second 21, the animation needs to show its original second 4.

At normal playback speed, the mapping is:

*Animation time = source in-point + timeline time − clip start*

The animation runtime must support rendering at a requested time. This works with animations prepared for our playback runtime; it doesn’t make an arbitrary web page seekable.

There is another detail: sending a seek request doesn’t mean the new frame is ready to display. Our preview runs the animation inside an iframe. After applying a seek, the page waits for fonts and two animation frames before acknowledging the request. Session and sequence identifiers prevent an outdated response from satisfying a newer seek.

The latest Timeline changes add layered preview playback and controls to move, resize, and rotate video and web-animation layers. Combined with the existing trimming support, this lets the same animation appear in several independently edited clips alongside video.

These changes are merged into the main branch but haven’t shipped in a new release yet. This currently covers editing and preview; video export is still future work.

Source: https://github.com/orime-org/breatic

event_model_payload.headline: FreeLLMAPI: 7.4 Billion Free AI Tokens a Month From 34 Providers Behind One Endpoint
event_model_payload.summary:
FreeLLMAPI stacks the free tiers of 34 AI providers behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, adding up to about 7.4 billion free tokens a month with smart routing and automatic failover. It has 50,376 stars.

What FreeLLMAPI Is: 7.4 Billion Free Tokens Behind One Endpoint

FreeLLMAPI is a self-hosted router that stacks the free tiers of 34 AI providers behind a single OpenAI-compatible /v1 endpoint. Every serious AI lab offers a free tier, a few million tokens a month or a few thousand requests a day, and on its own each one is a toy. Stacked together they add up to roughly 7.4 billion tokens a month across 474 model families and 635 free endpoints, from small and fast models to reasonably capable ones. Point any OpenAI client library at your local server and it routes across whichever providers you added keys for. The project is written in TypeScript, released under the MIT license, and it has 50,376 stars.

How the Router Works: Smart Routing, Failover and Per-Key Quotas

The router picks the best available model for each request and falls over to the next provider when one is rate-limited. It scores every model on live speed, capability and reliability, then retries the next model in your chain on a 429 or 5xx error, with cooldowns and key rotation. Per-key rate tracking keeps RPM, RPD, TPM and TPD counters for each platform, model and key, so routing stays under every free-tier cap. If a provider feels slow from your side, a Speed Test tells you whether your own connection is the bottleneck before you blame the router. The same model on several providers collapses into one entry with strict in-group failover, and named fallback-chain profiles let you keep a coding chain and a vision chain and switch between them per request.

What You Can Run on It: Chat, Code, Images, Video and Voice

FreeLLMAPI covers every OpenAI-style surface: chat completions, responses, completions for editor ghost-text autocomplete, image generation, video generation, audio speech and transcriptions, embeddings and models, streaming and non-streaming. There is also an Anthropic Messages API surface, so Claude Code and the official Anthropic SDKs run against your free pool, plus a native Gemini surface for Gemini CLI and opt-in Ollama emulation for Zed, JetBrains and other local-model clients. A Fusion mode fans one prompt out to a panel of diverse free models in parallel and has a judge model synthesize one answer from the drafts. Tool calling and structured outputs round-trip across providers, so coding agents get real tool calls rather than plain text.

Using It With Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Other Coding Agents

Most agents configure themselves with one command that reads your live catalog, backs up the existing config and merges into it. For Claude Code it is npx freellmapi setup-claude with your server URL and unified key, and there are matching commands for Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Cline, Roo Code, OpenCode, Aider and more, plus Continue, Goose, Qwen Code, Kilo Code, Crush, Zed, JetBrains AI and any OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic, Gemini or Ollama client. Conversations stay on one model for 30 minutes, and an optional compact handoff note keeps the thread coherent when a mid-chat switch happens. The opt-in prompt compression pipeline can deduplicate prompts, filter tool output and trim stale context before routing, and running your prompt text through an AI Text Cleaner first is another easy way to cut wasted tokens before a request ever leaves your machine.

Getting Started: Docker, the Desktop App and One Unified Key

The fastest start is the one-liner that sets up ~/freellmapi, generates an encryption key, pulls the Docker image and starts the container, then you open http://localhost:3001, add provider keys on the Keys page, reorder the fallback chain and grab your unified key from the header. That unified key is what you point your OpenAI SDK at, with base URL http://localhost:3001/v1 and model "auto" to let the router pick. There is also a native menu-bar desktop app for macOS and Windows, with the whole router and dashboard running locally from the tray, plus Android via Termux and a Raspberry Pi friendly footprint of about 40 MB RAM at idle. Provider keys are AES-256-GCM encrypted in SQLite and decrypted in memory per request, and your apps only ever see the single unified bearer token. The dashboard ships in 60 languages and shows p50/p95/TTFT analytics over 24 hour to 90 day windows.

The Honest Limits: Free Tiers, Latency and the $19 Live Catalog

FreeLLMAPI describes itself as built for personal experimentation, and the limits are real: no frontier models, variable latency, no SLA, and the effective intelligence of the endpoint dips late in the day as top models hit their daily caps, then resets at UTC midnight. Each provider's free tier has its own rules and limits, so the 7.4 billion figure is the sum of the listed free-tier capacity, not a guaranteed allowance for any one user. The router keeps its model catalog fresh on its own, pulling a signed catalog twice a day, but free installs track the monthly snapshot, so a model reaches them 30 days after it joins the live feed. The live catalog is a $19 per year premium add-on (or $49 once, lifetime), and it is the only paid part: the router itself stays MIT licensed and fully free, forever.

FAQs

What is FreeLLMAPI?

FreeLLMAPI is a self-hosted router that stacks the free tiers of 34 AI providers behind one OpenAI-compatible /v1 endpoint, adding up to about 7.4 billion free tokens a month across 474 model families and 635 free endpoints. It routes each request to the best available model, fails over automatically when a provider is rate-limited, and stores provider keys encrypted. It has 50,376 stars.

Is FreeLLMAPI really free?

Yes, the router is MIT licensed and fully free, forever. You bring your own free-tier keys from providers like Google, Groq, Cerebras, Mistral, OpenRouter and others, and the router aggregates them. The only paid part is the $19 per year live model catalog, which gets new models the same day instead of 30 days later on the free monthly snapshot.

How does the 7.4 billion tokens figure work?

It is the sum of the listed free-tier capacity across 34 providers, 474 model families and 635 free endpoints. Each provider's free tier has its own rules and request and token limits, so it is a total pool you draw from, not a single allowance, and the strongest models can hit their daily caps late in the day before resetting at UTC midnight.

Which coding agents work with FreeLLMAPI?

Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Cline, Roo Code, OpenCode, Aider, Continue, Goose, Qwen Code, Kilo Code, Crush, Zed, JetBrains AI and any OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic, Gemini or Ollama client. Most configure themselves with one setup command, and the router also exposes an MCP server and a ChatGPT-ready private tunnel.

What are the limits?

No frontier models, variable latency and no SLA. The effective intelligence dips late in the day as top models hit daily caps, then resets at UTC midnight. Free installs get new models 30 days after they join the live catalog, and the project describes itself as built for personal experimentation rather than production workloads.

What does the $19 per year premium add?

Premium keeps the signed model catalog live on every router you run, so new models, quota changes and provider fixes land the same day instead of 30 days later on the free monthly snapshot. One key covers every router you run. The router itself stays free, and premium is what funds the daily model testing and catalog maintenance.

Originally published at devpik.com/open-source/freellmapi. Repo: tashfeenahmed/freellmapi.

event_model_payload.headline: Explainroo UI: Make Animated Explainer Videos in Your Browser, Free and Open Source
event_model_payload.summary:
Explainroo UI is a free open source studio that turns a script into a narrated animated explainer video in your browser. Click any word to attach a drawing that pops on screen as the word is spoken, then export the result as MP4.

What Explainroo UI Is: A No-Code Studio for Animated Explainer Videos

Explainroo UI is a visual web studio for making animated technical explainer videos, and it asks nothing of you except a script. It turns system architectures, developer workflows, distributed systems, and code algorithms into narrated videos with hand-drawn vector animation, word-synchronized triggers, and one-click recording. It is built as the visual front end for the Explainroo programmatic video engine, and it runs entirely in your browser on Windows, Mac, and Linux. It is free and open source under the MIT license, and it has 28 stars on GitHub. The pitch is simple: explaining a technical idea usually means opening a video editor, a slide deck, and a screen recorder, then spending an afternoon stitching them together. Explainroo UI replaces that with a canvas, a script, and a record button. You write what you want to say, you point at the words where something should appear, and the studio does the timing, the narration, and the export.

How It Works: Write a Script, Click a Word, Record

The creation flow has three steps, and the second one is the whole idea. First, you paste your voiceover script into the editor, or you let the built-in AI Director write one for you. Second, you click any spoken word in your script, for example browser, database, or cloud, and attach a diagram component to it. That element animates onto the canvas at the exact split second the word is spoken. Third, you preview the video with synchronized voiceover narration and background music that ducks itself under the voice, then you record and export. The word-level synchronization is what makes the videos feel made rather than assembled. A server rack slides in as you say server, an arrow draws itself as you say sends, and the viewer never wonders what you are talking about, because the picture arrives with the word. Before you record, it is worth tidying the script: an AI Text Cleaner strips the filler and formatting junk out of a pasted draft, and if you are choosing between two versions of a script, a Text Diff shows exactly what changed between them. The studio coordinates narration text, speech audio, and vector animation into one synchronized 16:9 canvas, so there is no timeline to scrub and no keyframes to set by hand.

The AI Director: Let Gemini Write the Script

If you do not have a script yet, the built-in AI Director writes one. Give it any software topic or repository and it generates a complete multi-scene explainer video project using Google Gemini, with the narration broken into scenes and ready to attach visuals to. The AI Director is optional, and it needs your own Gemini API key, which you add to a .env file as GEMINI_API_KEY. Without a key, everything else still works: you paste your own script and build the video by hand. That split is a good design choice. The free core of the tool never phones home and never asks for an account, and the AI feature is a door you open yourself if you want it. The README is upfront that the key is yours and the cost is yours, which is the honest way to ship an AI feature in a free tool.

Four Themes and a Component Library

Every video gets its look from one of four visual themes, switched with a single click. Whiteboard is warm cream paper with slate ink strokes, made for system design and architecture tutorials. Dark Tech is a deep midnight canvas with glowing neon cyan schematics, built for cloud architecture and microservices. Blueprint is navy engineering paper with crisp white drafting lines and grid measurements, made for low-level protocols and compiler internals. Chalkboard is a classroom slate with soft textured chalk strokes and pastel highlights, made for computer science algorithms and math. All four render with Rough.js, which gives the strokes their natural pencil wobbles, marker edges, and cross-hatch fills, so the diagrams look hand-drawn rather than clip-art. The component library covers the pieces a technical explainer actually needs: architecture nodes like a client laptop, server rack, database, cloud and DNS cluster, API gateway, and message queue; UI mockups like a macOS browser window with a live URL bar, a Unix terminal with an active prompt, and a mobile smartphone viewport; infrastructure icons for Redis cache, auth bearer tokens, edge CDNs, and end users; and dynamic connectors, hand-drawn straight and curved animated arrows with request and response labels.

Captions and Music That Follow the Words

The audio engine is doing more work than it looks like. Narration comes from in-browser speech synthesis with control over rate, pitch, and voice, or you can upload your own voiceover as an MP3 or WAV file per scene, with live playback preview. The captions are Whisper-style dynamic subtitles in a floating pill that highlights the active spoken word in glowing yellow without covering the canvas, so a viewer watching on mute still follows the argument word by word. The background music is generative ambient harmonic chords that lower their own volume whenever the narrator speaks, which is the audio ducking the README promises, and it means you never have to mix two tracks by hand. The whole studio is also an installable Progressive Web App with responsive touch controls and offline precaching, so it works on a phone as well as a desktop. Keyboard shortcuts keep the flow fast: space toggles playback, Alt plus an arrow key jumps between scenes, and Escape closes any modal.

Exports: MP4, a Standalone HTML Player, and a CLI Bundle

When the video is ready, you have four ways out. The direct one is WebM or MP4 video, recorded in the browser with zero external dependencies, ready for YouTube, X, LinkedIn, and product demos. The clever one is the standalone offline HTML player: a single .html file with every scene, vector animation, subtitle, and voice synthesis embedded, which plays anywhere with a double-click and no dependencies at all. The developer one is the headless CLI bundle, a zip containing the standalone player, a project JSON file, the script as script.md, and the scenes as scenes.js, compatible with the Explainroo command line renderer. And the simple one is a PNG poster frame, a high-resolution 1280x720 snapshot of the canvas for documentation, thumbnails, and blog posts. You can also save and reload the full project state as a JSON backup at any time. The roadmap lists a drag and drop timeline, neural text-to-speech voices from ElevenLabs and Edge, cloud persistence, hardware-accelerated WebAssembly export, and a logo library for Docker, Kubernetes, AWS, React, Python, and PostgreSQL, but what ships today already covers the full job from script to finished video.

How to Run It: Download, Unzip, Double-Click

You do not need Git or a command line to run Explainroo UI. Download the studio zip from the releases page, extract it, and on Windows double-click start.bat, or on macOS and Linux run ./start.sh. The launcher installs dependencies and opens your browser at localhost:3000 automatically. Developers can clone the repo and run npm install followed by npm run dev instead, with Node.js 18 or newer. The Gemini key is the only optional setup, copied from .env.example to .env. That is the whole install, and it is the reason the tool is worth knowing about: the gap between wanting an explainer video and having one is usually a day of editing, and here it is a download and a script. For anyone who teaches, documents, or demos technical ideas, that is a real difference.

FAQs

What is Explainroo UI?

Explainroo UI is a free open source visual web studio for making animated technical explainer videos. You paste a narration script, click any word to attach a drawing that appears as the word is spoken, and export the finished video as MP4. It is built on the Explainroo video engine, licensed under MIT, and it runs in your browser on Windows, Mac, and Linux.

Is Explainroo UI free?

Yes. Explainroo UI is free and open source under the MIT license. There is no paid tier, no account, and no watermark. The only optional cost is your own Gemini API key if you want the AI Director to write scripts for you.

Do I need a Gemini API key?

Only if you want the AI Director to generate scripts. The AI Director uses Google Gemini and needs your own API key in a .env file. Everything else, including pasting your own script, attaching visuals, captions, music, and exporting, works without any key.

What video formats can I export?

You can record directly to WebM or MP4 video in the browser, download a standalone offline HTML player that plays with no dependencies, export a headless CLI bundle with the script and scenes for the Explainroo command line renderer, or save a 1280x720 PNG poster frame.

Does Explainroo UI run on Windows, Mac, and Linux?

Yes. On Windows you download the zip and double-click start.bat, and on macOS and Linux you run ./start.sh. It is also an installable Progressive Web App, and developers can run it from source with npm install and npm run dev on Node.js 18 or newer.

What is the difference between Explainroo UI and Explainroo?

Explainroo is the programmatic video engine that renders videos from code, and Explainroo UI is the visual no-code studio built on top of it. The UI gives you a canvas, a script editor, and a record button instead of a code file, and it can export a CLI bundle that the engine can render headlessly.
