event_model_payload.headline: ArtCraft: Photoshop Meets a 3D Studio for AI Art
event_model_payload.summary:
ArtCraft is like Photoshop meets a 3D studio for AI art. Build the scene first, place characters, pose them, set the camera, then generate with Midjourney, Sora, and others and animate it into video. It has 39,133 stars, 36,700 of them gained this month.

What Is ArtCraft?

ArtCraft calls itself the IDE for artists, and the name fits better than most project slogans do. It is an open-source desktop app for interactive AI image and video creation where you compose in 2D, stage scenes in 3D, and choose the models that fit your work, instead of typing a prompt into a box and hoping the result lands where you imagined it. Prompting becomes crafting: visual tools give you precise, repeatable control over composition, character identity, and camera placement.

It is a Rust project, dual-licensed under MIT or Apache-2.0 at your option, and it had 39,133 stars when we checked on November 6, 2026, with 36,700 of them gained this month alone. That kind of surge usually means a project solved a frustration a lot of people share, and here the frustration is obvious: generative models are powerful but hard to direct, and ArtCraft is built around directing them.

Build the Scene Before You Generate

The core idea is scene first, generation second. You place virtual actors in a consistent environment and plan multiple shots in the same room with Image to Location, layer backdrops, foregrounds, and props in 3D to build compositions with real depth, and turn an image into a 3D object you can position, rotate, and frame precisely with Image to 3D Mesh. Character Posing lets you pose characters and set your camera before generating the final shot, Scene Blocking with Kitbashing combines 3D asset kits to control camera angles and object placement, and Character Identity Transfer uses a posed mannequin to guide the placement and pose of your character.

The README makes a point of showing its work: the camera rings each feature row with its real preview image, so you can see the tools doing what they claim before you install anything. Background Removal isolates subjects to use as props, layers, or backdrops, and Mixed Asset Crafting combines image cutouts, worlds, and 3D meshes in one scene. When you are matching a backdrop to a prop, getting the palette right matters, and a quick pass through a Color Converter keeps your HEX, RGB, and HSL values consistent between the scene and the assets you bring in.

Prompting When You Want Speed

You do not have to stage a full scene for every idea. Start with a prompt when you want to explore quickly, then use the canvas and scene tools to refine the result. Text to Image explores ideas across a wide range of image models from a text prompt. Prompted Image Editing describes changes to an image with models such as Nano Banana Pro and GPT Image. Canvas Image Editing uses drawing, masks, and inpainting to guide exactly where an image changes, so you can fix one corner without regenerating the whole frame.

Image to Video animates an image with your choice of video models and generation controls, which is where the staging pays off a second time: a scene you blocked in 3D gives the video model a consistent world to move through instead of a single flat frame. Before you render, it is worth checking your framing, since a vertical 9:16 cut and a 16:9 cut are different compositions, not the same image cropped, and an Aspect Ratio Calculator works out the exact dimensions for each format.

The 62-Model Catalog

ArtCraft does not lock you to one provider. Its own catalog covers 62 models: 16 image models across Nano Banana, GPT Image, FLUX, and Seedream; 25 video models across Seedance, Kling, Veo, Sora, Vidu, MiniMax, and Flux; 5 music and sound models including Suno; 11 3D mesh models including Hunyuan 3D, Tripo3D, Meshy, and Rodin; and 5 world and Gaussian splat models including Marble and TripoSplat. On top of that it connects to Grok Imagine and Grok Video, Midjourney image generation, Sora 1 and 2 plus GPT Image, and World Labs Marble world generation.

A few models in the catalog are currently disabled or restricted, and more integrations are planned for Kling, Google, Runway, and Luma, plus aggregators such as OpenArt and Freepik for existing subscriptions. The catalog is the practical answer to the most common AI art question, which model should I use for this, because you pick inside one workspace instead of opening five tabs and five accounts.

What It Costs

Here is the part to understand before you start: the ArtCraft app itself is free, but you connect your own model subscriptions, and the description says so. Generation runs through the providers you have accounts with, so your cost depends on which models you use and how much you generate, not on ArtCraft. That is the honest trade of a bring-your-own-model tool: no subscription to the app, but no free generation either.

Downloads are straightforward. Stable releases for Windows and macOS are on the project site, the latest builds are on GitHub, and you can build from source including on Linux, with the setup documented in the repo. There is also an active Discord community and a YouTube channel with a two-minute demo that shows the full workflow from staging to finished video.

What to Watch Out For

First, this is a young project moving very fast: 36,700 stars in a month means features, models, and docs change often, so treat the README as the current truth and expect the catalog to keep growing. Second, some models in the catalog are disabled or restricted, so a model you saw in a demo may not be available in the desktop app on the day you try it. Third, because you bring your own subscriptions, costs are yours to manage across providers, and a heavy video session can add up if you are generating with the premium models.

None of that changes what makes it interesting. Most AI art tools ask you to describe a scene and accept what comes back. ArtCraft asks you to build the scene first, then generate inside it, and that inversion is why artists who care about composition keep coming back to it.

FAQs

What is ArtCraft?

ArtCraft is a free, open-source desktop app for interactive AI image and video creation, described as the IDE for artists. You compose in 2D, stage scenes in 3D with posed characters and a set camera, then generate with the models you choose. It is written in Rust, dual-licensed MIT or Apache-2.0, and had 39,133 stars in November 2026.

How is ArtCraft different from a normal AI image generator?

Normal generators take a text prompt and return an image. ArtCraft lets you build the scene first: place characters, pose them, set the camera, turn images into 3D objects, and layer backdrops and props in 3D. Only then do you generate, so the model works inside a composition you controlled instead of inventing one.

Which AI models does ArtCraft support?

Its own catalog covers 62 models across images, video, music, 3D meshes, and worlds, including Nano Banana, GPT Image, FLUX, Seedream, Kling, Veo, Sora, and Suno. It also connects to Grok, Midjourney, Sora, and World Labs. Some catalog models are currently disabled or restricted.

Is ArtCraft free?

The app is free and open source. But you connect your own model subscriptions, so generation costs depend on the providers and models you use. There is no subscription to ArtCraft itself.

What platforms does ArtCraft run on?

Stable releases are available for Windows and macOS, latest builds are on GitHub, and you can build from source, including on Linux. Setup instructions are in the repository.

Do I need to know how to code to use ArtCraft?

No. It is built for artists, designers, and filmmakers, not developers. You work visually: placing actors, posing characters, setting the camera, and choosing models. Building from source is the only part that needs a developer setup.

Originally published at devpik.com/open-source/artcraft. Repo: storytold/ArtCraft.

event_model_payload.headline: Does My Bama Bound AI Clip Have a Glitch Frame? Finding Cuts, Flashes, Freezes and Skipped Frames in Python
event_model_payload.summary:
Checked November 13, 2026 (15:00 CST, UTC+8). I build bamabound.app, which turns one photo of one person into a vertical clip of them holding a red I'M BAMA BOUND banner. Every clip in this post is a synthetic stand-in (a red "TEST BANNER" box swaying over a grainy green field, 720x1280, 30 fps, 8 s), not a real person and not a real generated clip.

People ask some version of this a lot: "There's a weird blink in the middle of my Bama Bound video. Is that a glitch, or did my editor do it?"

An AI clip is about eight seconds long (FAQ). At normal speed, a single odd frame is easy to feel and hard to find. You scrub, it's gone, you scrub back, you can't land on it. What you want is a list: frame 90, white flash, one frame long. Then you can look at exactly that frame, cut it, or send it to whoever made the clip.

This post builds that list with about 150 lines of Python, numpy and ffmpeg. I test it on five planted defects plus two clips that should come back clean, and compare it with ffmpeg's built-in scdet filter, which turned out to catch only two of the four defect types.

Four kinds of "jump", and what they look like in numbers

The whole method rests on one number per frame: how different is this frame from the one before it? Decode the clip very small (36 px wide, so film grain averages out), take the mean absolute RGB difference with the previous frame, and you get a 0-255 value. On my grainy test clip it sits around 1.1 for normal motion.

Defect What you see Shape of the difference curve
Hard cut the picture switches to a different shot one huge spike, and the picture stays different
Flash frame 1-3 frames of white/black/garbage a spike in, a spike out, and the frames either side match each other
Freeze motion stops, then resumes a run of near-zero differences
Skipped frames the banner "teleports" a little one moderate spike, a few times the usual motion

The skip is the sneaky one. Dropping 15 frames of a slowly swaying banner gave a difference of about 4 against a typical 1.1. That's visible to the eye, but nowhere near what a scene-cut detector is tuned for.

Judge each clip by its own motion

A fixed threshold doesn't work. A clip with lots of motion has big frame-to-frame differences everywhere. A calm one has tiny ones. So the script compares each difference with a rolling median over a one-second window around it. A spike counts when it is more than 4x that local median and above an absolute floor of 6. A skip counts at 2.5x local motion, 1.5x the clip's overall median and at least 1.0. A freeze is a run of frames under a tenth of the typical motion that lasts at least 0.3 s.

That 0.3 s number came from a false alarm, which I'll get to below.

The script 

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""jumpcheck.py - find sudden jumps in a short clip: hard cuts, flash frames,
freezes and skipped frames.

It decodes the clip at a small size (default 36 px wide), measures how much each
frame differs from the one before it (mean absolute RGB difference, 0-255),
and compares every difference with the clip's own typical motion (a rolling
median), so a slow clip and a busy clip are judged on their own terms.

    python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4            # human-readable report
    python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4 --json     # machine-readable
    python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4 --csv d.csv  # per-frame differences

Exit code 0 = nothing found (keyframe pulses are listed but not counted),
1 = at least one cut/flash/freeze/skip, 2 = could not read clip.
Needs ffmpeg/ffprobe on PATH and numpy.
"""
import argparse, json, subprocess, sys
import numpy as np


def probe(path):
    out = subprocess.run(
        ["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-select_streams", "v:0", "-show_entries",
         "stream=width,height,avg_frame_rate", "-of", "json", path],
        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout
    s = json.loads(out)["streams"][0]
    num, den = s["avg_frame_rate"].split("/")
    return int(s["width"]), int(s["height"]), float(num) / float(den)


def frames(path, w, h):
    cmd = ["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-an", "-vf",
           f"scale={w}:{h}:flags=area", "-pix_fmt", "rgb24", "-f", "rawvideo", "-"]
    raw = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    n = len(raw) // (w * h * 3)
    return np.frombuffer(raw[: n * w * h * 3], np.uint8).reshape(n, h, w, 3).astype(np.int16)


def keyframes(path):
    """Indices of I-frames. Low-bitrate encodes 'pulse' on every keyframe,
    which looks like a small skip but is just the encoder refreshing detail."""
    out = subprocess.run(
        ["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-select_streams", "v:0", "-show_entries",
         "frame=pict_type", "-of", "csv=p=0", path],
        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout.split()
    return {i for i, t in enumerate(out) if t.strip(",") == "I"}


def diff(a, b):
    return float(np.abs(a - b).mean())


def analyse(path, small_w=36, spike=4.0, floor=6.0, freeze_ratio=0.1, min_freeze_s=0.3):
    W, H, fps = probe(path)
    small_h = max(2, round(small_w * H / W / 2) * 2)
    f = frames(path, small_w, small_h)
    n = len(f)
    kf = keyframes(path)
    min_freeze = max(2, int(round(min_freeze_s * fps)))
    d = np.zeros(n)
    for i in range(1, n):
        d[i] = diff(f[i], f[i - 1])
    # typical motion around each frame: median of a 1-second window, excluding frame 0
    win = max(5, int(round(fps)))
    base = np.zeros(n)
    for i in range(1, n):
        lo, hi = max(1, i - win), min(n, i + win + 1)
        base[i] = np.median(d[lo:hi])
    typical = float(np.median(d[1:])) if n > 1 else 0.0
    events, i = [], 1
    is_spike = lambda k: d[k] > max(spike * base[k], floor)
    while i < n:
        if is_spike(i):
            # flash: spike in, spike out within 3 frames, and the frames either side match
            back = None
            for k in range(1, 4):
                j = i + k
                if j < n and is_spike(j) and diff(f[i - 1], f[j]) < max(spike * base[i], floor) / 2:
                    back = j
                    break
            if back:
                events.append({"type": "flash", "frame": i, "frames": back - i,
                               "time": round(i / fps, 3), "diff": round(float(d[i]), 2)})
                i = back + 1
                continue
            # does the picture stay changed? compare a frame before with a frame after
            after = min(n - 1, i + 2)
            kind = "cut" if diff(f[i - 1], f[after]) > max(spike * base[i], floor) else "jump"
            events.append({"type": kind, "frame": i, "time": round(i / fps, 3),
                           "diff": round(float(d[i]), 2), "typical": round(float(base[i]), 2)})
        elif d[i] < freeze_ratio * max(typical, 1e-6):
            j = i
            while j < n and d[j] < freeze_ratio * max(typical, 1e-6):
                j += 1
            if j - i + 1 >= min_freeze:
                events.append({"type": "freeze", "frame": i - 1, "frames": j - i + 1,
                               "time": round((i - 1) / fps, 3),
                               "seconds": round((j - i + 1) / fps, 3)})
            i = j
            continue
        elif d[i] > max(2.5 * base[i], 1.5 * typical) and d[i] > 1.0:
            events.append({"type": "keyframe" if i in kf else "skip", "frame": i, "time": round(i / fps, 3),
                           "diff": round(float(d[i]), 2), "typical": round(float(base[i]), 2)})
        i += 1
    return {"file": path, "frames": n, "fps": round(fps, 3), "size": f"{W}x{H}",
            "typical_diff": round(typical, 3), "max_diff": round(float(d.max()), 2),
            "events": events}, d


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.split("\n")[0])
    ap.add_argument("clip")
    ap.add_argument("--json", action="store_true")
    ap.add_argument("--csv")
    ap.add_argument("--width", type=int, default=36, help="analysis width in px (smaller = less grain)")
    ap.add_argument("--min-freeze", type=float, default=0.3, help="seconds of no change that count as a freeze")
    ap.add_argument("--spike", type=float, default=4.0, help="x typical motion that counts as a spike")
    a = ap.parse_args()
    try:
        rep, d = analyse(a.clip, small_w=a.width, spike=a.spike, min_freeze_s=a.min_freeze)
    except (subprocess.CalledProcessError, KeyError, IndexError, ValueError) as e:
        print(f"could not read {a.clip}: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    if a.csv:
        with open(a.csv, "w") as fh:
            fh.write("frame,time,diff\n")
            for i, v in enumerate(d):
                fh.write(f"{i},{i / rep['fps']:.3f},{v:.3f}\n")
    if a.json:
        print(json.dumps(rep, indent=2))
    else:
        print(f"{rep['file']}: {rep['frames']} frames @ {rep['fps']} fps, {rep['size']}, "
              f"typical frame-to-frame diff {rep['typical_diff']}, max {rep['max_diff']}")
        if not rep["events"]:
            print("  no cuts, flashes, freezes or skips found")
        for e in rep["events"]:
            extra = {k: v for k, v in e.items() if k not in ("type", "frame", "time")}
            print(f"  {e['type']:6} at {e['time']:6.3f}s (frame {e['frame']})  {extra}")
    real = [e for e in rep["events"] if e["type"] != "keyframe"]
    if any(e["type"] == "keyframe" for e in rep["events"]):
        print("  (keyframe = small pulse on an I-frame, usually encoder refresh; not counted)")
    return 1 if real else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

Run it:

python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4          # report, exit 1 if anything found
python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4 --json   # for CI or a batch script
python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4 --csv diffs.csv   # plot the curve yourself

Planting defects to test it

You can't trust a detector you've only run on clean clips. make_glitch.sh takes any clip and plants one known defect at a known frame:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Make a test copy of a clip with one known defect, to check a jump detector.
#   ./make_glitch.sh in.mp4 cut|flash|freeze|drop|lowbitrate N out.mp4
#   cut        N ignored: from 4 s on, the picture is flipped and hue-rotated (a "different shot")
#   flash      N white frames starting at frame 90
#   freeze     frame 150 held for N frames (same total length)
#   drop       N frames removed starting at frame 120 (clip gets shorter, motion jumps)
#   lowbitrate N ignored: CRF 38 with a keyframe every 30 frames (encoder pulse, not a defect)
set -euo pipefail
in=$1; kind=$2; n=$3; out=$4
enc=(-c:v libx264 -preset veryfast -crf 20 -pix_fmt yuv420p)
case $kind in
  cut) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -filter_complex \
        "[0:v]split[a][b];[a]trim=0:4,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS[a2];[b]trim=4,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS,vflip,hue=h=120[b2];[a2][b2]concat=n=2:v=1:a=0,fps=30[v]" \
        -map "[v]" -map 0:a? "${enc[@]}" -c:a copy "$out" ;;
  flash) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -vf "drawbox=0:0:iw:ih:color=white:t=fill:enable='between(n,90,$((90+n-1)))'" \
        "${enc[@]}" -c:a copy "$out" ;;
  freeze) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -filter_complex "[0:v]split[a][b];[a][b]freezeframes=first=150:last=$((150+n-1)):replace=150[v]" \
        -map "[v]" -map 0:a? "${enc[@]}" -c:a copy "$out" ;;
  drop) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -vf "select='not(between(n,120,$((120+n-1))))',setpts=N/30/TB" -an -r 30 "${enc[@]}" "$out" ;;
  lowbitrate) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -c:v libx264 -preset veryfast -crf 38 -g 30 -pix_fmt yuv420p -c:a copy "$out" ;;
  *) echo "unknown kind $kind" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac
echo "wrote $out ($kind $n)"

The base clip comes from a small synthetic generator (make_field_test_clip.sh: gradient sky, noisy field, red box with white text swaying on a sine, beeps over a hum). It's in the same folder as the scripts.

Results

Same base clip, one defect at a time:

Test clip jumpcheck.py found Exit
clean clip, grain 18 nothing (typical diff 1.07, max 1.54) 0
hard cut at 4.0 s cut at frame 120, diff 102.3 vs local 1.12 1
1 white frame at 3.0 s flash at frame 90, 1 frame 1
2 white frames at 3.0 s flash at frame 90, 2 frames 1
frame 150 held 15 frames freeze at 5.0 s, 0.5 s 1
15 frames dropped at 4.0 s skip at frame 120, diff 4.06 vs 1.11 1
clean clip, no grain nothing (typical 0.245) 0
clean clip scaled to 480x854 nothing 0
clean clip re-encoded CRF 38, keyframe every 30 7 keyframe pulses listed, not counted 0
file that doesn't exist error message 2

For comparison: ffmpeg's scdet

ffmpeg ships a scene-change filter, so the obvious question is why not just use it:

ffmpeg -i clip.mp4 -vf "scdet=threshold=10,metadata=print:file=scd.txt" -f null -

On the same planted clips at threshold=10:

Defect Highest lavfi.scd.score Flagged?
clean 0.17 no
hard cut 24.5 (frame 120) yes
1 white frame 36.8 (frame 90) yes, but only the entry. The exit frame scored low, so it looks just like a cut
15-frame freeze 2.4 no
15 dropped frames 0.9 no

That isn't a bug. scdet is built to find scene changes, and its score is roughly "how much did the frame difference jump compared with the previous difference". The return from a flash is a big difference right after another big difference, so it scores low. Freezes and small skips aren't scene changes at all. If all you need is real cuts, scdet is fine. To tell a flash from a cut, or catch the quieter defects, you need the raw curve.

Two false alarms that shaped the defaults

1. Low-bitrate keyframe "pulses." I re-encoded the clean clip at CRF 38 with a keyframe every 30 frames. The first version of the script reported seven "skips" at frames 29, 58, 87 and so on, exactly 29 frames apart. ffprobe -show_entries frame=pict_type showed an I-frame at every one of them. At low bitrate, every keyframe refreshes detail the P-frames had smeared away, and that registers as a small jump. The script now asks ffprobe for I-frame positions, labels those events keyframe and leaves them out of the exit code.

The cost of that choice is that a real skip landing on a keyframe gets hidden. This happened once in the dataset grid I mention below. Before I made the test clip deterministic, a 10-frame drop got labelled keyframe because x264 had put an I-frame right at the jump. If you have a clip that already feels wrong, also read the keyframe lines.

2. Slow motion looks like a freeze. With grain turned off, the test banner moves less than a pixel per frame at the slow ends of its sway. After encoding, some frames come out identical. The first version flagged eight "freezes" of 3-7 frames (0.1-0.23 s) in a perfectly fine clip. Raising the minimum to 0.3 s removed all of them and still caught the planted 15-frame freeze. A 0.1 s pause in an AI clip is rarely what people mean by "it froze".

Where it stops working

  • Tiny skips are invisible. On the grainy clip, dropping 1, 2 or 5 frames wasn't detected. The motion jump is smaller than the grain. On the grain-free clip, 5 dropped frames were caught (diff 1.59 vs typical 0.244) but 1-2 weren't. Freezes of 3 and 6 frames were not reported (by design, under 0.3 s); 9 and 15 were. A full grid of these cases is in the dataset linked at the end.
  • A cut to a similar-looking shot can slip through. My cut fixture flips the picture and rotates the hue, so it's an obvious change. A cut between two nearly identical framings won't produce a big spike.
  • The freeze after-effect. When a freeze ends, the motion catches up in one frame. On the grain-free clip that catch-up was also reported as a skip. It isn't a second defect, just the other end of the same freeze.
  • Thresholds were tuned on synthetic clips. Real footage with camera shake will need --spike raised.

What to do with the list

  • It's your own edit. Look at the reported frame first. Flashes and freezes usually come from a transition, a bad cut point or a dropped frame in the export. Trim with frame accuracy (re-encode, don't stream-copy) and run the check again.
  • The clip came out of the generator like that. The studio's help page separates a failed generation from one that looks wrong. Looking different from your photo isn't a failed order on its own. If you write to support, a frame number and a timestamp make the report concrete. The address is on the help page.

For reference, the pricing page listed these per-clip prices when I checked on November 13, 2026: 480p $7.98, 720p $9.98, 1080p $16.98, 4k $24.98, tax added at checkout. Check the page itself before you rely on them.

Measured grid

I ran the planted defects at several sizes (flash 1-3 frames, freeze 3-15, drop 1-15) on a grainy and a grain-free source, with fixed random seeds so it reproduces exactly. The 30 rows are in the bamabound-guides dataset on Hugging Face (config jump_detection), along with the script that rebuilds them.

event_model_payload.headline: CloudWatch Logs retention policy for the whole account
event_model_payload.summary:
A CloudWatch Logs retention policy is one of those settings nobody thinks about on the first deployment. Every Lambda function writes logs, and CloudWatch keeps them forever by default. After a few years of Serverless you end up with hundreds of log groups, and half of them belong to functions that no longer exist.

Since November 9, 2026, you can fix that centrally. An account-level retention policy defines how long logs stay in all log groups or in a selected subset. That sounds like a checkbox in the console. However, there is one detail in it that can delete data without warning. In this article I show you how the rules work, how to roll them out safely with a dry run, and how to manage them as code with AWS CDK.

In short

CloudWatch Logs can now set retention through policies for the whole account or for prefixes such as /aws/lambda. When several policies match, the longest one wins. The catch: a policy also replaces longer settings on individual log groups, so every change deserves a dry run first.

What you will learn in this article

  • How account-level policies decide the retention of log groups
  • Why a 90-day baseline can delete some logs earlier than you expect
  • How to check the impact first with a dry run and a small TypeScript tool
  • How to manage the policy as code with AWS CDK

Why log retention gets forgotten so often

CloudWatch Logs stores log data indefinitely by default. The documentation says so, and in day-to-day work you hardly notice. A Lambda function creates its log group /aws/lambda/ on the first invocation if you did not define it in your infrastructure code. It then says “Never expire”, and nobody ever looks at it again.

In addition, these log groups stay behind when you delete a stack. The function is gone, the logs remain. That costs storage, and it is also a privacy topic: logs like to contain email addresses, IP addresses or order numbers. The GDPR includes the principle of storage limitation (Art. 5(1)(e)), and “forever” is rarely a good answer to it. This is not legal advice, but it is a good reason to stop postponing the topic.

Until now you had two options. Either every team sets retention per log group in code. Or a platform group builds a Lambda function that catches new log groups via EventBridge and sets a retention afterwards. Both work, both have gaps. That is exactly where the new feature comes in.

How a CloudWatch Logs retention policy works

An account-level retention policy is an entry per account and Region that you create through the PutAccountPolicy API with the type RETENTION_POLICY. It has four parts:

Part Meaning Allowed values
Name unique name in the account free text, must not start with aws/
Retention how long log events are kept 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180, 365, 400, 545, 731, 1096, 1827, 2192, 2557, 2922, 3288, 3653 days or NEVER_EXPIRE
Enforcement mode does the rule also apply to existing log groups? RETROACTIVE or NEW_ONLY
Selection which log groups no filter (all) or LogGroupNamePrefix="/aws/lambda"

You can create up to 20 of these policies per Region. The feature costs nothing extra, and according to the announcement it is available in all commercial Regions except Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates. Important: a policy only applies in the Region where you create it. If you work in eu-central-1 and eu-west-1, you need it twice.

The longest policy wins

Unlike other account-level policies in CloudWatch, retention policies may overlap. If several match a log group, the one with the longest retention applies. NEVER_EXPIRE counts as the longest. This leads to a nice pattern: one baseline for everything, longer periods for certain prefixes, and exceptions that never expire.

Example with three policies: the longest matching policy determines the effective retention.

The catch: longer settings get replaced too

Now comes the part you should not skim. A matching account-level policy fully replaces the setting of the log group. That works in both directions. If a log group keeps data for ten years and you create a 90-day baseline for everything, CloudWatch deletes everything in it that is older than 90 days. The documentation explicitly warns about this.

The opposite case is surprising as well. Many teams deliberately use 7 or 14 days for Lambda logs. Account-level policies, on the other hand, require at least 30 days. If such a log group falls under your baseline, it suddenly gets 30 or 90 days and costs more storage than before. So a baseline is a fixed value for everything it matches, and it is no upper limit.

RETROACTIVE or NEW_ONLY?

With RETROACTIVE, the policy applies to every matching log group, including existing ones. With NEW_ONLY, it only applies to log groups created after the policy. Existing ones keep their own setting. NEW_ONLY is the cautious start, yet it does not clean up the old leftovers. I would begin with a dry run for RETROACTIVE and decide after that.

Two timing details: a new or updated policy only takes effect after about 24 hours. Until then, the old value applies. Also, CloudWatch typically deletes expired events within 72 hours, in rare cases later. From the moment they expire, though, they no longer count towards storage costs.

🎬 How CloudWatch Logs determines the effective retention of a log group – this animated diagram only runs on my site: watch it on sascha-ms.de

Step by step: roll out retention with the AWS CLI

This is how I would introduce a CloudWatch Logs retention policy in an existing account. You need:

  • AWS CLI v2 in a recent version whose put-account-policy command knows the --dry-run parameter
  • the permissions logs:PutAccountPolicy and logs:PutRetentionPolicy, for deleting logs:DeleteAccountPolicy and logs:DeleteRetentionPolicy, for reading logs:DescribeAccountPolicies and logs:DescribeLogGroups
  • an idea of which logs must stay longer (audit, billing, contracts)

1. Take stock

First, check which log groups never expire today and how much they store:

aws logs describe-log-groups \
  --query 'logGroups[?!retentionInDays].[logGroupName, storedBytes]' \
  --output table

The result is a table with names and stored bytes. Write down the log groups that should deliberately live longer. Those are exactly the ones that need their own policy in a moment.

2. Create the exceptions first

Create the longer periods before the baseline. That way there is no moment in which only the short baseline applies. In this example, the fictional bike rental keeps its audit logs for two years:

aws logs put-account-policy \
  --policy-name audit-2y \
  --policy-type RETENTION_POLICY \
  --policy-document '{"retentionInDays": 731, "enforcementMode": "RETROACTIVE"}' \
  --selection-criteria 'LogGroupNamePrefix="/bikerental/audit"'

3. Check the baseline with a dry run

Next comes the baseline for everything. With --dry-run, CloudWatch saves nothing. Instead, it reports how many log groups would keep data longer, shorter or unchanged:

aws logs put-account-policy \
  --policy-name baseline-90d \
  --policy-type RETENTION_POLICY \
  --policy-document '{"retentionInDays": 90, "enforcementMode": "RETROACTIVE"}' \
  --dry-run

The response contains a dryRunResult object with the fields decreasedRetentionLogGroupCount, increasedRetentionLogGroupCount and unchangedRetentionLogGroupCount. It also lists up to 20 of the largest affected log groups. For example, you immediately see whether a large archive group would get shorter. If decreasedRetentionLogGroupCount is greater than zero, look closely: those are the log groups that lose data.

4. Create it and check after 24 hours

If everything looks right, send the same command without --dry-run. After about a day, describe-log-groups shows the effective retention and the name of the policy that decides it:

aws logs describe-log-groups \
  --log-group-name-prefix /aws/lambda \
  --query 'logGroups[].[logGroupName, retentionInDays, retentionPolicyName]' \
  --output table

The retentionPolicyName field only shows up when an account-level policy applies. If NEVER_EXPIRE applies, retentionInDays is missing from the response. To list all policies, run aws logs describe-account-policies --policy-type RETENTION_POLICY.

A TypeScript tool for plan and dry run

The dry run returns counts and the 20 largest log groups. Often that is enough. But if you want to see the complete list of groups that lose data before an approval, a small tool helps. It loads all log groups and existing policies, recalculates the rules locally and then also asks for the real dry run.

Its core is pure logic without AWS calls and therefore easy to test. The effectiveRetention function implements both rules from above: the longest matching policy wins, and it replaces the log group’s own value.

// src/retention.ts
// Pure planning logic for account-level CloudWatch Logs retention policies.
// No AWS calls in here, so everything can be unit-tested offline.

/** Retention values (in days) that account-level policies accept. */
export const ALLOWED_DAYS = [
  30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180, 365, 400, 545, 731, 1096, 1827, 2192, 2557, 2922,
  3288, 3653,
] as const;

export type Retention = number | "NEVER_EXPIRE";
export type EnforcementMode = "RETROACTIVE" | "NEW_ONLY";

export interface RetentionPolicy {
  name: string;
  /** Log group name prefix; undefined = all log groups in the account. */
  prefix?: string;
  retention: Retention;
  mode: EnforcementMode;
  /** When the policy was created (epoch ms). Needed for NEW_ONLY. */
  createdAt: number;
}

export interface LogGroupInfo {
  name: string;
  /** Retention set on the log group itself; undefined = never expire. */
  retentionInDays?: number;
  creationTime: number;
  storedBytes: number;
}

export type ChangeKind = "shorter" | "longer" | "unchanged";

export interface PlannedChange {
  group: LogGroupInfo;
  before: Retention;
  after: Retention;
  kind: ChangeKind;
  /** Name of the policy that decides the retention after the change. */
  decidedBy?: string;
}

/** Parses CLI input like "90" or "never" into a valid retention value. */
export function parseRetention(input: string): Retention {
  const value = input.trim().toLowerCase();
  if (value === "never" || value === "never_expire") return "NEVER_EXPIRE";
  const days = Number(value);
  if (!Number.isInteger(days) || !(ALLOWED_DAYS as readonly number[]).includes(days)) {
    throw new Error(
      `Invalid retention "${input}". Allowed: ${ALLOWED_DAYS.join(", ")} or "never".`,
    );
  }
  return days;
}

/** Builds the policyDocument string for PutAccountPolicy. */
export function buildPolicyDocument(retention: Retention, mode: EnforcementMode): string {
  return JSON.stringify({ retentionInDays: retention, enforcementMode: mode });
}

/** Builds the selectionCriteria string, or undefined for "all log groups". */
export function buildSelectionCriteria(prefix?: string): string | undefined {
  if (prefix === undefined || prefix === "") return undefined;
  if (prefix.includes('"')) throw new Error("Prefix must not contain double quotes.");
  return `LogGroupNamePrefix="${prefix}"`;
}

/** Reads a policy as returned by DescribeAccountPolicies. */
export function parsePolicy(p: {
  policyName?: string;
  policyDocument?: string;
  selectionCriteria?: string;
  lastUpdatedTime?: number;
}): RetentionPolicy {
  const doc = JSON.parse(p.policyDocument ?? "{}") as {
    retentionInDays?: Retention;
    enforcementMode?: EnforcementMode;
  };
  const match = /LogGroupNamePrefix\s*=\s*"([^"]*)"/.exec(p.selectionCriteria ?? "");
  return {
    name: p.policyName ?? "unknown",
    prefix: match?.[1],
    retention: doc.retentionInDays ?? "NEVER_EXPIRE",
    mode: doc.enforcementMode ?? "RETROACTIVE",
    // The API only returns lastUpdatedTime, which is the best approximation we have.
    createdAt: p.lastUpdatedTime ?? 0,
  };
}

/** Does a policy apply to a given log group? */
export function policyMatches(policy: RetentionPolicy, group: LogGroupInfo): boolean {
  const prefixOk = policy.prefix === undefined || group.name.startsWith(policy.prefix);
  const modeOk = policy.mode === "RETROACTIVE" || group.creationTime >= policy.createdAt;
  return prefixOk && modeOk;
}

/** Compares two retention values. NEVER_EXPIRE is the longest. */
export function compareRetention(a: Retention, b: Retention): number {
  const toNumber = (r: Retention) => (r === "NEVER_EXPIRE" ? Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY : r);
  return toNumber(a) - toNumber(b);
}

/**
 * Effective retention of a log group: if at least one account policy matches,
 * the longest matching policy wins and REPLACES the log group's own setting
 * (even if that setting was longer). Otherwise the log group's own value counts.
 */
export function effectiveRetention(
  group: LogGroupInfo,
  policies: RetentionPolicy[],
): { retention: Retention; decidedBy?: string } {
  const matching = policies.filter((p) => policyMatches(p, group));
  if (matching.length === 0) {
    return { retention: group.retentionInDays ?? "NEVER_EXPIRE" };
  }
  const winner = matching.reduce((best, p) =>
    compareRetention(p.retention, best.retention) > 0 ? p : best,
  );
  return { retention: winner.retention, decidedBy: winner.name };
}

/** Simulates adding (or replacing) a policy and lists the effect per log group. */
export function planChange(
  groups: LogGroupInfo[],
  existing: RetentionPolicy[],
  candidate: RetentionPolicy,
): PlannedChange[] {
  const after = [...existing.filter((p) => p.name !== candidate.name), candidate];
  return groups
    .map((group) => {
      const before = effectiveRetention(group, existing).retention;
      const next = effectiveRetention(group, after);
      const diff = compareRetention(next.retention, before);
      const kind: ChangeKind = diff < 0 ? "shorter" : diff > 0 ? "longer" : "unchanged";
      return { group, before, after: next.retention, kind, decidedBy: next.decidedBy };
    })
    .sort((a, b) => b.group.storedBytes - a.group.storedBytes);
}

/** Groups the plan by kind, e.g. for a short summary. */
export function summarize(plan: PlannedChange[]): Record {
  const summary: Record = { shorter: 0, longer: 0, unchanged: 0 };
  for (const change of plan) summary[change.kind] += 1;
  return summary;
}

/** Human-readable bytes (base 1024). */
export function formatBytes(bytes: number): string {
  const units = ["B", "KiB", "MiB", "GiB", "TiB"];
  let value = bytes;
  let unit = 0;
  while (value >= 1024 && unit < units.length - 1) {
    value /= 1024;
    unit += 1;
  }
  return `${value.toFixed(unit === 0 ? 0 : 1)} ${units[unit]}`;
}

The command line uses the AWS SDK for JavaScript v3. Starting with version 3.1165.0, @aws-sdk/client-cloudwatch-logs knows the dryRun parameter and the retentionPolicyName field. Install and run it like this:

npm install
npx tsx src/cli.ts inventory
npx tsx src/cli.ts plan --name baseline-90d --days 90
npx tsx src/cli.ts apply --name baseline-90d --days 90 --yes

The expected output of plan looks roughly like this. Every line with SHORTER is a log group that keeps less data after the change:

Local plan: 2 shorter, 41 longer, 12 unchanged
  SHORTER         3653 -> 90           8.0 GiB  /bookshop/archive
  SHORTER NEVER_EXPIRE -> 90           5.0 GiB  /aws/lambda/search
Dry run (AWS): matched 55, shorter 2, longer 41, unchanged 12, not analyzed 0

There are two limits you should know. If a policy already applies to a log group, the API only shows the policy value and no longer the group’s own one. And for NEW_ONLY, the tool uses the time of the last update as an approximation. If the numbers differ, trust the AWS dry run. The Vitest tests cover the rules, for example that NEVER_EXPIRE always wins.

Retention policy as code with AWS CDK

A setting that affects this many log groups belongs in version control. There is one catch: as of this writing (November 10, 2026), the CloudFormation resource AWS::Logs::AccountPolicy does not list the RETENTION_POLICY type yet. Until that changes, an AwsCustomResource helps in AWS CDK. It calls putAccountPolicy on create and update and deleteAccountPolicy on delete.

// lib/log-retention-stack.ts
// CloudFormation's AWS::Logs::AccountPolicy does not list RETENTION_POLICY yet,
// so this stack calls the CloudWatch Logs API through an AwsCustomResource.
import { Stack, type StackProps } from "aws-cdk-lib";
import * as iam from "aws-cdk-lib/aws-iam";
import {
  AwsCustomResource,
  AwsCustomResourcePolicy,
  PhysicalResourceId,
} from "aws-cdk-lib/custom-resources";
import { Construct } from "constructs";

export interface RetentionRule {
  /** Unique policy name, must not start with "aws/". */
  name: string;
  /** Log group name prefix; leave empty for all log groups. */
  prefix?: string;
  /** 30, 60, 90, ... 3653 or "NEVER_EXPIRE". */
  retention: number | "NEVER_EXPIRE";
  mode?: "RETROACTIVE" | "NEW_ONLY";
}

export class AccountRetentionPolicy extends Construct {
  constructor(scope: Construct, id: string, rule: RetentionRule) {
    super(scope, id);

    const params: Record<string, string> = {
      policyName: rule.name,
      policyType: "RETENTION_POLICY",
      policyDocument: JSON.stringify({
        retentionInDays: rule.retention,
        enforcementMode: rule.mode ?? "RETROACTIVE",
      }),
    };
    if (rule.prefix) {
      params.selectionCriteria = `LogGroupNamePrefix="${rule.prefix}"`;
    }

    const putCall = {
      service: "CloudWatchLogs",
      action: "putAccountPolicy",
      parameters: params,
      physicalResourceId: PhysicalResourceId.of(`retention-${rule.name}`),
    };

    new AwsCustomResource(this, "Policy", {
      onCreate: putCall,
      onUpdate: putCall,
      onDelete: {
        service: "CloudWatchLogs",
        action: "deleteAccountPolicy",
        parameters: { policyName: rule.name, policyType: "RETENTION_POLICY" },
      },
      policy: AwsCustomResourcePolicy.fromStatements([
        new iam.PolicyStatement({
          actions: [
            "logs:PutAccountPolicy",
            "logs:PutRetentionPolicy",
            "logs:DeleteAccountPolicy",
            "logs:DeleteRetentionPolicy",
          ],
          resources: ["*"],
        }),
      ]),
      installLatestAwsSdk: false,
    });
  }
}

export class LogRetentionStack extends Stack {
  constructor(scope: Construct, id: string, props?: StackProps) {
    super(scope, id, props);

    // Baseline for everything in this account and region.
    new AccountRetentionPolicy(this, "Baseline", { name: "baseline-90d", retention: 90 });

    // Longer retention for audit logs of the fictional bike rental.
    new AccountRetentionPolicy(this, "Audit", {
      name: "audit-2y",
      prefix: "/bikerental/audit",
      retention: 731,
    });
  }
}

Run npx cdk synth to check the template and npx cdk deploy to roll it out. Expected result: two resources of type Custom::AWS and one IAM policy with exactly the four Logs actions. If you delete the stack, the policies disappear as well. A dry run of delete-account-policy shows you beforehand what will then apply to each log group.

A tip from the architecture corner: once prefixes decide about retention, log group names suddenly become an architecture decision. Write the convention down, for example in an architecture decision record. Otherwise an audit log will eventually end up under a prefix that cleans up after 90 days.

Common mistakes with log retention

  • Creating the baseline before the exceptions. The exceptions go in first, otherwise only the short period applies for a moment. The 24-hour delay softens that a bit, but I would not rely on it.
  • Skipping the dry run. A look at decreasedRetentionLogGroupCount takes seconds. Deleted logs do not come back.
  • Trusting the value in your code. If your team sets 14 days in a CDK stack, but an account-level policy applies, the policy value wins. Every team should know that.
  • Forgetting Regions. Each Region needs its own policies, including the one where only “a little bit” runs.
  • Granting too many permissions. AWS recommends giving logs:PutAccountPolicy only to administrators who own logging for the whole account.
  • Starting several dry runs at once. Only one dry run can run per account at a time. Scripts that check in parallel will get errors.

Keeping an eye on cost and security

The policies themselves are free. What changes is the storage cost of log data, and it can move in both directions. Old log groups without expiry get cheaper, while short Lambda log groups below 30 days may get more expensive. How much that means for you follows from the inventory in step 1 together with the CloudWatch Logs price list.

Security is mostly about control. Whoever may change account-level policies can indirectly delete logs. Treat these permissions like delete permissions. For logs with a legal retention requirement, I would also check whether they belong in a central log archive account to which application teams have no write access.

My take

To be honest: I have been waiting for this for a long time. “Never expire” as the default was always a poor compromise for Serverless accounts with many small functions. Finally there is a built-in solution, without a custom cleanup Lambda.

Still, I would like different semantics. A baseline that replaces longer values on individual log groups is handy for platform teams and surprising for application teams. An option like “only set it if nothing is set” would save a lot of discussions. Until then, communication is the only fix: tell the teams that their value in code no longer has the last word. And put it into your runbook before someone searches for logs during an incident that no longer exist.

My suggestion for the start: a 90-day baseline with RETROACTIVE, exceptions for audit and contracts created first, everything checked with a dry run and managed as code. That takes an hour and cleans up years of leftovers.

FAQ

How long does CloudWatch Logs keep logs by default?

Indefinitely. Without its own setting and without an account-level policy, log events never expire.

Can I set a 7-day retention with an account-level policy?

No. Account-level policies require at least 30 days. Shorter periods still only work per log group, and only as long as no account-level policy applies to that group.

Does the retention policy cost extra?

No, according to AWS there are no additional costs for the policies. Only the storage costs of the log data change.

How do I delete a retention policy again?

Use aws logs delete-account-policy --policy-name --policy-type RETENTION_POLICY. Add --dry-run to see the effect of the deletion first.

Your next step

Run the inventory from step 1 in your most important account today. The number of log groups set to “Never expire” is usually argument enough. If you are working on costs anyway, my article about NAT gateway costs with Lambda fits right in.

Now it is your turn: which baseline retention do you consider sensible, and which logs have to stay longer in your setup? Let me know in the comments.

event_model_payload.headline: A small offline check for route data before making a travel animation
event_model_payload.summary:
A map animation makes movement look continuous, even when the underlying record is sparse. That visual effect can be useful for storytelling, but it can also hide missing samples, time-zone mistakes, and values that do not represent valid coordinates. Before turning an exported route into a public clip, it helps to run a few small checks and then review the map itself.

This article builds an offline Python check for a deliberately simple CSV format. It does not parse the Google Timeline export format, reconstruct a route, prove where anyone was, or determine whether a location can safely be shared. The examples and tests use synthetic values. I am associated with Timeline Visualizer, and AI assisted in drafting this article and code. Timeline Visualizer is a browser-based google timeline visualizer that turns exported location history into an animated travel video. It offers route customization and MP4 export; custom music is part of the optional Pro upgrade. This standalone code is not a feature of the product or an integration with it.

Choose a narrow input contract

The example accepts rows with three fields: lat, lon, and timestamp. Latitude and longitude are decimal degrees. The timestamp is an ISO 8601 value with an explicit UTC offset, such as 2025-05-08T09:00:00+00:00. A trailing Z is also accepted as UTC. These fields are a teaching format, not a claim about the fields present in a particular service's export.

A real conversion layer needs its own documentation and tests. If an input represents coordinates as integers scaled by a power of ten, for example, those values must be converted correctly before this checker receives them. If a timestamp is a Unix epoch, it must be converted to an offset-aware value deliberately. Guessing a format from a number's length can produce plausible but incorrect coordinates, so keep source parsing separate from validation.

The tool returns row numbers and short warning labels. It deliberately avoids printing the actual coordinates. That reduces accidental exposure in console output, although row numbers can still reveal information when combined with the original file. Treat both the input and any report as private. The function operates on data already in memory and makes no network calls; that does not make a machine or its backups automatically secure.

A small checker 

import csv
import math
from datetime import datetime


def audit(rows, gap_minutes=120):
    issues = []
    previous = None
    for number, row in enumerate(rows, 1):
        try:
            lat, lon = float(row['lat']), float(row['lon'])
            stamp = datetime.fromisoformat(
                row['timestamp'].replace('Z', '+00:00')
            )
            if stamp.utcoffset() is None:
                raise ValueError('timestamp must include offset')
            if not (math.isfinite(lat) and math.isfinite(lon)
                    and -90 <= lat <= 90 and -180 <= lon <= 180):
                raise ValueError('invalid coordinate')
        except (KeyError, TypeError, ValueError):
            issues.append((number, 'invalid row'))
            previous = None
            continue
        if previous is not None:
            delta = (stamp - previous).total_seconds() / 60
            if delta < 0:
                issues.append((number, 'out of order'))
            elif delta > gap_minutes:
                issues.append((number, 'large time gap'))
        previous = stamp
    return issues


def read_csv(path):
    with open(path, encoding='utf-8', newline='') as handle:
        return list(csv.DictReader(handle))

The bounds check rejects values outside the possible latitude and longitude ranges. math.isfinite matters because Python accepts strings such as nan and inf as floating-point values; those are not usable positions. A numeric value inside the range can still be wrong. Swapped latitude and longitude may pass, and a plausible coordinate can belong to the wrong city. This code reports basic validity, not geographic truth.

The ordering check compares each valid timestamp to the previous valid timestamp. A negative interval is flagged as out of order. An interval strictly greater than the chosen threshold is flagged as a large time gap. Two points exactly 120 minutes apart are not flagged under the default setting. A gap is a prompt to inspect the source, not proof that a device failed or that a traveler moved directly between the two points.

When a row is invalid, the code clears the previous timestamp. The next valid row begins a new comparison sequence. This avoids pretending that the checker knows how to bridge a malformed row. Depending on the application, a different policy might be appropriate, but it should be explicit and covered by tests. For example, a production pipeline may want a separate warning that a comparison was interrupted.

Exercise the boundary cases

The following small tests use fabricated coordinates and times. Save the checker as route_audit.py and run this snippet in the same directory. They test the code shown above, not the Timeline Visualizer product or any real export.

from route_audit import audit


def row(lat, lon, stamp):
    return {'lat': lat, 'lon': lon, 'timestamp': stamp}


a = '2025-05-08T09:00:00+00:00'
b = '2025-05-08T09:30:00+00:00'
c = '2025-05-08T13:00:00+00:00'

assert audit([row('48', '2', a), row('48.1', '2.1', b)]) == []
assert audit([row('48', '2', a), row('48', '2', c)]) == [(2, 'large time gap')]
assert audit([row('48', '2', b), row('48', '2', a)]) == [(2, 'out of order')]
assert audit([row('nan', '2', a)]) == [(1, 'invalid row')]
assert audit([row('91', '2', a)]) == [(1, 'invalid row')]
assert audit([row('48', '2', '2025-05-08T09:00:00')]) == [(1, 'invalid row')]
assert audit([row('48', '2', a), {}, row('48', '2', c)]) == [(2, 'invalid row')]
assert audit([
    row('48', '2', '2025-05-08T09:00:00Z'),
    row('48', '2', '2025-05-08T11:00:00+02:00'),
]) == []
print('8 synthetic assertions passed')

These eight assertions passed locally against the accompanying example. The last test uses two representations of the same instant with different offsets. Python compares aware datetimes by instant, so the interval is zero. The test is useful because sorting timestamp strings lexicographically is not generally a safe substitute for parsing offsets. Local dates are still important for a human itinerary, but that is a separate presentation decision.

Decide what a warning means

A warning should lead to a question, not an automatic correction. For a large gap, inspect the original record and any itinerary information you already have. It may correspond to a device being offline, but it may also be an intentional stop. For out-of-order rows, determine whether the file was meant to be ordered by recording time, import order, or another field. Sorting blindly can obscure an upstream issue or change the intended sequence.

Consider the threshold in context. Two hours may be reasonable for a dense city walk and unhelpful for a route sampled only a few times per day. Pass a different gap_minutes value when the sampling policy is known, and record that choice with the review. This example does not validate the threshold itself; a production implementation should reject negative, non-finite, or otherwise inappropriate settings and return structured errors suitable for its caller.

Do not use a single numeric check as a privacy guarantee. A valid point may be a home, school, workplace, or medical location. A seemingly broad map can identify a person through a distinctive combination of places and times. Review the route and audience explicitly, remove unnecessary segments, obtain consent when others are represented, and remember that a shared video can be copied beyond the initial recipients.

Turn checks into a reviewable workflow

Keep the raw export private and work on a copy. Run validation before selecting a visual style, then make a short list of warnings to inspect. Check the first and last locations, the order of major stops, missing intervals, and any labels visible at the intended playback size. If the source is uncertain, leave a gap or describe the uncertainty instead of drawing a confident line that the data does not support.

After editing, play the actual exported video from start to finish. Confirm that the map scale provides enough context without exposing more than the audience needs. If music is included, make sure the license covers the intended use. If a video will be compressed by a messaging or social platform, check the compressed copy as well as the original. A clear opening frame and a short pause at an important stop can do more for comprehension than additional motion effects.

The boundary between data quality, privacy, and presentation is important. The Python function only catches a few mechanical problems. A person still needs to decide what the journey is meant to communicate and what should remain private. A small, well-documented checker is valuable precisely because its limitations are visible: it helps organize review without replacing judgment or presenting an animation as authoritative evidence.

event_model_payload.headline: Azure API Management CI/CD: APIOps Pipelines with GitHub Actions
event_model_payload.summary:
What has to pass before a merged pull request may change the production API Management instance without anyone opening the portal? Part 5's publish workflow already ran a dry run on every pull request and published on merge, but nothing required the dry run to pass, it signed in with the same identity that published to dev, and nothing read the spec or the policies before the CLI did. A pipeline you can trust with prod needs four gates, each catching something the others can't: checks that need no Azure at all, a dry run that can only read, a publish to dev that API Management itself validates, and a person who approves prod.

The companion repo keeps Part 5's layout: apiops/ holds the artifact tree, the extract filter and configuration.prod.yaml, and the APIOps CLI is still pinned at @azure-tools/apiops-cli@1.0.5. The publish workflow is what changes. The dry run becomes a required check that runs on every pull request and can only read, dev gets the merged commit, prod gets it after an approval, and a manual run publishes the full tree when prod has fallen behind. Each stage signs in through OIDC with its own user-assigned managed identity, so the repository holds no Azure secret. As in Part 5, nothing is deployed. Both workflows pass actionlint, the three validate steps ran locally against the sample, the claim that the dry run only reads comes from the CLI's 1.0.5 source, and no workflow has run on GitHub or exchanged a token with Entra ID. Where a step depends on how GitHub or Azure behaves at run time, I link the documentation it rests on.

From a local change to production

A change starts on a branch that edits something under ApimOrdersDemo/apiops/. Its pull request gets two checks. validate lints the specs, checks the policy files and compares each spec with the base branch, without signing in to Azure. dry-run signs in as id-apiops-plan, which can only read, and plans the change against dev, then against prod with the prod overrides. Both are required, so a merge waits for them. The merge lands one commit on main. publish-dev publishes that commit to dev as id-apiops-dev, then publish-prod waits in the prod environment until a reviewer approves and publishes the same commit to prod as id-apiops-prod. The nightly extract from Part 5 keeps running on the side and turns portal edits into drift pull requests, which pass through the same two checks as every other change.

The rule behind the identities: only a job running on main can reach one that writes.

The workflow is about 200 lines, most of them checkout, Node setup and CLI flags. Here is its job graph, with steps, runners, permissions and concurrency left out:

jobs:
  changes:
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'

  validate:      # required check, no Azure sign-in
    needs: changes
    if: needs.changes.outputs.validate == 'true'

  dry-run:       # required check, id-apiops-plan (Reader), no environment
    needs: changes
    if: needs.changes.outputs.apiops == 'true'

  publish-dev:   # id-apiops-dev
    if: github.event_name != 'pull_request'
    environment: dev

  publish-prod:  # id-apiops-prod, after a reviewer approves
    needs: publish-dev
    environment: prod

On a pull request, the run takes changes and then validate and dry-run side by side. On a push to main or a manual run, it takes publish-dev and then publish-prod. Every job has an if: or a needs: that ties it to one of the two paths, so no run does both. The sections below show the parts of each job that matter.

Triggers: pull requests, pushes to main, and a manual full publish 

on:
  # No paths filter on pull_request: a required check from a path-filtered workflow stays Pending
  # on every PR that doesn't match. The changes job decides instead, and a skipped job counts as passed.
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ['ApimOrdersDemo/apiops/**']
  # Full publish without --commit-id, to reconcile prod after a rejected or cancelled run.
  workflow_dispatch:

pull_request has no paths filter, on purpose. GitHub's workflow syntax reference spells out what a path filter does to a required check: when a workflow is skipped by path filtering, its checks "will remain in a 'Pending' state", and a pull request that requires them "will be blocked from merging." The samples repo has two dozen folders next to ApimOrdersDemo. With Part 5's paths: ['ApimOrdersDemo/apiops/**'] and dry-run marked as required, every pull request that touched only a Functions demo would wait forever for a check that never starts.

So the workflow starts on every pull request and decides inside. A skipped job reports Success, even when it is a required check, which makes a job-level if: the answer: green for pull requests that don't touch apiops/, a real dry run for those that do. The changes job computes it:

  changes:
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      apiops: ${{ steps.diff.outputs.apiops }}
      validate: ${{ steps.diff.outputs.validate }}
    steps:
      # A change to the policy script alone runs validate against the unchanged artifacts. It plans
      # nothing, so dry-run stays skipped.
      - id: diff
        run: |
          changed() { if git diff --quiet HEAD~1 HEAD -- "$@"; then echo false; else echo true; fi; }
          echo "apiops=$(changed ApimOrdersDemo/apiops)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "validate=$(changed ApimOrdersDemo/apiops ApimOrdersDemo/scripts/check-policies.mjs)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

On a pull request, actions/checkout checks out the merge commit GitHub builds for it, and that commit's first parent is the tip of the base branch. HEAD~1..HEAD is everything the pull request changes. It's also the range --commit-id diffs in the dry run (Part 5: ~1 against ), so the two can't disagree about whether apiops/ changed, and a checkout with fetch-depth: 2 is all the history either needs. A paths-filter action from the Marketplace does the same with more options, but a git diff --quiet doesn't add a third-party action to a workflow that signs in to Azure. The price is a runner start, a few seconds, on every pull request in the repository.

There are two outputs because the two checks read different files. dry-run plans the artifacts, so apiops/ is all it cares about. validate also runs scripts/check-policies.mjs, which lives outside apiops/, and with one output a pull request that changed only the script would merge without the new script running once. That pull request now gets validate against the unchanged artifacts and a skipped dry-run, which would have nothing to plan.

push keeps its path filter. Nothing requires a check on a push, so a push that doesn't touch apiops/ can skip the whole workflow. Per-commit publishing still assumes one commit per merge: a rebase merge of three commits lands three commits on main, and the run publishes only the last one. Allow merge commits or squash merges in the repository settings and turn rebase merging off.

workflow_dispatch takes no inputs. A manual run follows the same publish-dev and publish-prod path as a push, with one difference in the publish command:

          ${{ github.event_name == 'push' && format('--commit-id {0}', github.sha) || '' }}

On a push, the expression becomes --commit-id . On a manual run it's empty, and the CLI publishes the full tree. That's the reconcile path. When a reviewer rejects a prod approval or a waiting run gets cancelled, that commit's change never reaches prod, and the next per-commit run only publishes its own diff. A full publish PUTs every artifact (Part 5: safe to re-run, not free) and brings prod back to what main says. Start it from main: the dev and prod environments only accept the main branch, so a manual run from anywhere else fails at publish-dev.

Validation that needs no Azure

validate has no permissions block, so it gets the workflow's contents: read and no id-token. It couldn't sign in to Azure if it tried, which also makes it the one check that passes on a fork's pull request. It needs changes like dry-run does but reads its own output, so both start when apiops/ changed, validate alone starts when only the policy script did, and both count as passed when neither changed. After checkout (fetch-depth: 2, which gives it the base version of each spec) and Node setup, it runs three steps from ApimOrdersDemo/apiops, like every job that touches the artifacts. Each one reads what is inside a file, which the dry run never does: it plans calls, and a valid policy plans the same PUT as a broken one.

Linting the OpenAPI specs 

      - name: Lint the OpenAPI specs
        run: npx --yes @stoplight/spectral-cli@6.17.1 lint --ruleset .spectral.yaml 'apim-artifacts/apis/*/specification.yaml'

Spectral is pinned like the CLI, and the glob is quoted so Spectral expands it instead of the shell. The ruleset sits next to the artifacts in apiops/.spectral.yaml, so editing it is a change under apiops/ and runs the check that uses it:

extends: [[spectral:oas, recommended]]
rules:
  # API Management names each operation after its operationId, and operations//policy.xml hangs off
  # that name. Without one, the import generates a name from method and path.
  operation-operationId: error
  # Partners find the contact in the developer portal, not in the spec.
  info-contact: off

Two edits fit spectral:oas to API Management. operation-operationId goes from warning to error, because the import names each operation after its operationId and the operation policies in this repo hang off that name: apis/orders/operations/get-order/policy.xml belongs to whatever operation is called get-order. On the sample the step reports 0 errors and 8 warnings (six missing tags, and get-order has no description in either version), and warnings don't fail it. Delete operationId: get-order from the v1 spec, and it does:

  59:9    error  operation-operationId  Operation must have "operationId".                             paths./orders/{orderId}.get
✖ 5 problems (1 error, 4 warnings, 0 infos, 0 hints)

Gotcha: the linter has to know where the gateway enforces security. Redocly CLI 2.76.0 with its recommended config fails both specs with six errors, one security-defined per operation, because neither spec declares a security scheme. That's deliberate: the subscription key and the Entra token are checked in policy (Parts 2 and 3), not described in the spec. Turn the rule off in redocly.yaml, or declare the key header and the bearer scheme in the spec so the developer portal shows them too. Spectral's oas rules only check that a scheme an operation references exists, so they stay quiet.

Checking policies when they aren't quite XML 

apis/orders/policy.xml:27: parser error : attributes construct error

That's xmllint --noout on a policy API Management accepts. For XML, the quote before POST ends the attribute. API Management doesn't mind, because the CLI sends policies as rawxml, which the ARM API calls "a non XML encoded policy document". The next tool to reach for would be a schema, and there isn't one: I found no official XSD for policies on Learn, in the VS Code extension or in the policy snippets repo. So the check is a script of about 140 lines, Node built-ins only. It's JavaScript because the job already has Node for npx. The script never runs the C# in the expressions; it only finds where each one starts and ends.

      - name: Check the policies
        run: node ../scripts/check-policies.mjs apim-artifacts

It blanks every policy expression and parses what's left as XML. It then requires one inbound, backend, outbound and on-error section in every API, operation and product policy, each with a directly inside, and compares apis/orders/policy.xml with apis/orders-v2/policy.xml byte for byte. The blanking is what makes the parse possible:

// Expressions are C#, and policies travel as rawxml, so condition="@(x == "POST")" is a valid policy
// and invalid XML. Replace each @(...) and @{...} with spaces, keeping line breaks for line numbers.
function blankExpressions(src) {
  let out = ''
  for (let i = 0; i < src.length; i++) {
    const close = src[i] === '@' && { '(': ')', '{': '}' }[src[i + 1]]
    if (!close) {
      out += src[i]
      continue
    }
    let depth = 0
    let end = -1
    for (let j = i + 1; j < src.length && end < 0; j++) {
      if (src[j] === '"' || src[j] === "'") j = skipLiteral(src, j)
      else if (src[j] === src[i + 1]) depth++
      else if (src[j] === close && --depth === 0) end = j
    }
    if (end < 0) throw new PolicyError(src, i, 'unclosed policy expression')
    out += src.slice(i, end + 1).replace(/[^\n]/g, ' ')
    i = end
  }
  return out
}

The scan counts brackets and skips C# string and char literals, so a ) inside "..." doesn't end the expression. Spaces instead of an empty string keep every tag on its original line, which is the line the error message reports.

On the sample's six policy files it prints 6 policy files OK. On a copy with three typical mistakes, it exits 1: the get-order operation policy without in inbound, an unquoted attribute in the partner product's policy, and Part 5's Orders.Read role added to v1 only:

apis/orders/operations/get-order/policy.xml:  has no , so the broader scope's inbound section never runs
products/orders-partners/policy.xml: line 4: malformed markup (unquoted attribute, or < in an attribute value?)
apis/orders/policy.xml: differs from apis/orders-v2/policy.xml; change both

The rule is the reason the script exists. An operation policy without it skips the product rate limit, the token check and the backend route, and nothing reports an error. In this sample the call reaches the function without the managed identity token or the function key and gets a 401 from the backend instead of the gateway. The comparison is the sample-specific part: replace the pair in MUST_MATCH with yours, or delete it.

What the script can't know is which policy elements exist. parses and passes, and so does a {{named-value}} nobody created. Without a schema, only API Management can reject those, and its first chance is the PUT in publish-dev.

Catching breaking changes before they become a new version

Copy the v2 spec over the v1 spec, commit, and the third step fails:

1 changes: 1 error, 0 warning, 0 info
error   [response-body-type-changed] at /head/apim-artifacts/apis/orders/specification.yaml
    in API GET /orders
        the response's body `type` changed from `array

event_model_payload.headline: Freestyle Job vs Declarative Pipeline in Jenkins: Which One Should You Use?
event_model_payload.summary:
A beginner-friendly comparison of Jenkins Freestyle jobs and Declarative Pipelines on AWS EC2, with examples and a clear recommendation."
tags: aws, jenkins, devops, cicd

When I started learning Jenkins on AWS, the first question I hit was: "Should I create a Freestyle job or a Pipeline?" Both can build and deploy your code, but they work very differently. In this article I explain both in simple terms, compare them, and help you decide which one to use on your EC2-hosted Jenkins server.

What is a Freestyle Job?

A Freestyle job is the classic, beginner-friendly way to create a build in Jenkins. You configure everything through the web UI by clicking and filling in forms:

  • Choose a source code repository (GitHub)
  • Add a build trigger (manual, webhook, or poll SCM)
  • Add build steps (for example, "Execute shell")
  • Add post-build actions (for example, notifications)

Example: Docker build in a Freestyle job (Execute shell step)

docker build -t myuser/cloudcart:latest .
docker login -u $DOCKER_USER -p $DOCKER_PASS
docker push myuser/cloudcart:latest
docker run -d -p 8081:80 myuser/cloudcart:latest

Pros

  • Very easy to learn, with no coding needed
  • Fast to set up for simple tasks
  • Good for first labs and quick tests

Cons

  • The configuration lives inside Jenkins, not in your Git repository
  • Hard to copy, review, or version-control
  • Complex flows (multiple stages, parallel steps) get messy
  • If the Jenkins server is lost, the job setup is lost too

What is a Declarative Pipeline?

A Declarative Pipeline defines your whole CI/CD flow as code, in a file called a Jenkinsfile stored in your GitHub repo. It follows a clear, structured syntax made of stages and steps.

Example: Jenkinsfile

pipeline {
    agent any

    environment {
        IMAGE_NAME = "myuser/cloudcart"
    }

    stages {
        stage('Checkout') {
            steps {
                git branch: 'main', url: 'https://github.com/myuser/cloudcart.git'
            }
        }

        stage('Build Docker Image') {
            steps {
                sh 'docker build -t $IMAGE_NAME:latest .'
            }
        }

        stage('Push to Docker Hub') {
            steps {
                withCredentials([usernamePassword(credentialsId: 'dockerhub-creds',
                    usernameVariable: 'DOCKER_USER', passwordVariable: 'DOCKER_PASS')]) {
                    sh 'echo $DOCKER_PASS | docker login -u $DOCKER_USER --password-stdin'
                    sh 'docker push $IMAGE_NAME:latest'
                }
            }
        }

        stage('Deploy') {
            steps {
                sh 'docker rm -f cloudcart || true'
                sh 'docker run -d --name cloudcart -p 8081:80 $IMAGE_NAME:latest'
            }
        }
    }

    post {
        success { echo 'Pipeline completed successfully!' }
        failure { echo 'Pipeline failed. Check the logs.' }
    }
}

Pros

  • Pipeline as Code: it is versioned in Git with your application
  • A visual Stage View shows exactly which stage passed or failed
  • Easy to review, reuse, and roll back
  • Supports parallel stages, conditions, and approvals
  • Survives a Jenkins restart and can resume

Cons

  • Slightly steeper learning curve (you need to learn the syntax)
  • A small typo in the Jenkinsfile can break the build

Freestyle vs Declarative Pipeline: Side-by-Side

Feature Freestyle Job Declarative Pipeline
Configuration Web UI (clicks) Code (Jenkinsfile)
Stored in Git No Yes
Learning curve Very easy Moderate
Multi-stage workflows Difficult Built in
Stage visualization No Yes (Stage View)
Parallel execution Limited Yes
Reusability Low High
Best for Simple jobs, learning Real CI/CD projects

When Should You Use Which?

Use a Freestyle Job when:

  • You are a beginner running your first Jenkins lab
  • The task is small (one script, a quick test, a cleanup job)
  • You just want to understand how Jenkins works

Use a Declarative Pipeline when:

  • You are building a real CI/CD workflow (build → test → push → deploy)
  • You want your pipeline stored in GitHub with your code
  • You work in a team or want a production-style setup
  • You plan to integrate tools like Docker, SonarQube, ECR, or Kubernetes

How to Create a Pipeline Job on Jenkins (EC2)

  1. Open Jenkins at http://:8080
  2. Click New Item, enter a name, and select Pipeline
  3. Under Pipeline, choose Pipeline script from SCM
  4. Select Git and paste your repository URL
  5. Set the branch (for example main) and the Script Path as Jenkinsfile
  6. Click Save, then Build Now
  7. Open Stage View to watch each stage run

Tip: Make sure port 8080 is open in your EC2 Security Group, and store secrets such as Docker Hub credentials in Manage Jenkins → Credentials, never inside the Jenkinsfile.

My Recommendation

Start with a Freestyle job to understand the basics: how Jenkins pulls code, runs a shell command, and shows console output. Once you are comfortable, move to Declarative Pipelines. They are the industry standard for CI/CD, they are cleaner, and they make your project look far more professional on your GitHub and resume.

Conclusion

Freestyle jobs are great for learning, but Declarative Pipelines are what you will use in real projects. Treating your pipeline as code gives you version control, visibility, and repeatability, which are the core ideas of DevOps on AWS.

If you are learning Jenkins on EC2 too, try converting one of your Freestyle jobs into a Jenkinsfile today. It is the best way to learn.

Author: Vishal Patil
LinkedIn: vishalpatil-devops-aws
GitHub: VishalPatil-DevOps-AWS
