event_model_payload.headline: Building Safer AI Memory: Inside RagLeap Memory v0.3.1
event_model_payload.summary:
Encrypted memory export, AES-256-GCM, tamper detection, and the engineering work behind safer memory portability.

AI systems are becoming increasingly dependent on persistent memory.

An AI employee needs to retain useful context across tasks, retrieve relevant information, and operate within clearly defined boundaries. But memory is not just about storing information. It also involves protecting that information when it moves between systems.

With RagLeap Memory v0.3.1, we've taken another step towards building a stronger, security-conscious memory infrastructure for open-source AI employees.

This release introduces optional encrypted memory export and import, powered by AES-256-GCM through ragleap-security.

This article explains what changed, how the encryption works, what we tested, and — just as importantly — what this release does not claim to protect.

1. Why encrypted memory portability matters

Memory portability is useful when operators need to:

  • Move memory exports between environments.
  • Back up selected memory scopes.
  • Transfer memory data securely.
  • Preserve useful context across deployments.
  • Manage memory exports with stronger confidentiality guarantees.

However, a portable memory file can contain sensitive information.

A plain export may be convenient, but anyone who obtains that file could potentially inspect its contents.

RagLeap Memory 0.3.1 adds an optional encryption layer to exported memory files while preserving the existing plain-export behaviour for users who do not enable encryption.

The goal is straightforward: make memory portability safer without unexpectedly changing existing workflows.

2. AES-256-GCM encrypted exports

The new encryption capability uses AES-256-GCM through the ragleap-security package.

The memory package provides the export/import workflow, while the security package handles the underlying encryption.

Install the optional cryptography dependency:

pip install "ragleap-memory[crypto]==0.3.1"

The base package remains available without the optional extra:

pip install ragleap-memory==0.3.1

If encryption is requested without the optional dependency, the package raises an error explaining which extra is required.

This keeps the encryption dependency optional and avoids changing the behaviour of installations that do not need it.

3. New encryption APIs

Version 0.3.1 adds optional encryption and decryption parameters to the existing file and stream APIs.

The new export signature is:

export_file(
    scope,
    path,
    encrypt_with=None,
    passphrase=None,
    context=None,
)

Import operations support:

import_file(
    ...,
    decrypt_with=None,
    passphrase=None,
    context=None,
)

And the same decryption options are available through import_stream.

The implementation supports:

  • Key for encryption and decryption.
  • KeyRing for key selection and rotation workflows.
  • Passphrase-based encryption using scrypt-derived keys.
  • Context-bound encrypted exports.

Passphrase derivation happens once per file rather than once per individual memory entry.

This provides flexibility for different operational requirements without forcing every user into one key-management approach.

4. Tamper detection and context binding

Encryption alone is not the complete story.

The release also strengthens the relationship between encrypted entries and their original export.

Each encrypted line is bound to:

  • A fixed cryptographic label.
  • The SHA-256 hash of the exact header line.
  • Its position in the export.
  • The supplied context.

This means changes to encrypted data, moving entries, duplicating entries, or attempting to reuse entries across different export contexts will cause decryption to fail.

Incorrect keys or contexts also result in decryption failure.

The import process checks the expected entry count, so dropped or additional lines are rejected.

Errors are reported with the relevant line number rather than silently accepting corrupted data.

These checks are intended to make accidental modification and tampering detectable.

5. No silent downgrade between encrypted and plain exports

A security-sensitive import operation should not silently change its interpretation of a file.

RagLeap Memory 0.3.1 explicitly distinguishes encrypted and plain exports.

The new behaviour includes:

  • Encrypted exports require the appropriate decryption key or passphrase.
  • Supplying encryption credentials for a plain export causes the import to refuse it.
  • Unsupported header versions are rejected.
  • Version 2 headers identify encrypted exports.
  • Existing version 1 plain exports continue to work.

Importantly, existing calls without the new arguments retain their 0.3.0 behaviour.

This makes the release additive rather than a breaking change for existing users.

6. Existing import safeguards remain in place

Decryption does not bypass the existing memory import controls.

After decryption, data still passes through the established import path, including:

  • Trust limits.
  • Scope validation.
  • Quotas.
  • Size limits.
  • A single database transaction.
  • Existing import safety checks.

The principle is important: encryption should protect the exported file, but it should not become a shortcut around the controls governing what enters the memory system.

7. Testing beyond ordinary unit tests

Security-sensitive changes require more than checking whether encryption and decryption work in a basic example.

For this release, we performed several layers of verification.

Test results:

Verification Result
VPS test suite, Python 3.10 532 passed
Sandbox test suite, Python 3.10 532 passed
Sandbox test suite, Python 3.12 532 passed
Mutation testing 232/232 caught
GitHub CI checks on implementation PR 55/55 passed

Mutation testing deliberately introduces changes into the implementation to determine whether the tests detect them.

In this release, all 232 tested mutations were detected in the reported sandbox runs.

We also performed release-artifact verification:

  • The five Python files in the published wheel were compared with the source at the release tag.
  • Fresh installations were tested with and without the optional crypto extra.
  • The source distribution test suite was run against the installed wheel.
  • A real database export created using RagLeap Memory 0.3.0 was successfully opened and imported.
  • RagLeap Memory 0.3.0 rejected a 0.3.1 encrypted export with the expected unsupported-version behaviour.

The published wheel and source distribution were also checked against their recorded SHA-256 digests and release provenance.

These checks provide evidence that the published package corresponds to the tested release source.

8. Important security limitations

We want to be precise about what this release protects.

Encrypted export files are protected — not the entire memory environment.

The current implementation does not encrypt:

  • The underlying SQLite database.
  • Process memory while exporting or importing.
  • Other application data outside the exported file.

There are additional limitations:

  • The export header reveals the number of entries.
  • Encrypted line lengths reveal approximate entry sizes.
  • Anyone possessing the appropriate key can read or forge an export.
  • Replaying an older valid export is not detected by this release.
  • Decrypted content remains untrusted input and must still pass the import safeguards.
  • No independent security audit has been performed.

Large imports are also subject to the configured size limit, which defaults to 64 MiB.

We believe transparent security boundaries are essential. Encryption should not be presented as a guarantee that every part of a memory system is secure.

9. Where this fits into RagLeap's memory direction

RagLeap is building an open-source, self-hosted AI employee platform.

Our memory direction is not simply about sharing personal context between different chat applications.

We are working towards a stronger memory infrastructure that can support AI employees and enterprise workflows.

That requires several capabilities to work together:

  • Persistent and structured memory.
  • Scoped access and isolation.
  • Reliable retrieval.
  • Security and controlled data portability.
  • Memory governance and lifecycle management.
  • Integration with the wider AI employee architecture.

RagLeap Memory 0.3.1 is one step in that direction.

It does not complete the enterprise memory roadmap, but it adds an important security capability while preserving compatibility with existing workflows.

10. Install RagLeap Memory 0.3.1

Standard installation:

pip install ragleap-memory==0.3.1

With encrypted export/import support:

pip install "ragleap-memory[crypto]==0.3.1"

Project resources:

  • GitHub: https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core
  • PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/ragleap-memory/
  • Documentation: https://docs.ragleap.com/

Contributions, testing, security feedback, and technical discussions are welcome through the official repository.

Final thoughts

AI memory is becoming a foundational part of intelligent systems.

As AI employees take on more responsibilities, their memory infrastructure needs to be reliable, controlled, portable, and designed with security boundaries in mind.

With RagLeap Memory 0.3.1, we have added encrypted memory export and import, context binding, tamper detection, and extensive release verification.

We will continue developing RagLeap's memory infrastructure with a focus on security, reliability, and self-hosted control.

RagLeap — Open-source AI employees that ask before they act.

event_model_payload.summary:
In a school sports event, students wearing ODD jersey numbers enter the ground first. After they finish, students wearing EVEN jersey numbers enter the ground.

Let's use Python to display the order.

Displaying Odd Jersey Numbers

odd_no=1
print(odd_no,end=" ")
odd_no=odd_no+2
print(odd_no,end=" ")
odd_no=odd_no+2
print(odd_no,end=" ")
odd_no=odd_no+2
print(odd_no,end=" ")
odd_no=odd_no+2
print(odd_no,end=" ")
odd_no=odd_no+2

odd_no=1
while odd_no<=10:
print(odd_no,end=" ")
odd_no=odd_no+2

output 1 3 5 7 9

even_no=2
print(even_no,end=" ")
even_no=even_no+2
print(even_no,end=" ")
even_no=even_no+2
print(even_no,end=" ")
even_no=even_no+2
print(even_no,end=" ")
even_no=even_no+2
print(even_no,end=" ")
even_no=even_no+2

even_no=2
while even_no<=10:
print(even_no,end=" ")
even_no=even_no+2

output 2 4 6 8 10

combined program
print("Odd Jersey Numbers:")

odd_no=1
while odd_no<=10:

print("\nEven Jersey Number:")

eeven_no=2
while even_no<=10:
print(even_no,end=" ")
even_no=even_no+2

Odd Jersey Numbers:
1 3 5 7 9

Even Jersey Number:
2 4 6 8 10

event_model_payload.headline: Upgrade Evidence for Packages: Helping AI Agents Patch Safely
event_model_payload.summary:
AI agents now open dependency upgrades faster than most engineering teams can review them. Safe patching is not just about bumping a version, it is about proving the bump held.

According to Sonatype's 2026 State of the Software Supply Chain report, 27.76% of 36,870 AI-generated upgrade recommendations pointed to versions that do not exist in any registry.

This ai agent package upgrade evidence guide breaks down why unverified upgrades fail and what proof every change should carry. It also shows how to record that proof in your pipeline.

You will see where human approval belongs, so your team can let agents patch with confidence and keep a clean, reviewable audit trail for every dependency change.

Why Do AI Agent Dependency Upgrades Fail Without Evidence?

Transitive dependencies change what nobody reviewed

An agent that bumps one direct package rarely changes just one package. The new version can pull in a dozen transitive dependencies, and each carries its own code, maintainers, and risks.

Reviewers usually read the manifest diff, yet the real change lives in the lockfile. Public data does not fill the gap either. Sonatype's analysis found that nearly 65% of open source CVEs lacked an NVD-assigned CVSS score.

Therefore, severity labels alone cannot tell an agent which upgrade is safe, or tell a reviewer why it was chosen.

A green build is not proof of a safe upgrade

A passing build only shows that the code compiles and the tests you wrote still pass. It does not show that the version exists in the registry. It also cannot show that the version is free of known flaws, or that the changed code paths were exercised.

Moreover, an agent explains its choice in fluent text, which feels like evidence but is not. Without a stored record of what was checked, nobody can reconstruct the decision later.

For software supply chain security reviews, that missing record is the real failure, not the bad version itself.

What Is AI Agent Package Upgrade Evidence?

AI agent package upgrade evidence is the verifiable record that proves an automated dependency change was necessary, correct, tested, and approved.

Detection tools stop at the alert, so AI agent package upgrade evidence has to be produced by the step that actually changes the code.

Think of it as a commit-level receipt. Each upgrade carries six items, and a reviewer should be able to answer every question without opening a terminal.

Together they form a package upgrade audit trail that survives staff changes and audit cycles. Notice that the registry check sits next to the test results.

The first confirms the package is real, while the second confirms your application still behaves.

How to Build an Upgrade Evidence Record Step by Step

Reliable ai agent package upgrade evidence starts in the pipeline, so the pipeline below treats evidence as a build artifact. If the file is missing or incomplete, the merge fails.

Capture the dependency diff before and after

Snapshot the lockfile before the agent runs, then diff it afterward. Record every direct and transitive change, not only the package the agent targeted.

Next, confirm each new version exists in the registry, since models can name releases that were never published. A simple lookup such as npm view handles this for npm packages, and the result belongs in the record.

Store the advisory ID that triggered the change as well, so the reason for the upgrade travels with the code. Repeat this for every ecosystem in the repository, because mixed stacks hide gaps.

Attach regression testing results to the change

Run automated dependency upgrade testing against the new dependency tree and store the report with the change ID.

Regression testing should cover the code paths that import the upgraded package, not just the overall pass rate.

If any test fails, the agent either repairs the code or abandons the upgrade, and the record should show which happened. Keep the report as a build artifact so auditors can open it months later. No passing tests means no evidence, and no evidence means no merge.

A minimal evidence record looks like this:

{
  "change_id": "upg-0042",
  "package": "lodash",
  "ecosystem": "npm",
  "from": "4.17.15",
  "to": "4.17.21",
  "advisory_ids": ["CVE-2021-23337"],
  "transitive_changes": 0,
  "registry_verified": true,
  "tests": { "suite": "regression", "passed": 187, "failed": 0 },
  "approval": { "tier": "patch", "approved_by": "reviewer@example.com" },
  "rollback_ref": "git:9f3c2ab"
}

A CI gate can then fail closed:

- name: Verify upgrade evidence
  run: |
    npm view "lodash@$NEW_VERSION" version
    jq -e '.registry_verified == true and .tests.failed == 0 and .rollback_ref != null' "evidence/$CHANGE_ID.json"

Where Should Human Approval Sit in Safe Package Patching?

Not every upgrade deserves the same scrutiny. A practical human approval workflow ties review depth to the version change. Patch releases with complete evidence can auto-merge to staging after a spot check. Minor releases need one reviewer who reads the evidence pack. Major releases get a full review and a tested rollback plan.

Tool comparisons such as LibX vs Snyk vs Dependabot show that scanners handle detection well. Yet dependency security only improves when the fix is also tested and recorded.

Automated vulnerability remediation closes that loop by upgrading the package, generating the code change, testing it, and handing the reviewer an evidence pack.

As a result, the reviewer's job shifts from hunting for facts to approving them.

Package Upgrade Evidence Checklist for Engineering Teams

Use this checklist to judge whether your ai agent package upgrade evidence is strong enough before an agent merges anything.

Each item maps to a field in the evidence record, so the checklist doubles as a review template.

Teams that adopt even four of these items gain a defensible package upgrade audit trail for the next software supply chain security review.

  • Lockfile diff stored, including transitive dependencies.
  • Advisory ID linked to the reason for the change.
  • Registry lookup confirms the exact version exists.
  • Regression tests run and attached as an artifact.
  • Approval tier matches the version change.
  • Rollback reference points to a tested commit.
  • Evidence file required by the CI gate, with the build failing when it is missing.

Verified Upgrades Beat Fast Upgrades

Agents will keep proposing upgrades, and the teams that benefit most will be the ones that demand proof with every change.

Xccelera builds an AI security dependency upgrader and vulnerability auto-resolver. It finds vulnerable and outdated dependencies, upgrades them, remediates the affected code, and tests each fix before it ships.

Every scan, upgrade, and fix is recorded as evidence, and human approval stays in the loop where your policies require it. That combination turns agent speed into something engineering leaders can trust and auditors can verify.

If your backlog of security upgrades keeps growing faster than your review capacity, start by asking what evidence each patch leaves behind.

event_model_payload.headline: A practical portrait review workflow and crop-boundary check
event_model_payload.summary:
A profile photo has a small job: help another person recognize you and get a sense of how you present yourself. That can be harder than it sounds. A picture that looks appealing at full size may be unreadable on a phone, while a technically sharp image may feel too formal for the setting. Instead of searching for one perfect portrait, build a small set of honest, varied images and review them together.

AI Dating Photo Generator is a browser-based tool that creates dating profile portraits from your own photos, lets you choose a scene, and offers a way to review or refine results. If you decide to explore the ai dating profile photo generator, treat generated images as options to evaluate rather than as proof of what you look like in every situation. I am associated with the project, and this guide was drafted with AI assistance. Examples are hypothetical, and it does not claim independent product testing or guaranteed results.

Start with recognition, not decoration

Before changing a background or choosing an outfit, decide what a viewer should be able to recognize. A clear view of your face, an expression that feels natural, and a recent appearance are more important than a dramatic location. A useful first image should still make sense at the small size at which most people will encounter it.

Compare a candidate with a recent, unedited photograph. Check features that matter for recognition, including the shape of your face, hairstyle, facial hair, and any distinctive marks you normally show. Lighting and a different camera angle can change how someone looks, but a generated image should not make a meeting in person feel like a surprise. If you would need to explain that the picture represents an old hairstyle or a substantially different appearance, choose a more current alternative.

Gather a useful source set

When selecting input images, use photographs you have permission to upload and share. Prefer images of yourself over pictures containing other people. A varied source set can include a straight-on portrait, a gentle three-quarter angle, and a picture in even daylight. Avoid relying entirely on images with heavy filters, deep shadows, face coverings, or very low resolution.

More files are not automatically better. Review each photo for focus, current appearance, and whether your face is large enough to distinguish. Set aside any image whose ownership or consent is uncertain. If a group photograph is your only option, consider taking a fresh individual picture instead of uploading other people’s faces unnecessarily.

Keep the original files in a private location. Before using any external service, read its current terms and privacy information, including what it says about uploads, retention, deletion, and permitted uses. Do not assume that a file disappears immediately after you close a browser tab. If the available information does not meet your comfort level, use an offline photo or another method instead.

Choose a setting that supports the subject

A background should add context without competing with your face. A simple outdoor scene, an uncluttered room, or a neutral wall can be easier to read than a busy street full of signs and strangers. Think about the mood you want to convey: relaxed, approachable, creative, or active. A setting can suggest a mood without making a factual claim about your occupation or lifestyle.

Review the boundaries where hair, clothing, and shoulders meet the background. Generated portraits may contain odd edges, inconsistent shadows, or details that look plausible at a glance but not on inspection. Look at hands, jewelry, glasses, fabric patterns, and objects close to the body. If a feature looks wrong, refine or discard the image rather than hoping nobody notices.

A convincing scene is not necessarily an accurate one. Avoid selecting a location that implies you visited a place or participated in an activity if you did not. A neutral illustrative setting is easier to interpret honestly than a picture that appears to document a specific trip or event. When in doubt, pair a generated portrait with real, recent photographs that show your everyday appearance.

Check light, color, and framing

Good lighting reveals the face without flattening every detail. Look for a balance between visible eyes, natural skin tones, and enough contrast to separate the subject from the background. Very bright highlights can erase detail, while strong backlighting can turn a face into a silhouette. Color should feel consistent across the image; a warm face against an implausibly cool shadow may be distracting.

Test the crop before deciding. Leave some space around the head and shoulders so the image can survive different app layouts. A square preview may crop differently from a tall profile card. Keep important facial features away from the extreme edges, and verify that hair or the top of the head is not unintentionally cut off.

Look at the image on both a larger display and a phone. At a large size, inspect artifacts. At a small size, ask whether the expression is readable and whether the subject stands out from the background. A photo can pass one test and fail the other. Keep only images that work in the context in which they will be seen.

Build variety across a set

A profile usually benefits from more than several nearly identical close-ups. Consider a clear primary portrait, a different angle or setting, and a candid or activity image that reflects something you actually enjoy. Each picture should contribute information rather than repeat the same expression in a slightly different crop.

Variety does not mean presenting incompatible versions of yourself. A collection that switches dramatically between ages, hair colors, body shapes, or styles can undermine recognition. Place images side by side and ask whether someone meeting you would reasonably identify the same person in all of them. Keep your real appearance as the reference point.

If an activity photo includes friends, ask for their permission before publishing it. Avoid showing documents, address details, workplace identifiers, vehicle plates, or other information you do not intend to disclose. You can crop a photograph to reduce incidental exposure, but check that the resulting image still makes sense and does not misleadingly change the context.

Use a short review checklist

A repeatable checklist is more useful than endlessly comparing minor differences. For each candidate, answer the following questions:

  1. Is the picture recent enough to represent my current appearance?
  2. Can a viewer see my face clearly at the expected display size?
  3. Are the eyes, hands, accessories, and background free of distracting artifacts?
  4. Does the image avoid implying an experience, place, or identity that is not mine?
  5. Do I have permission to use every visible person’s image and the underlying photograph?
  6. Does this picture add something distinct to the rest of the set?
  7. Am I comfortable with the platform receiving and displaying the image?

If an answer is no, decide whether a simple crop or a different candidate addresses the problem. If not, leave it out. This process is not a score for attractiveness; it is a way to reduce confusion, privacy risks, and avoidable visual distractions.

Get feedback without outsourcing the decision

A trusted friend can notice a misleading crop or an expression that does not look like you. Give them a narrow question, such as whether they would recognize you from the first image or which of two crops is clearer on a phone. Broad requests for a rating can produce conflicting opinions without helping you make a practical choice.

Remember that friends may have different preferences from the people you hope to meet. Treat their feedback as information, not a rule. You remain responsible for selecting pictures that feel comfortable, accurate, and consistent with the expectations of the app you use. Check that app’s rules on altered or generated images before uploading.

A small crop-metadata check

A developer building an internal review workflow can start by validating declared crop coordinates before recording a review. The function below only checks integer bounds against supplied dimensions. It does not open a file, identify a person, verify consent, inspect image metadata, or detect manipulated content. Coordinates use a top-left origin and a half-open rectangle: a crop ending exactly at the right or bottom edge is allowed. This is a standalone teaching example, not a feature of the product mentioned above.

def check_crop(width, height, left, top, crop_width, crop_height):
    values = (width, height, left, top, crop_width, crop_height)
    if any(type(value) is not int for value in values):
        return False
    if width <= 0 or height <= 0 or left < 0 or top < 0:
        return False
    if crop_width <= 0 or crop_height <= 0:
        return False
    return left + crop_width <= width and top + crop_height <= height

I ran six local synthetic cases for full-frame and edge-aligned crops, overflow, negative offsets, zero size, and a Boolean argument. Those cases establish only that this function returns the expected Boolean for the supplied values; they are not tests of an image editor or service. A production pipeline would also need to define orientation, units, metadata provenance, error handling, and data retention before using such a check. Keep consent records separate and do not log private photographs just to test a rectangle.

For example, (800, 600, 10, 20, 790, 580) is within bounds, while increasing the crop width to 791 extends one pixel beyond the declared right edge. The function deliberately rejects Boolean values even though Python treats bool as a subclass of int; this is a policy choice for this example rather than a universal validation rule. If an application accepts other numeric types or rotated coordinates, specify those rules explicitly and test them separately.

Maintain the profile over time

Revisit your pictures when your appearance or circumstances change. A new haircut, glasses, or a different everyday style may make an older image less useful as a primary portrait. You do not need to replace every picture at once; review the set periodically and swap out anything that no longer feels representative.

Keep a small private shortlist of approved images and their original sources. This makes it easier to update a profile without repeating the entire selection process. Remove files you no longer want to retain, and use any available deletion controls on services where you uploaded them. The result should be a profile that is easy to recognize, considerate of other people’s privacy, and comfortable for you to maintain.

event_model_payload.headline: What Does a Production Incident Actually Cost? A Practical Way to Calculate It
event_model_payload.summary:
A production incident is rarely just a few minutes of downtime.

An API starts failing. An alert fires. Engineers join a Slack channel, open dashboards, inspect logs, follow traces, check recent deployments and start trying to understand what changed.

Eventually, the issue gets resolved.

But how much did that incident actually cost?

Most engineering teams track uptime, error rates and Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR). Far fewer calculate the engineering time consumed by incidents and translate it into a financial number.

That number can make a big difference when prioritizing reliability improvements.

1. Start with the engineering cost

The easiest place to start is the time engineers spend investigating and resolving incidents.

You need four inputs:

  • Number of incidents per month
  • Average resolution time per incident
  • Average number of engineers involved
  • Loaded hourly cost per engineer

The formula is:

Monthly engineering incident cost =

Incidents per month × Hours per incident × Engineers involved × Cost per engineer-hour

Let's use an example.

Assume an engineering team experiences:

Input Value
Incidents per month 8
Average resolution time 3 hours
Engineers involved 3
Loaded engineer-hour cost $75

The calculation:

8 × 3 × 3 × $75 = $5,400/month

That's $64,800 annually in engineering time.

This is not necessarily what the company loses in revenue. It is the estimated cost of engineering capacity spent handling production incidents.

2. Engineering time is only one part of the cost

A complete incident-cost analysis should distinguish between several categories.

Engineering time

The direct cost of engineers investigating, mitigating, fixing and validating an incident.

Customer impact

Customers may experience failed requests, interrupted workflows, degraded performance or loss of access to important features.

Revenue impact

For transaction-heavy products, failed payments, abandoned checkouts and interrupted business workflows can have measurable financial consequences.

Support and recovery

Support teams may spend additional time responding to tickets, communicating with customers and processing service credits or refunds.

Opportunity cost

Time spent repeatedly investigating incidents is time engineers cannot spend building features, improving architecture or addressing technical debt.

These costs should be calculated separately wherever possible. Otherwise, it's easy to count the same impact twice.

3. Why investigation time matters

MTTR is often discussed as one number, but the incident lifecycle has several stages:

  1. Detection – How long does it take to recognize the problem?
  2. Investigation – How long does it take to understand the cause?
  3. Remediation – How long does it take to implement and validate the fix?

A significant part of engineering effort can disappear into investigation.

Why?

Because information is fragmented.

An engineer might have to move between an error tracker, a log explorer, a distributed tracing system, a session replay tool and Git history.

They then manually correlate timestamps, trace IDs, affected requests and recent deployments.

The problem isn't always a lack of telemetry. It's the time required to connect the available evidence.

4. How to reduce the cost

Reducing incident cost doesn't necessarily mean preventing every failure. It also means making failures faster to understand and resolve.

Some practical improvements:

Correlate observability signals.

Make it possible to move from an error to its relevant logs, traces and request context without manually searching across systems.

Connect incidents to deployments and code changes.

Understanding what changed recently can help narrow down the investigation.

Improve incident context.

Group recurring errors, identify affected services and make relevant evidence available from the beginning.

Reduce repetitive investigation.

Use automation and AI-assisted analysis to gather evidence and suggest likely root causes.

Keep remediation reviewable.

Suggested fixes should be inspectable by engineers before they are merged or deployed.

The objective is to reduce time spent reconstructing what happened.

5. Calculate your own incident cost

Start with your actual incident frequency, average resolution time, team size and loaded engineering cost.

Don't assume every incident has the same financial impact. Start with the measurable engineering component and add customer or revenue impact separately when reliable data is available.

Modulis has an incident cost calculator that uses these four inputs.

For example, its default scenario of 8 incidents per month, 3 hours per incident, 3 engineers and $75 per engineer-hour gives an estimated $5,400 monthly engineering cost.

The estimate does not include lost revenue or customer churn.

Final thought

Production reliability is often presented as a technical investment.

But incidents also consume an economic resource: engineering capacity.

When a team repeatedly spends hours finding the same kinds of problems, the cost accumulates quietly.

Measuring that cost gives engineering leaders a better way to prioritize observability, debugging improvements and incident-response automation.

The goal isn't just fewer production incidents. It's less engineering time lost when they happen.

Disclosure: I work with Modulis, an AI-powered engineering intelligence platform that connects production errors with logs, traces, session context and Git changes to support faster incident investigation.

Original article: https://modulis.ai/blog/cost-of-a-production-incident/

event_model_payload.headline: I ranked 7 Android cloud services by one question: will the device still be the same device in three months?
event_model_payload.summary:
Disclosure first: I work with DuoPlus, on the growth side. So yes, it's on this list, and yes, it's near the top. I'll tell you where it falls short too, and I checked every other product's claims against its own website this week instead of going from memory.

Why this list exists: most cloud phone and device cloud roundups rank by "how many devices" or "how cheap." That's not what breaks for the teams I talk to. They're small QA shops, two-person dev teams, agencies looking after a dozen client apps. The question that actually costs them time is boring: when I open this Android environment next month, is it still logged in, still configured, still mine? Or am I starting from zero again?

So that's the ranking criterion. Fit for small dev/QA teams and agencies that need stable, isolated Android environments that last. Not gaming, and not one-off test runs (though some tools below are great at those).

1. DuoPlus

https://www.duoplus.net/share/market

DuoPlus gives you real ARM Android cloud phones, on Android 10, 11, 12 and 15. Each one is an isolated, independent device environment with its own data and login state, and it stays a fixed, long-term environment, so the phone you set up for a client in March is the same phone in June.

The part agencies care about is handover. You can share a device with a teammate in one click and they pick it up already logged in. When someone goes on leave, nobody spends an afternoon re-entering passwords and waiting on 2FA codes from the client.

Other things I actually use: per-device proxy and region settings, local environments in 150+ countries/regions, bulk install/uninstall/launch of apps across a batch of devices, root, and an API. Billing is per-minute. There are browser, desktop and mobile clients. There are also cloud numbers, which I use for testing our own app's signup and OTP flows without passing someone's personal SIM around the office.

Fits: agencies holding client app accounts long-term, small QA teams that want persistent devices they can hand to each other, anyone doing regional checks.

Drawbacks, honestly: it's Android only, so if your release checklist includes iOS you need a second tool. And it's not a test-automation grid with built-in reporting. If what you want is "upload APK, run Espresso suite on 40 device models, get a video per failure," the next three entries do that better.

2. Genymotion SaaS

https://www.genymotion.com/

Genymotion is the one I'd point a pure dev team at. Their site lists Genymotion SaaS ("optimized for team work, CI/CD and agentic AI"), a PaaS version on AWS, Alibaba, GCP and Azure, and Genymotion Desktop for PC and Mac. Integrations they name: Detox, GitHub Actions, CircleCI, Bitrise, Jenkins.

These are Android virtual devices built to be spun up from a pipeline, and they also pitch browser-based support and demo use.

Fits: dev teams that want Android devices wired into CI, plus support teams that need to reproduce a customer's bug from a browser tab.

Less ideal when: you need one specific device to hold a client's logged-in state for months and get passed between people. That's not what a CI emulator is shaped for.

3. AWS Device Farm

https://aws.amazon.com/device-farm/

Real physical phones and tablets hosted by AWS. You can run automated tests (Appium, Espresso, Calabash, or their built-in suite with no scripting), do manual remote sessions, and get videos, logs and performance data back. You can set location, language and network conditions.

The interesting bit for this list: their private device lab option gives you iOS and Android devices for your exclusive use and, per their page, lets you persist settings between sessions. That gets much closer to "my device stays my device."

Fits: teams already on AWS who need real hardware coverage, including iOS, hooked into Jenkins or Android Studio.

Less ideal when: you're a five-person agency without anyone who wants to own AWS config. And the shared pool is built for test runs, not long-lived logged-in accounts.

4. BrowserStack App Live

https://www.browserstack.com/app-live

BrowserStack says 30,000+ real iOS and Android devices. You can upload dev APK/AAB/IPA builds or install production apps from the stores, debug with logs and crash reports, and test on up to four devices at once. Their Custom Device Lab adds exclusive device access with options like app persistence and SIM binding.

Fits: QA teams who need wide model coverage across iOS and Android, fast.

Less ideal when: the job is keeping a handful of long-term environments for ongoing client work. You'd be paying for breadth you don't use, and persistence lives in the custom lab tier, not the default.

5. GeeLark

https://www.geelark.com/

GeeLark offers ARM-based cloud phones for Android apps plus multi-account browser profiles for web, both in one workspace. Team features are solid on paper: team members can be added free, roles and permissions, operation logs, groups/tags/notes for organising profiles. They also mention MCP so you can connect an AI agent to manage the phones and profiles, and they list GPS/SIM simulation across 150+ countries.

Fits: social and marketing teams who want phones and browser profiles managed side by side, with scheduling and AI content tools on top.

Less ideal when: you're a dev/QA team. A big chunk of the product is about posting, content generation and engagement automation, which you'll pay attention to (and maybe pay for) without needing.

6. VMOSCloud

https://www.vmoscloud.com/

VMOSCloud runs Android cloud phones with a strong lean toward social media automation: an AI workflow feature that turns text prompts into actions, a Synchronizer that mirrors one device's actions across many, and a Team Hub with roles and permissions. Their homepage lists Google Play Integrity, SafetyNet and Widevine L1. "App Test" appears in their industry list, though most of the page is about growing social accounts.

Fits: operators running many social accounts who want synchronized control.

Less ideal when: you want a dev-first tool. I'd also read their data policy closely if you plan long-term use: their FAQ says data is automatically deleted once the subscription ends, which is fine, just plan exports around it.

7. Redfinger

https://www.cloudemulator.net/

One of the older names. Redfinger has Android, Windows, web and iOS access, a Redfinger for Business line, and servers in the US, Taiwan and Singapore. Their site mentions device simulation for testing alongside gaming and cross-border marketing.

Fits: individuals and small teams who want a simple cloud Android device on several platforms.

Less ideal when: you need team handover and region coverage beyond those three server locations.

Honourable mentions: LDCloud and UgPhone

Both are positioned mainly for gaming. LDCloud (https://www.ldcloud.net/) leads with 24/7 AFK play, multi-instance and sync operation. UgPhone (https://www.ugphone.com/) lists tiers on Android 10, 12 and 13 with servers in places like Hong Kong, Germany, Japan, the USA and Singapore. For client QA work, I wouldn't start here.

How I'd actually choose

If I'm honest, the decision usually comes down to one question. Is the device disposable (run tests, throw away) or durable (holds state, gets handed between people for months)?

Disposable: Genymotion, AWS Device Farm, BrowserStack. Pick by whether you need iOS and how much CI you already have.

Durable: that's where DuoPlus, GeeLark, VMOSCloud and Redfinger sit, and I'd rank them by how painless handover and regional setup are for a non-engineer on your team. That's why DuoPlus is first on my list.

Plenty of teams end up with one of each. What hurts is using a disposable tool for durable work and wondering why everyone keeps logging in again.

If you've ranked these differently for your own team, I'd like to hear why in the comments, especially if you run client work on BrowserStack's custom lab.

event_model_payload.headline: Normalizing U.S. Company Names Before You Match Them
event_model_payload.summary:
Company names from different sources rarely agree character for character. "The Acme Group, L.L.C.", "ACME GROUP LLC" and "Acme Group" could be one entity or three. A normalized name gives you a stable comparison key, as long as you remember what the key discards.

What usually needs cleaning

Case and spacing. Pick one case, trim the ends, and collapse repeated spaces.

Punctuation. Periods, commas, and quotes are noise. Curly and straight apostrophes should end up identical, or be removed. An ampersand is safest as the word "and."

Accents. "Peña" and "Pena" should compare equal. Unicode normalization followed by an ASCII fold handles the common cases.

Legal endings. LLC and L.L.C., Inc. and Incorporated, Corp. and Corporation, Co. and Company, Ltd. and Limited, plus LP, LLP, and PLLC. Map the spellings to one short form and move it out of the name into a field of its own. It tells you the entity type, and "Acme Inc" and "Acme LLC" can be two separate legal entities.

A leading "The". Sources disagree on whether to keep it, so the key should not depend on it.

Trade names. A string like "Acme Group LLC dba Bright Path" holds two names. Split on dba, d/b/a, aka, or fka and keep both parts, labeled. Matching on the trade name alone can attach a record to the wrong legal entity.

Same name, different state

Identical names across states are common, because each state checks name availability only against its own registry. A key that ignores the state will merge strangers. Put the state, or the registry the record came from, into the key, and treat a cross-state match as a lead to confirm with other fields.

A teaching example

This is a teaching example, not production code. It returns the state, the core name, the entity-type ending, and any trade name found after dba, aka, or fka.

import re
import unicodedata
ENDINGS = {"INCORPORATED": "INC", "CORPORATION": "CORP", "COMPANY": "CO", "LIMITED": "LTD"}
ENDINGS.update({e: e for e in ("LLC", "INC", "CORP", "CO", "LTD", "LP", "LLP", "PLLC")})
ALIAS = re.compile(r"\b(?:D[./]?B[./]?A|A[./]?K[./]?A|F[./]?K[./]?A)\b\.?", re.I)

def words(text):
    text = unicodedata.normalize("NFKD", text).encode("ascii", "ignore").decode()
    text = text.upper().replace("&", " AND ").replace(".", "").replace("'", "")
    return re.findall(r"[A-Z0-9]+", text)

def company_key(raw, state):
    legal, *alias = ALIAS.split(raw, maxsplit=1)
    core = words(legal)
    ending = ENDINGS.get(core[-1], "") if core else ""
    while core and core[-1] in ENDINGS:
        core.pop()
    core = core[1:] if core[:1] == ["THE"] else core
    return state.upper(), " ".join(core), ending, " ".join(words("".join(alias)))

Two calls show the behavior, including an edge case:

company_key("The Acme Group, L.L.C. d/b/a Bright Path", "tx")
# ('TX', 'ACME GROUP', 'LLC', 'BRIGHT PATH')
company_key("Peña & Co.", "or")
# ('OR', 'PENA AND', 'CO', '')

The second result leaves a dangling AND, because "& Co." is really part of how that firm writes its name. Rules like these are blunt, and every ruleset produces cases like this one.

Order matters as well. Split off the trade name before removing punctuation, or "d/b/a" falls apart into loose letters that look like part of the name.

To keep the rules honest, build a small table of pairs you know are the same entity and pairs you know are not, and rerun it whenever you change a rule. A fix for one case often breaks another.

What the key throws away

Normalization is lossy on purpose. Store the raw name next to the key, keep the ending and the trade name as separate fields, and never treat an equal key as proof of identity. Confirm with something the name cannot fake: a registry ID, a formation date, or a principal address.

This post was drafted with the help of AI tools.

event_model_payload.headline: BIGF v2.4 Lab: Enforcing Deterministic AI Agent Boundaries with OPA, Rego & RFC 8785
event_model_payload.summary:
Welcome to the **VITI Labs* hands-on guide.*

System prompts are not security boundaries. If an autonomous AI agent is allowed to delegate tasks to sub-agents (Agent-to-Agent / A2A) or execute financial and infrastructure mutations, governance must happen outside the LLM at a deterministic runtime gate.

In this lab, you will build and test a complete Business Impact Governance Framework (BIGF v2.4) policy gate using Open Policy Agent (OPA), Rego, and RFC 8785 JSON Canonicalization (JCS).

Architecture: How the Gate Works

Every A2A delegation or actuation request passes through three deterministic stages before execution:

  1. Ingress Sanitization (BIGF-DCS): Raw JSON floats (IEEE 754) are rejected immediately (422 Unprocessable). All currency and threshold values must be encoded as 10-4 fixed-point strings ("2450.5000").
  2. Cryptographic Lineage (RFC 8785 JCS + SHA-256): The child contract must carry the exact SHA-256 hash of its canonicalized parent contract (parent_jcs_sha256) to prevent privilege injection or chain tampering.
  3. Monotonic Narrowing (B × S × T): A child agent can never expand its parent's authority:
    • B-Axis (Business Impact): child.max_exposure_fp4 <= parent.max_exposure_fp4 and currencies must match.
    • S-Axis (Situational State / BIII): child.min_biii_fp4 >= parent.min_biii_fp4 (integrity requirements can only tighten), and live telemetry BIII must meet the threshold.
    • T-Axis (Time & Telemetry): child.max_ttl_sec <= parent.max_ttl_sec, and the contract must fall strictly within the parent's [iat, exp] window.

Step 1: Project Structure

Create a directory bigf-opa-lab with four files:

bigf-opa-lab/
├── jcs_hash.py        # RFC 8785 canonicalizer & SHA-256 lineage generator
├── bigf_gate.rego     # Deterministic BIGF v2.4 OPA policy
├── bigf_gate_test.rego# Runnable OPA unit test suite (200 OK, 403 Halt, 422 Reject)
└── input_valid.json   # Sample A2A parent-to-child delegation payload

Step 2: RFC 8785 Canonicalizer (jcs_hash.py)

Before OPA evaluates a delegation chain, the orchestrator or ingress proxy canonicalizes the parent contract per RFC 8785 (sorted keys, zero insignificant whitespace, UTF-8) and verifies parent_jcs_sha256.

import hashlib
import json

def canonicalize_jcs(obj: dict) -> bytes:
    """RFC 8785 deterministic JSON canonicalization (UTF-8)."""
    return json.dumps(
        obj,
        sort_keys=True,
        separators=(",", ":"),
        ensure_ascii=False
    ).encode("utf-8")

def compute_jcs_sha256(obj: dict) -> str:
    """Computes the deterministic SHA-256 lineage hash."""
    return hashlib.sha256(canonicalize_jcs(obj)).hexdigest()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    parent_contract = {
        "bigf_version": "2.4.0",
        "contract_id": "a2a-parent-9f8e7d6c",
        "delegation_depth": 1,
        "exp": 1794509100,
        "iat": 1794508800,
        "invariants": {
            "b_axis": {
                "currency": "EUR",
                "max_exposure_fp4": "10000.0000",
                "regulatory_anchor": ["DORA", "NIS2"]
            },
            "s_axis": {
                "allowed_transitions": ["INVOICE_VERIFY", "SETTLEMENT_EXECUTE"],
                "min_biii_fp4": "0.8000"
            },
            "t_axis": {
                "max_ttl_sec": 300
            }
        },
        "iss": "ed25519:3b6a27bcceb6a42d62a3a8d02a6f0d73653215771de243a63ac048a18b59da29",
        "parent_jcs_sha256": None,
        "sub": "agent:procurement-eu-01"
    }
    print("parent_jcs_sha256:", compute_jcs_sha256(parent_contract))

Step 3: The Deterministic Rego Gate (bigf_gate.rego)

Save this policy as bigf_gate.rego. Notice how Rego enforces fail-closed physics: if any violation fires, allow defaults to false and the gate emits a structured 403 HARD HALT or 422 REJECTED decision record.

package bigf.v2_4.gate

import rego.v1

# Fail-closed default
default allow := false

# 1. BIGF-DCS Ingress Guard: Reject any raw JSON floating-point numbers
dcs_float_violations contains msg if {
    some path, val in walk(input)
    is_number(val)
    # In JSON/Rego, non-integers (e.g., 2450.5) fail exact integer division check
    round(val) != val
    msg := sprintf("422 BIGF-DCS Type Violation: IEEE 754 float detected at %v", [path])
}

# Fixed-point string parser (10^-4 scaling via to_number on validated strings)
parse_fp4(str) := num if {
    is_string(str)
    regex.match(`^\d+\.\d{4}$`, str)
    num := to_number(str)
}

# 2. Cryptographic Lineage & Depth Checks
violations contains "CRYPTO_AXIS: parent_jcs_sha256 mismatch" if {
    input.child.parent_jcs_sha256 != input.computed_parent_jcs_sha256
}

violations contains "CRYPTO_AXIS: Invalid delegation depth increment" if {
    input.child.delegation_depth != input.parent.delegation_depth + 1
}

# 3. B-Axis (Business Impact Monotonic Narrowing)
violations contains "B_AXIS: Currency mismatch between parent and child" if {
    input.child.invariants.b_axis.currency != input.parent.invariants.b_axis.currency
}

violations contains "B_AXIS: Child exposure exceeds parent ceiling" if {
    child_exp := parse_fp4(input.child.invariants.b_axis.max_exposure_fp4)
    parent_exp := parse_fp4(input.parent.invariants.b_axis.max_exposure_fp4)
    child_exp > parent_exp
}

violations contains "B_AXIS: Requested action amount exceeds child ceiling" if {
    req_amt := parse_fp4(input.request.amount_fp4)
    child_exp := parse_fp4(input.child.invariants.b_axis.max_exposure_fp4)
    req_amt > child_exp
}

# 4. S-Axis (Situational Integrity & Transition Subset)
violations contains "S_AXIS: Child weakened min_biii_fp4 requirement" if {
    child_biii := parse_fp4(input.child.invariants.s_axis.min_biii_fp4)
    parent_biii := parse_fp4(input.parent.invariants.s_axis.min_biii_fp4)
    child_biii < parent_biii
}

violations contains "S_AXIS: Live telemetry BIII below required threshold" if {
    live_biii := parse_fp4(input.telemetry.live_biii_fp4)
    req_biii := parse_fp4(input.child.invariants.s_axis.min_biii_fp4)
    live_biii < req_biii
}

violations contains "S_AXIS: Requested transition not permitted by child contract" if {
    not input.request.transition in input.child.invariants.s_axis.allowed_transitions
}

violations contains "S_AXIS: Child transitions exceed parent scope" if {
    some t in input.child.invariants.s_axis.allowed_transitions
    not t in input.parent.invariants.s_axis.allowed_transitions
}

# 5. T-Axis (Time Window & TTL Bounds)
violations contains "T_AXIS: Child TTL exceeds parent max_ttl_sec" if {
    input.child.invariants.t_axis.max_ttl_sec > input.parent.invariants.t_axis.max_ttl_sec
}

violations contains "T_AXIS: Child validity window escapes parent [iat, exp]" if {
    input.child.iat < input.parent.iat
}

violations contains "T_AXIS: Child expiration exceeds parent expiration" if {
    input.child.exp > input.parent.exp
}

violations contains "T_AXIS: Contract expired at evaluation timestamp" if {
    input.telemetry.now_utc > input.child.exp
}

# Final Deterministic Gate Decision
allow if {
    count(dcs_float_violations) == 0
    count(violations) == 0
}

# Canonical Decision Record (CDR) Output
decision := {
    "status": "422 UNPROCESSABLE",
    "state": "INGRESS_SCHEMA_VIOLATION",
    "privileges_propagated": 0,
    "violations": dcs_float_violations,
} if {
    count(dcs_float_violations) > 0
} else := {
    "status": "403 HARD HALT",
    "state": "UNVERIFIED_CRITICAL_STATE",
    "privileges_propagated": 0,
    "violations": violations,
} if {
    count(violations) > 0
} else := {
    "status": "200 OK",
    "state": "VERIFIED_EXECUTION",
    "approved_amount_fp4": input.request.amount_fp4,
    "biii_fp4": input.telemetry.live_biii_fp4,
    "lineage_sha256": input.child.parent_jcs_sha256,
}

Step 4: Runnable OPA Unit Tests (bigf_gate_test.rego)

Save this test suite alongside bigf_gate.rego to verify all three enforcement outcomes (200 OK, 403 HARD HALT, and 422 UNPROCESSABLE):

package bigf.v2_4.gate_test

import data.bigf.v2_4.gate
import rego.v1

base_input := {
    "computed_parent_jcs_sha256": "7d1a54127b222502f5b79b5fb0803061152a44f92b37e23c6527baf665d4da9a",
    "parent": {
        "delegation_depth": 1,
        "iat": 1794508800,
        "exp": 1794509100,
        "invariants": {
            "b_axis": {"currency": "EUR", "max_exposure_fp4": "10000.0000"},
            "s_axis": {
                "allowed_transitions": ["INVOICE_VERIFY", "SETTLEMENT_EXECUTE"],
                "min_biii_fp4": "0.8000"
            },
            "t_axis": {"max_ttl_sec": 300}
        }
    },
    "child": {
        "delegation_depth": 2,
        "iat": 1794508810,
        "exp": 1794508920,
        "parent_jcs_sha256": "7d1a54127b222502f5b79b5fb0803061152a44f92b37e23c6527baf665d4da9a",
        "invariants": {
            "b_axis": {"currency": "EUR", "max_exposure_fp4": "2450.5000"},
            "s_axis": {
                "allowed_transitions": ["SETTLEMENT_EXECUTE"],
                "min_biii_fp4": "0.8500"
            },
            "t_axis": {"max_ttl_sec": 110}
        }
    },
    "request": {
        "transition": "SETTLEMENT_EXECUTE",
        "amount_fp4": "2450.5000"
    },
    "telemetry": {
        "live_biii_fp4": "0.9100",
        "now_utc": 1794508850
    }
}

# Test 1: Valid attenuated delegation -> 200 OK
test_valid_monotonic_delegation if {
    gate.allow with input as base_input
    gate.decision.status == "200 OK" with input as base_input
}

# Test 2: Privilege escalation (child tries to raise exposure above parent) -> 403 HARD HALT
test_reject_exposure_escalation if {
    bad := json.patch(base_input, [{"op": "replace", "path": "/child/invariants/b_axis/max_exposure_fp4", "value": "15000.0000"}])
    not gate.allow with input as bad
    gate.decision.status == "403 HARD HALT" with input as bad
}

# Test 3: Telemetry degradation (live BIII drops below 0.8500) -> 403 HARD HALT
test_reject_low_biii if {
    degraded := json.patch(base_input, [{"op": "replace", "path": "/telemetry/live_biii_fp4", "value": "0.7900"}])
    not gate.allow with input as degraded
    gate.decision.status == "403 HARD HALT" with input as degraded
}

# Test 4: IEEE 754 float injected into payload -> 422 UNPROCESSABLE
test_reject_ieee754_float if {
    float_payload := json.patch(base_input, [{"op": "replace", "path": "/request/amount_fp4", "value": 2450.5}])
    not gate.allow with input as float_payload
    gate.decision.status == "422 UNPROCESSABLE" with input as float_payload
}

Step 5: Run It in 10 Seconds

Install the OPA binary (or run via Docker) and execute the test suite:

opa test . -v

Expected output:

bigf_gate_test.rego:
data.bigf.v2_4.gate_test.test_valid_monotonic_delegation: PASS (1.2ms)
data.bigf.v2_4.gate_test.test_reject_exposure_escalation: PASS (0.8ms)
data.bigf.v2_4.gate_test.test_reject_low_biii: PASS (0.7ms)
data.bigf.v2_4.gate_test.test_reject_ieee754_float: PASS (0.9ms)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PASS: 4/4

Four deterministic checks executed in under 4 milliseconds—zero CAB meetings, zero floating-point drift, and cryptographic lineage enforced before a single byte hits production.

Explore the full BIGF v2.4 specification & open-access whitepapers:

Just google it: BIG framework Erkki Laine (available on Zenodo & ORCID under CC BY-NC 4.0) ✌️

event_model_payload.headline: Turn PDFs into Clean Markdown for ChatGPT and RAG (Without Uploading Them)
event_model_payload.summary:
If you've ever pasted a PDF into ChatGPT or Claude and got an answer about the wrong section, the model probably wasn't the problem. The text was.

A PDF doesn't store "a heading", "a table" or "a paragraph". It stores pieces of text placed at positions on a page. When you copy that text out, you get whatever order the PDF happens to keep it in, and the structure is gone. For an LLM, and even more for a RAG pipeline, structure is half the information.

This post covers what goes wrong, what clean Markdown for AI should look like, and a short Python chunker that splits it for retrieval while keeping page numbers.

Disclosure: I built QuickCatPDF, the free converter I use in the examples. The format and the chunking code work with any converter that produces similar Markdown.

What breaks when you copy text out of a PDF

Copy and paste from a typical report and you'll usually see some of these:

  • Lines broken mid-sentence, because every visual line ends with a newline.
  • Two columns mixed together, line by line.
  • The page header and footer repeated on every page ("Annual Review 2026 · Page 7").
  • Tables flattened into a run of numbers with no idea which value belongs to which column.
  • Words split by hyphens at line ends ("docu- ment").
  • Links gone. In a PDF, a link's address isn't part of the text at all. It's stored separately as an annotation on top of the page, so plain copy-paste only gives you the visible words.

None of this stops a model from reading the text, but it makes it worse at finding the right part and at quoting numbers from tables correctly.

What "clean Markdown for an LLM" looks like

Markdown is a good middle ground: models read it naturally, it's compact, and it keeps the structure that matters.

---
title: "Annual Review 2026"
source: "annual-review.pdf"
pages: 4
---



# Annual Review 2026

## Introduction

Revenue grew in every quarter...

## Results by quarter

| Quarter | Revenue | Growth |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | 1.2M | 4% |
| Q2 | 1.4M | 17% |

A few details are worth copying, whatever tool you use:

  1. Front matter naming the source file and page count. When you paste several documents into one chat, the model knows which is which.
  2. Page markers as HTML comments (). Models read them, rendered Markdown hides them, and your RAG answers can cite a page.
  3. Real headings (#, ##, ###) instead of bold lines.
  4. Pipe tables, so every value stays in its row and column.
  5. No page furniture: page numbers and repeated headers and footers removed, hyphenated words joined, wrapped lines merged into single paragraphs.

Three questions people keep asking

"How do I keep headings when converting PDF to Markdown?"
Most converters detect headings from the text's size and weight. That works when the PDF's headings are visibly larger or bold. If a document's headings are the same size and weight as the body text, there's no signal to detect, and they come out as plain paragraphs. In that case, add the ## markers by hand for the main sections. It takes a minute and makes a big difference for chunking.

"How do I keep tables?"
Pick a converter that outputs pipe tables, then check one table against the original. Tables without lines (columns separated only by white space, like bank statements) are the hardest case for any tool.

"Why are my hyperlinks lost?"
Because of the annotation point above: the address isn't in the text layer. A converter has to read the link annotations and match them to the words underneath. Plain copy-paste and many text extractors skip that step.

Chunking for RAG without losing page numbers

Headings are natural chunk boundaries, and the page comments let every chunk carry the page it started on. Here's a small, dependency-free chunker:

import re

def chunk_markdown(md: str, max_chars: int = 4000):
    """Split Markdown on ## headings, keeping the page number each chunk starts on."""
    md = re.sub(r"\A---\n.*?\n---\n", "", md, flags=re.S)  # drop front matter
    page = 1
    chunks, current, heading = [], [], None

    def flush():
        text = "\n".join(current).strip()
        if text:
            chunks.append({"heading": heading, "page": start_page, "text": text})

    start_page = page
    for line in md.splitlines():
        m = re.match(r"", line)
        if m:
            page = int(m.group(1))
            if not "".join(current).strip():
                start_page = page
            continue
        if line.startswith("## ") or sum(len(l) for l in current) > max_chars:
            flush()
            current, start_page = [], page
            if line.startswith("## "):
                heading = line[3:].strip()
        current.append(line)
    flush()
    return chunks

Each chunk comes back as {"heading": "Results by quarter", "page": 1, "text": "..."}, ready to embed. Store heading and page as metadata, and your answers can say "see page 1, Results by quarter" instead of pointing at the whole document.

If you prefer page-sized chunks (useful for contracts and forms), split on the comments instead.

Watch your token budget

A rough rule for English is about 4 characters per token, fewer for other scripts. That's close enough to decide whether a document fits in one prompt or needs chunking. Treat it as an estimate, not an exact count.

Doing it without uploading the PDF

Many PDFs you'd want to ask an AI about are exactly the ones you shouldn't hand to random websites: contracts, financial reports, internal docs. You'll decide later where the text goes. The conversion step doesn't need to send it anywhere.

The converter I built, QuickCatPDF's PDF to Markdown for LLMs, runs in the browser:

  1. Drop in up to 20 PDFs.
  2. Keep Front matter and Page markers as comments ticked.
  3. Optionally limit the Pages.
  4. Click Convert to Markdown, then copy or download. It shows the character count and a token estimate.

In my test, a 4-page report converted in about half a second into 4.6 KB of Markdown. Scanned PDFs are read with OCR in the browser too. You can check that nothing is uploaded: load the page, turn on airplane mode, and convert.

For plain Markdown for GitHub, Obsidian or Notion (with bold, italics, links and optional images), there's a separate PDF to Markdown tool.

Quick checklist

  • Don't paste raw PDF text into an LLM when structure matters. Convert to Markdown first.
  • Keep front matter and page markers, and drop the headers and footers.
  • Check one heading and one table against the original.
  • Chunk on ## headings and keep the page number as metadata.
  • Estimate tokens at about 4 characters per token for English.

What's the worst PDF you've had to feed into an LLM? Tables, multi-column layouts, scans? I'm collecting hard cases.

event_model_payload.headline: Pi-hole on Kubernetes with PowerDNS and external-dns
event_model_payload.summary:
A home or office network needs two things from its DNS. Devices should
find the services that run in the network by name, such as
pihole.home.example. Ads and trackers should not resolve at all. Pi-hole
does the second part. It answers with 0.0.0.0 for every domain on its
deny list and blocklists, and forwards the rest. The names of the local
services belong in a zone that a server holds with authority. PowerDNS
Authoritative Server holds that zone here, and external-dns writes a
record into it for every Kubernetes Service that asks for a name.

This post puts the three together from three
recipes that kadet-hub publishes for
Kapitan. The project is
pihole-powerdns
in kadet-hub/examples. Its check script deploys it to a new
kind cluster on every change and once a week, and fails
when a step below stops working. All names are under .example, which
RFC 2606 reserves, so none of them belongs to a real domain.

What each recipe brings

A recipe is a directory of Kapitan classes, published as a signed OCI
artifact. All three render with the kubernetes
generator 1.14.0.

  • pihole 1.0.0 runs Pi-hole 2026.10.1, rebuilt from the Docker Compose example of docker-pi-hole. It renders a StatefulSet with a 1Gi claim for /etc/pihole and a Service with DNS on port 53 over UDP and TCP and the web interface on ports 80 and 443.
  • powerdns 1.0.0 runs PowerDNS Authoritative Server 5.1.5 with its zones in SQLite on a 1Gi claim. An init container creates the zone that applications.powerdns.zone names. The HTTP API listens on port 8081 and takes the key from a Secret.
  • external-dns-powerdns 1.0.0 runs external-dns 0.23.0, rebuilt from the external-dns project's Helm chart 1.23.0. It includes powerdns and writes into its zone through the API.

The fetch inventory

Kapitan 0.36.3 reads the inventory before it
fetches dependencies, so a recipe cannot be fetched by the inventory that
uses it. The recipes are pinned in a separate fetch inventory,
fetch/targets/recipes.yml:

parameters:
  kapitan:
    dependencies:
      - type: oci
        source: ghcr.io/kadet-hub/recipes/pihole:1.0.0@sha256:09ded1b7816cc669ecc45b539fc349c9cace2a53b1c23962561c7b3c3589746c
        output_path: inventory/classes/recipes/pihole
      - type: oci
        source: ghcr.io/kadet-hub/recipes/external-dns-powerdns:1.0.0@sha256:5e497b87ee50d7027666310355f5e12bb850c0d67f7e6a1d5ec2249843219fb3
        output_path: inventory/classes/recipes/external-dns-powerdns
      - type: oci
        source: ghcr.io/kadet-hub/recipes/powerdns:1.0.0@sha256:5330189e01e87845dd0dbaae1270929b566f1e62f0591502b07d69ed68e92fda
        output_path: inventory/classes/recipes/powerdns

Version and digest come from the signed
index, downloaded and verified as in the next
section. A recipe's index record also lists the recipes it includes:

jq -c '.recipes["external-dns-powerdns"]["1.0.0"].includes[] | [.name, .version]' index.json

["powerdns","1.0.0"]

Every recipe unpacks into inventory/classes/recipes/, so the
project can hold one version of powerdns. It has to be the one that
external-dns-powerdns includes. The index also lists powerdns 1.0.1,
whose readiness probe connects to the API port instead of the DNS port.
That version fits this project once an external-dns-powerdns version that
includes it is published.

Verify, then pull by digest

The registry's
consumer docs
give the steps, and check runs them for all three recipes. For pihole:

id=https://github.com/kadet-hub/registry/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main
gh release download --repo kadet-hub/registry --pattern 'index.json*'
gh attestation verify index.json --bundle index.json.sigstore.json --owner kadet-hub --cert-identity "$id"
d=sha256:09ded1b7816cc669ecc45b539fc349c9cace2a53b1c23962561c7b3c3589746c
tmp=$(mktemp -d)
gh attestation verify "oci://ghcr.io/kadet-hub/recipes/pihole@$d" --owner kadet-hub --cert-identity "$id"
oras pull -o "$tmp" "ghcr.io/kadet-hub/recipes/pihole@$d"
mkdir -p inventory/classes/recipes/pihole
tar -xf "$tmp/pihole.tar" -C inventory/classes/recipes/pihole --no-same-owner

The first attestation check proves that the
registry's release workflow signed the index. The second proves the same
for the recipe. check also requires the index to list 1.0.0 under
pihole with that digest and yanked: null. The recipes pin the
kubernetes generator by digest, and check verifies and pulls it into
lib/kubernetes the same way. Kapitan then compiles without --fetch,
which checks neither digests nor attestations.

One zone, two targets

The zone is set once, in the class inventory/classes/home.yml:

parameters:
  home:
    zone: home.example

The target dns renders PowerDNS and external-dns
into the namespace dns. inventory/targets/dns.yml:

classes:
  - home
  - recipes.external-dns-powerdns
parameters:
  namespace: dns
  kapitan:
    vars:
      target: dns
  applications:
    powerdns:
      api_key: ?{base64:dns/powerdns-api-key||random:str:40}
      zone: ${home.zone}

applications.powerdns.zone names the zone that PowerDNS creates at its
first start. external-dns-powerdns uses the same value as its
--domain-filter, so external-dns writes only names in that zone. The
API key is a ref. The first compile creates a random
value of 40 characters and stores it under refs/dns/powerdns-api-key.
The base64 backend only encodes, so use one that encrypts, such as gpg or
Vault, for an install that matters.

The target pihole renders Pi-hole into the namespace pihole.
inventory/targets/pihole.yml:

classes:
  - home
  - recipes.pihole
parameters:
  namespace: pihole
  kapitan:
    vars:
      target: pihole
  applications:
    pihole:
      password: ?{base64:pihole/password||random:str:32}
  components:
    pihole:
      env:
        # kind's cluster DNS. On a LAN this is the resolver Pi-hole forwards to.
        FTLCONF_dns_upstreams: kube-dns.kube-system.svc.cluster.local
        # The home zone goes to PowerDNS. FTL's dnsmasq resolves the name of
        # the Service once, when FTL starts.
        FTLCONF_misc_dnsmasq_lines: server=/${home.zone}/powerdns.dns.svc.cluster.local
      service:
        annotations:
          # external-dns writes this name into the zone.
          external-dns.kubernetes.io/hostname: pihole.${home.zone}

Pi-hole 6 accepts each setting of its pihole.toml as an environment
variable named FTLCONF_

_. The recipe passes
components.pihole.env through, so the wiring needs no change to the
recipe.

misc.dnsmasq_lines adds lines to the configuration of dnsmasq, the DNS
server inside FTL, Pi-hole's core. The line
server=/home.example/powerdns.dns.svc.cluster.local sends every query
for the zone and its subdomains to PowerDNS. Every other name goes to the
servers in dns.upstreams. dnsmasq accepts a host name in server= and
resolves it when it reads its configuration (parse_server in
src/dnsmasq/option.c of FTL v6.8). The Service powerdns must
therefore exist when Pi-hole starts. If the Service is deleted and
created again with a new cluster IP, Pi-hole needs a restart.

Pi-hole's own setting for this is conditional forwarding,
dns.revServers. It writes the same server= line, but each entry also
requires the network range of a reverse zone and sends the PTR queries
for that range to the same server. PowerDNS holds no reverse zone here,
so misc.dnsmasq_lines carries only the forward zone.

The annotation on the Service pihole asks external-dns for the name
pihole.home.example. The recipe runs external-dns with
--publish-internal-services, so the record holds the Service's cluster
IP. Any Service in any namespace gets a record the same way.

Compile and deploy

The recipes are written for the omegaconf inventory backend. With
Kapitan 0.36.3 and its omegaconf extra installed as the consumer docs
describe:

printf 'global:\n  inventory-backend: omegaconf\n' > .kapitan
kapitan compile
kapitan compile --reveal

The first compile creates the refs. The second writes their values into
the Secrets. The compile renders 10 files for dns, two of them the
CRDs of external-dns's chart, and 3 for pihole.

kubectl create namespace dns
kubectl label namespace dns pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
kubectl apply -R -f compiled/dns
kubectl -n dns rollout status statefulset/powerdns
kubectl create namespace pihole
kubectl label namespace pihole pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline
kubectl apply -R -f compiled/pihole

PowerDNS and external-dns run as users other than root and pass the Pod
Security level restricted. Pi-hole's image starts as root and drops to
the user pihole for FTL, so its namespace gets baseline. dns goes
first, so that the Service powerdns exists when FTL resolves its name.

Asking Pi-hole

check starts a client pod from Pi-hole's image, which brings dig and
curl, and asks Pi-hole through its Service:

dig @pihole.pihole.svc.cluster.local +short pihole.home.example A
dig @pihole.pihole.svc.cluster.local +noall +comments +authority missing.home.example A

The first answer is the cluster IP of the Service pihole, read from
PowerDNS. The second is NXDOMAIN with the zone's SOA record in the
authority section. Its contact is hostmaster.home.example, which
PowerDNS derives from the zone name. Neither the cluster's DNS nor the
root servers answer with that record, so the NXDOMAIN came from PowerDNS
through Pi-hole.

Blocking is tested with ads.example. It is NXDOMAIN until it is on a
list, whatever the blocklist holds that Pi-hole downloads at its first
start. check logs in to Pi-hole's API with the password from the Secret
pihole and puts the domain on the deny list:

sid=$(jq -nc --arg p "$password" '{password: $p}' |
  curl -fsS --data @- http://pihole.pihole.svc.cluster.local/api/auth | jq -er .session.sid)
curl -fsS -H "X-FTL-SID: $sid" --data '{"domain": "ads.example"}' \
  http://pihole.pihole.svc.cluster.local/api/domains/deny/exact

FTL answers the API before it reloads its lists, so check asks again
for up to 20 seconds. Then Pi-hole answers 0.0.0.0, the answer of its
default blocking mode, over UDP and TCP.

What the CI run showed

Run 41952672519
of the examples workflow tested commit 32c55f0 of
kadet-hub/examples#138
on 5 November 2026, on GitHub's ubuntu-24.04 runner, with the kind
node image kindest/node:v1.37.0. The durations below come from the
log's timestamps or are what check printed, in whole seconds.

Verifying the index, the three recipes and the generator and pulling them
took 24 seconds. Installing Kapitan with uv and the two compiles took 11
more. kind had the cluster ready 43 seconds later. From the first
kubectl apply until Pi-hole's rollout finished took 53 seconds, image
pulls included. Starting the client pod, the queries and the deny entry
took 2 seconds together.

external-dns had written pihole.home.example into PowerDNS by the first
query, and Pi-hole answered it with the Service's cluster IP over UDP and
TCP. For missing.home.example, Pi-hole returned NXDOMAIN with this
SOA record in the authority section:

home.example. 3600 IN SOA a.misconfigured.dns.server.invalid. hostmaster.home.example. 2026110501 10800 3600 604800 3600

ads.example was NXDOMAIN before the deny entry and 0.0.0.0 over UDP
and TCP after it.

The wiring is the one line in misc.dnsmasq_lines. In a local run
without it, external-dns still wrote the record into PowerDNS, but Pi-hole
returned no address for pihole.home.example, and check failed. The
cluster's DNS, Pi-hole's only upstream then, knows nothing about
home.example.

What it leaves out

Clients on the LAN. The Service pihole is ClusterIP, so only pods
reach it. Devices on the network need it exposed, for example with
components.pihole.service.type: LoadBalancer, and their DHCP server has
to hand out its address. For a Service of that type, external-dns writes
the load balancer's address. kind has no load balancer, so none of this is
tested. Pi-hole answers every client that reaches it
(FTLCONF_dns_listeningMode: ALL), so expose port 53 only to the
networks it serves.

Ingress. external-dns-powerdns 1.0.0 reads Services only
(--source=service), and its ClusterRole grants no access to Ingresses.
An Ingress host does not become a record without a change to the recipe.

The upstream. FTLCONF_dns_upstreams points at the cluster's DNS, as in
the pihole recipe's test, because a CI runner may not reach public
resolvers. On a LAN it names the resolvers Pi-hole should ask, separated
by ;.

The SOA. The powerdns recipe 1.0.0 sets no default-soa-content, so the
zone's SOA names a.misconfigured.dns.server.invalid as its primary name
server, PowerDNS's default. The NS record names ns1.home.example, which
has no address record. Neither matters while Pi-hole forwards the zone,
but both show up for anyone who queries the SOA.

The API. PowerDNS serves its API to every address, and every pod that
reaches the Service powerdns with the key can change the zone. No
recipe renders a NetworkPolicy that limits this to external-dns.

DHCP and the blocklist. Pi-hole's DHCP server needs Pi-hole on the LAN
itself, and the recipe does not set it up. The check does not test the
blocklist Pi-hole downloads, only the deny list.

Originally published at kadet-hub.org.

event_model_payload.headline: Terraform for Beginners: Build Cloud Infrastructure by Writing Simple Code
event_model_payload.summary:
A short story to start

Imagine you spent a whole afternoon clicking around the Azure or AWS website to set up a server, a network, a database and a few security rules. It works. Well done.

Now your manager says: "Great, can you build exactly the same thing again for testing, and another copy in Europe?" Can you remember every click? Every setting? Every small box you ticked?

Most people cannot. That is the problem Terraform solves. Instead of clicking, you write down what you want in a simple text file. Terraform reads the file and builds it for you, the same way, every time.

1. What is Terraform, in one sentence?

Terraform is a tool that turns a simple text file into real cloud infrastructure.

This idea is called Infrastructure as Code, or IaC for short. Your servers, networks and databases are described in code, just like an app.

A good way to picture it is a building plan. An architect does not build a house by shouting instructions to workers one by one. She draws a plan. Builders follow the plan. If you want ten identical houses, you use the same plan ten times. Terraform files are your plan.
