Each team has its own backlog, its own way of working and other projects competing for the same people. Someone has to keep those plans moving as one.

  • Run one scrum across all teams. Ours started weekly, went to twice a week to clear blockers, and became daily near the first cutover.
  • Ask every team the same three questions. What are you working on, and what is the estimate? What is blocked or likely to slip, and what is the alternative? What still has to happen for the next environment to cut over on its date?
  • Keep one board. One epic, with each team's own tickets linked in.
  • Spell out requirements early. When one team settles on a solution, share what it needs from the others the same day.
  • Post outcomes in the shared channel. Two-person working sessions are fine, but the result belongs where every team sees it.
  • Follow up instead of waiting. It never hurts to over-communicate.
  • Plan around the calendar. Change freezes, public holidays and time off for key people all punch holes in a quarter. Keep a tab for who is out and when, and set each environment window around it.

Dates will still move, and ours did on the first environment. Build slack around the known gaps so one slip does not push every later window.

4. Data: the part that decides the cutover

Compute can be redeployed. Data has to be moved, kept in sync and proven correct, so it shapes the whole cutover. There is no single right method, only questions you have to answer.

Can you take downtime? Decide this first, with the product owner. A short window removes a whole class of design. We could take one.

One direction or two? Bidirectional replication buys an easy rollback and costs you conflict handling and weeks of testing. We tested replicating back from the upgraded engine to the old one and hit problems. We chose one direction: seed the new database from a shared snapshot, replicate old to new with native replication, and roll back by export and import. That rollback carries downtime, so tell the product team before they agree.

Native or heterogeneous tooling? Every engine has its own replication. Tools such as AWS DMS or Oracle GoldenGate cover moves across engines. Pick the option with the fewest steps to script and test. For us that was native.

Where else does the data live? Rarely in one place. Ours was in three, each with its own method:

Store How it moved Rollback
Relational database Snapshot seed, then one-way native replication Export and import
Search cluster Snapshot to a shared bucket and restore, then a remote reindex of the current day during the window Reindex back
Object storage Bidirectional bucket replication, left on for days after cutover Files already in both accounts

What feeds it and what reads it? List every inbound loader and every downstream reader. We stopped the loaders before the window and repointed them after. The downstream warehouse stayed on the old database for one more day.

What can testing break? Readiness tests that write to the new database while replication is running can break the replication. Plan which tests write, and when.

5. Network and edges: where it usually breaks

The application and the database get the attention. The surprises come from DNS, load balancers and allowlists.

DNS. If the domain's hosting moves too, stage it so a rollback never touches the registrar. We moved ours into Route 53 like this:

  1. Create the new hosted zone as an empty shell. Not live, and no records created early.
  2. Add temporary names in the old zone that point at the new load balancers, so the new stack can be tested before cutover.
  3. At cutover, repoint the old zone's records to the new load balancers.
  4. The next day, sync the records into the new zone.
  5. After 24 hours, publish the new name servers at the registrar next to the old ones.
  6. After another 24 hours, remove the old name servers and watch the URL monitors.

Load balancers. Decide where TLS terminates, what the listener rules are, and whether each endpoint gets its own load balancer or shares one with host and path routing. Have services call each other through a load balancer or a DNS name, not through the cluster's internal networking.

Allowlists. A new account means new outbound addresses. Every partner and internal service that allowlisted the old ones needs the new ones before cutover. Give every outbound call (email delivery, analytics, partner APIs) its own line in the inventory. Check inbound routes too, such as loaders that still run on-premises.

Object storage. If browser or mobile clients read buckets directly, the CORS rules move with the buckets. If bucket names change, find every place a name is stored.

Edge protection. Check what sits in front of production that the lower environments lack. One of our APIs was behind a web application firewall only in production, and a deployment that rewrote its DNS record would have broken it.

6. Cutover: rehearse it the same way every time

Cut over the lowest environment exactly the way you will cut over production. People will ask why QA needs this much ceremony. QA is the only rehearsal production gets.

  • Use one runbook format for every environment. Ours had a preparation tab, a cutover tab, a rollback tab and a DNS tab. Every row had a date, time, duration, team, owner and status.
  • Write the application test cases before the first environment. Run the same set in every environment.
  • Get a sign-off from each team. Once before the window and again after it.
  • Script every cutover and rollback command. Store the scripts before the night.
  • Say ahead of time what a lower environment cannot prove. A production-only firewall, a registrar change and a disaster-recovery copy are typical.
  • Give cleanup its own change request. We had two people present for every bucket deletion.

Our rehearsals showed that deployments had to finish before the window, that published DNS had to be checked against expected results, and that the cutover needed an application redeploy. Each of those would have been a surprise in production.

For a sense of scale, our production runbook budgeted about forty minutes from cutting traffic to sign-off.

7. Monitoring, retention and cost: decide early

Monitoring. Set up monitoring and central logging in the new environment before the cutover. Put full coverage of databases and application URLs on the production readiness list. Stay on one approved logging path. If the cluster auto-instruments applications, a new service comes up already covered.

Retention. Autoscaling without retention is a bill that grows quietly. Set retention at every layer as it is built: log indices, database logging tables, buckets and container images. We left some of these until after cutover, and I would not do that again.

Cost. The cost lessons are mostly about deciding early:

  • Pick instance classes before the build, so reserved capacity can be planned.
  • Run the consolidated cluster on reserved instances.
  • Create temporary instances with volumes that delete on termination.
  • Question any design that copies data between accounts more than it needs to.
  • Ask whether every log line is needed before paying to ship and store it.

My take

A migration is mostly coverage. Know what you have, decide what changes now and what waits, move the data with a rollback you have tested, and rehearse the cutover in every environment. In my experience the hard moments come from things nobody wrote down far more often than from the technology.

It is also never one person's work. Application, database, DevOps and network engineers build it. The lead's job is to keep the scope honest, the plan visible and the teams talking to each other.

With a clear scope, a complete architecture diagram, a regular scrum and a firm timeline, and with AI tools to speed up the inventory and runbook work, three to five months is a fair plan for most platform migrations.

event_model_payload.headline: I built a terminal Pomodoro timer that plays lo-fi music - here's what I learned about the science behind it
event_model_payload.summary:
I used to have the same tab open almost every day: YouTube search results for "lofi pomodoro".

Not even a specific playlist. Usually something like:

https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=lofi+pomodoro

I'd pick a playlist, start working, and let the combination of lo-fi beats + Pomodoro timer do its thing.

That worked for a while. Then I hit the very predictable problem: I used those playlists so much that I got tired of them.

I wanted to customize the music, but I still wanted it synchronized with a Pomodoro timer. Work session starts? Music starts. Break starts? Music stops and ambient sound takes over. Work resumes? Music resumes.

So I built a CLI lo-fi music player that ties music playback to Pomodoro work and break sessions. Then I went down a rabbit hole researching whether lo-fi music and Pomodoro timers actually help you focus, or if the whole thing is just aesthetic productivity theater.

Here's what I found.

The tool first

Install it as a command-line tool from PyPI with uv:

uv tool install lofi-pomodoro
pomodoro

You can also install it with pip (pip install lofi-pomodoro). The default lo-fi playlist is downloaded on the first local-music run and cached for later sessions. The timer starts with 25-minute work sessions, 5-minute short breaks, and 15-minute long breaks.

Spotify support is included in the standard install. With Spotify open on a device, this resumes or keeps the current playback and synchronizes it with work sessions:

pomodoro --spotify

Or pass a built-in preset or playlist URI after --spotify:

pomodoro --spotify lofi
pomodoro --spotify spotify:playlist:37i9dQZF1DX0SM0LYsmbMT

Built-in presets include lofi, lofi-beats, jazz, deep-focus, and chill. Spotify playback control requires Premium. On first use, the CLI asks for a Spotify Client ID and opens a browser for authorization; no separate Spotify extra needs to be installed.

Keyboard controls during the session:

  • s — skip track
  • p — pause/unpause timer and music
  • i — ignore this track forever (saved to .ignored_songs)
  • q — quit the session
  • a — add +5 minutes to the current work session

The terminal prompt looks like this:

Press 's' to skip, 'p' to pause/unpause, 'i' to ignore a local track, 'q' to quit

You can also point it at your own folder:

pomodoro --music-folder ~/my-music --volume 0.7

GitHub: WittmannF/lofi-pomodoro

A Quick Introduction to Pomodoro

If you're not familiar with the Pomodoro Technique, it's a time-management method developed by Francesco Cirillo in the late 1980s.

The basic idea is simple:

  1. Pick a task and focus on it for 25 minutes.
  2. Take a 5-minute break.
  3. Repeat, taking a longer break after four focus sessions.

That's the traditional 25/5 approach, although the full technique also includes planning, tracking interruptions, and reviewing your work.

Personally, I use it more as a starting point than a strict set of rules. The timer helps me begin working, but I don't necessarily stop when it rings.

Now, the science

I expected to find either:

  1. "Lo-fi makes you focus" is real science.
  2. "Lo-fi makes you focus" is pure placebo.

The actual answer is less satisfying and more useful: the evidence is mixed, but the mechanism makes sense if you separate two different problems.

Pomodoro is mostly about effort regulation: when do I work, when do I stop, and how do I avoid negotiating with myself every five minutes?

Lo-fi is mostly about environment regulation: what audio background keeps me calm, masks distractions, and doesn't compete too much with the task?

There isn't strong direct evidence that "Pomodoro + lo-fi" is the optimal combination. But there is evidence for both sides of the design: structured breaks can reduce the cost of self-regulation, and certain kinds of background music can support mood and attention without hijacking cognition.

That's the "best of both worlds" argument. Not magic. Just two small interventions solving different parts of the focus problem.

1. Pomodoro is not magic, but timers reduce self-negotiation

The most relevant paper I found was Biwer et al. (2023), Understanding effort regulation: Comparing 'Pomodoro' breaks and self-regulated breaks.

They studied 87 university students during authentic self-study sessions. One group chose their own breaks. Two groups used systematic breaks: 24 minutes study / 6 minutes break, or 12 minutes study / 3 minutes break.

The result was not "Pomodoro users completed way more work." Task completion was similar.

But the systematic-break groups reported:

  • lower fatigue and distractedness
  • higher concentration and motivation
  • similar task completion in less time

The authors' explanation is the part I care about as a developer: deciding when to stop is itself cognitive work. A timer externalizes that decision. Instead of constantly asking "should I take a break now?", you postpone that negotiation until the bell.

That matches how Pomodoro feels in practice. The timer does not make me smarter. It removes one class of decisions.

2. Fixed timers can also backfire

A newer study by Smits, Wenzel & de Bruin (2025) compared self-regulated breaks, Pomodoro breaks, and Flowtime breaks during a two-hour study session.

The results were more cautious: there were no overall differences in productivity, task completion, or flow. Pomodoro breaks led to a faster increase in fatigue, and Pomodoro/Flowtime led to a faster decrease in motivation compared with self-regulated breaks.

So no, the honest conclusion is not "always force 25/5."

The better conclusion is: timers are useful when you need structure, especially when you are procrastinating or task-switching too much. But if you are genuinely in flow, a rigid timer can be annoying.

That's why I added a to extend the current work session by five minutes. The timer gives structure, but it should not punish momentum.

3. The Mozart Effect is mostly fake

You've probably heard that listening to classical music makes you smarter. This comes from a 1993 paper by Rauscher, Shaw & Ky in Nature — 36 college students showed a temporary improvement in spatial reasoning after listening to Mozart K. 448.

The media distorted "temporary spatial reasoning boost in 36 adults" into "Mozart makes babies smarter." Georgia's governor proposed distributing Mozart CDs to newborns. Baby Einstein became a franchise.

The problem: the effect is entirely explained by arousal and mood. Thompson et al. (2001) showed that when you statistically control for how much participants enjoyed and were energized by the music, the Mozart Effect disappears. Any pleasant, energizing stimulus — including a Stephen King passage — produces the same effect.

It's not Mozart. It's not classical music. It's mood and arousal.

4. Lyrics consistently hurt reading and writing tasks

This one is well-established and important.

When you read or write, your brain uses the phonological loop — the inner voice that "speaks" words as you process them. Background speech and song lyrics compete directly with this system, even when you're not consciously listening to them.

Salamé & Baddeley (1989) demonstrated this with serial recall tasks — 769 citations later, the finding has been consistently replicated. A 2023 paper in Journal of Cognition confirmed: "music with lyrics interferes with cognitive tasks."

The language of the lyrics matters too: if the lyrics are in the same language as the text you're reading, interference is higher than if the song is in a foreign language (Sun et al., 2024).

Practical implication: for reading, writing, coding with complex logic — instrumental only. For mechanical or physical tasks, lyrics cause much less harm.

5. Lo-fi probably works because it's predictable and low-friction

The key mechanism is probably cognitive load.

Your auditory cortex constantly predicts what comes next in music. When predictions are confirmed, the brain stops allocating resources to musical analysis — the music recedes into the background.

Lo-fi achieves this through:

  • Simple, repetitive harmony — your brain builds the model fast
  • Consistent 70–90 BPM tempo — no surprises
  • Imperfections (vinyl crackle, tape hiss) — paradoxically signal that the music isn't competing for attention. It sounds "not produced to grab you."
  • No lyrics — no phonological loop competition
  • Masking — the consistent audio field masks sudden environmental sounds (notifications, conversations) that would otherwise trigger involuntary attentional orienting

There is some direct lo-fi evidence, but I would not oversell it.

Kirk et al. (2022) compared jazz, piano, lo-fi, and no-music groups and found that focus music groups showed better sustained-attention performance and increased heart-rate variability compared with no music. But this was a controlled study with specific tracks, not proof that every YouTube lo-fi playlist improves coding.

Orpella et al. (2025), in PLOS ONE, tested music advertised for "work flow" and "deep focus" during a flanker task. Only the "work flow" condition produced significant mood and performance benefits. The "deep focus" label alone was not enough.

That's an important warning: the playlist name is not the mechanism. The actual acoustic features matter.

6. Volume matters more than you think

Mehta, Zhu & Cheema (2012) tested three noise levels — 50 dB, 70 dB, 85 dB — and found 70 dB (roughly café volume) was the sweet spot for creative work. Below that: mild under-arousal. Above 85 dB: performance degraded.

For deep analytical work (reading, writing, learning new material), 45–60 dB is better — less stimulation, less interference with complex processing.

The Yerkes-Dodson curve applies: moderate arousal enhances performance; too much or too little hurts. Music is an arousal lever.

7. White noise is genuinely useful for ADHD

This was the most surprising finding.

Séderlund et al. (2010) proposed the stochastic resonance model: ADHD brains have lower baseline dopamine, which means lower internal neural "noise." Your brain needs a certain noise floor to detect weak signals. When that floor is too low (as in ADHD), weak signals don't get processed properly.

White noise adds external noise to bring subthreshold signals above the detection threshold — improving working memory and focus for ADHD individuals.

This explains the paradox: white noise helps ADHD individuals but slightly impairs neurotypical people. Neurotypical people already have adequate internal noise; adding more pushes them past the optimal point.

Multiple studies since have confirmed this (Helps et al., 2014; Baijot et al., 2016).

8. Why I like the combination

The strongest case for a lo-fi Pomodoro timer is not that it maximizes raw cognitive performance.

It's that it creates a repeatable work environment:

  • the timer reduces self-negotiation about breaks
  • the music reduces environmental randomness
  • instrumental tracks avoid lyric interference
  • breaks create a clean boundary between "focus" and "rest"
  • Spotify/custom folders prevent the playlist fatigue I hit with YouTube

That's why I wanted the music synchronized with the timer. If the timer says "work", the soundscape should support work. If the timer says "break", the soundscape should stop asking for focus.

Implementation notes (for the devs)

The timer loop and local audio player live in pomodoro/__main__.py. The first-run playlist download and cache are handled in pomodoro/playlist_cache.py; Spotify playback and PKCE authentication live in pomodoro/spotify_player.py.

The main thread runs the cycle state machine and renders the Rich progress bar. Background workers handle local or Spotify playback and read keyboard input without requiring Enter. Queues carry skip, pause, and ignore commands between the key listener and the music player. The terminal listener restores terminal settings on exit.

The project is published on PyPI and has GitHub Actions coverage for Python 3.12, 3.13, and 3.14. CI runs the unit tests and smoke-tests the CLI, including Spotify playlist arguments. pygame-ce replaced pygame to provide the audio mixer on Python 3.14.

Current scope

Spotify mode controls playback during work sessions; break sounds such as rain, fireplace, or wind are still played locally. In local mode, you can use the cached default playlist or point the timer at your own music folder. The timer is available from PyPI, and Spotify support ships with the standard installation.

The full research document on music and cognition is in the repo at docs/music-science-studying.md if you want to go deeper.

GitHub: WittmannF/lofi-pomodoro

Happy to answer questions about the implementation or the research.

event_model_payload.headline: Exact text in an open-weight image model: what actually controls it
event_model_payload.summary:
Most image models treat lettering as texture. You ask for a sign that says "SATURDAY 2 PM" and you get something that reads like it, at a glance, from a distance. That is fine for a mood board and useless for a shop menu, a price tag or a poster someone has to print.

We build MOSS Image Studio, a browser studio around OpenMOSS's MOSS-Image — a 5B open-weight model released under Apache 2.0 that was trained with text rendering as a first-class goal rather than an accident. While building the sample library for our own blog we have generated a few hundred images with it, mostly posters with real copy in them. This post is what we learned about the parts you control, and the parts you do not.

The model is only half of it

Run the same weights through a sloppy prompt and you get the usual mush. The difference between "plausible sign" and "printable menu" comes from four things, in this order:

  1. The text is quoted, not described. Write the lines you want verbatim, in quotes, and label their role — headline 'PRINT CLUB', line 'SATURDAY 2 PM', footer 'STUDIO BASEMENT'. Role words are ordinary language to the model; it will sometimes print them into the picture. Keep them plain.
  2. Fewer, larger lines beat many tiny ones. Five lines at a readable size render far more reliably than a twelve-line block of small type. If the layout needs dense type, expect to iterate.
  3. Position is a separate decision. Describing "lots of empty space in the upper third" is a suggestion; a layout box is a constraint. That is why we built a box editor: you place the text area on the canvas, and the model fills it.
  4. The scene sentence leaks. Anything in the prompt is fair game for the picture. Name a "café" and a café sign may appear with invented text on it. Remove the objects that carry unwanted writing instead of asking for their absence — "no signs" is a suggestion too.

If you run it locally in ComfyUI

ComfyUI ships templates for MOSS-Image, and the setup is the part people get wrong. The four text-to-image templates load the instruction-tuned SFT checkpoint, moss_image_sft_int8_convrot.safetensors, at the documented settings (25 steps, CFG 2.5, the er_sde sampler). The Base checkpoint moss_image_base_int8_convrot.safetensors is a different model with different settings (50 steps, CFG 3, euler) — pairing the wrong template with the wrong checkpoint is the most common reason people conclude the model "can't do text".

Three files, three folders:

  • diffusion model → models/diffusion_models/
  • text encoder qwen3.5_9b_w4a8_gptq.safetensors → models/text_encoders/, loaded with CLIPLoader of type moss_image (not qwen, not flux)
  • VAE flux2-vae_small.safetensors → models/vae/

The full walkthrough with the templates is in our ComfyUI guide. Local ComfyUI is the right answer if you want the weights on your own GPU and no per-image cost; it is not the right answer if you want to make one poster tonight.

Where it still fails

Being honest matters more here than a feature list.

  • Long copy at small sizes. Paragraphs, legal lines, dense price tables: characters start to drift. Break them into separate lines or drop them.
  • Languages outside training. Latin and Chinese render well. Anything rarer is a gamble; check every glyph before printing.
  • Consistency across images. Two generations of the same brief are two different designs. If you need a series that matches, generate one and remix it in the box editor rather than re-rolling the prompt.
  • Numbers in sequence. A price list of six items will usually get the numbers right per line, not in order of importance. Reorder and rerun.

What we would tell someone starting today

Write the copy first, in a text file, before you open any tool. Decide how many lines it is and how large each one has to be. Then generate one image to see whether the model agrees with your plan, adjust the text (usually by cutting), and only then touch the scene. Most failed posters we see are copy problems wearing a rendering costume.

MOSS Image Studio is an independent studio built on the open MOSS-Image model; it is not affiliated with OpenMOSS. If you want to try the prompts in this post without installing anything, the studio gives you three images without a card.

event_model_payload.headline: Three Kinds of "Uncensored" Local LLM, and Why the Most Permissive One Is Often the Worst Choice
event_model_payload.summary:
"Uncensored" gets used as though it names one thing. It names at least three, they're produced by different techniques, and they have meaningfully different quality profiles. If you're picking a local model, the distinction is worth more than another benchmark table.

1. Permissive mainstream models. Gemma, Qwen, Mistral, straight from the labs. These still have guardrails, but a model running locally with a system prompt you wrote behaves very differently from the same weights behind a hosted product with a safety layer, a usage policy and a legal team in front of it. For most people this is the right starting point, and it's also where the strongest models are.

2. Fine-tunes. Dolphin, Hermes and similar. Someone took a base model and retrained it on examples that comply instead of refusing. Done well, they stay coherent and keep most of the base model's capability. They're the usual answer for fiction and roleplay, where the base model's reflex to moralise is actively in the way.

3. Abliterated models. This is the interesting one technically. Researchers found that refusal behaviour in these models isn't diffuse — it occupies an identifiable direction in activation space, and you can project it out. The result is a model that will answer almost anything, produced without retraining.

The part that gets left out of the recommendation threads: abliteration is surgery, and surgery has side effects. These models typically lose measurable ground on reasoning benchmarks and can behave erratically on unusual prompts. You removed a behaviour that was entangled with other behaviours.

So the ordering most people should use is the opposite of the one they reach for. Start at 1. Move to 2 if a specific task keeps hitting a refusal you can't work around. Go to 3 only when you can say precisely why the first two don't do the job.

A note on licences, since it's adjacent and it bites. Gemma, Qwen and Mistral are Apache 2.0. Llama has its own community licence with extra conditions. Read the licence in the exact repository you download from, not a summary and not the base model's — variants and quantised re-uploads don't reliably inherit terms. And check whether the licensor still exists: a non-commercial licence from a dissolved company is unfixable at any price, because there's nobody left to buy a commercial licence from.

Practical checklist:

  • Start with a permissive mainstream model and a system prompt you wrote yourself.
  • Only move down the list when a real task forces you to.
  • Verify what you're running — plenty of stacks silently fall back to a smaller model when VRAM runs out, and never tell you.
  • GGUF or safetensors. An .exe from a random site calling itself an "uncensored AI installer" is malware in a costume.

The headline version: the most permissive model available is rarely the best model available, and the gap is widest exactly where people assume it's narrowest.

https://getpocketcore.com/

event_model_payload.headline: Choosing an AI Project Management Tool for a Self-Managed Environment
event_model_payload.summary:
When project plans, task boards, and status updates live in separate places, teams can struggle to connect planning with delivery. That gets harder when project data must stay in an environment your organization controls.

A useful comparison goes beyond whether a product can be self-hosted. Check how it turns plans into assigned work, tracks dependencies and progress, and connects AI to project activity. Also distinguish hosting the application from hosting the AI model: those can be separate requirements.

Comparison table

Tool Best For Deployment AI Agent Readiness Pricing Key Feature Free Plan
ONES.com Development teams planning requirements, tasks, and delivery in a self-managed environment Cloud, On-Premise, Private Cloud, Air-gapped Yes, AI agent + MCP 30-day free trial for up to 20 users; annual tiered pricing. Project planning and delivery workflows with an Assistant that can create linked tasks and analyze progress No — 30-day trial
Jira Software teams coordinating issues, agile work, and development activity Cloud, Data Center Native agent Varies by plan Issue-centered project tracking for software teams Yes, plan-dependent
ClickUp Teams bringing projects and everyday task coordination together Cloud AI assistant Varies by plan Tasks, views, and AI assistance in a shared workspace Yes, plan-dependent
Wrike Teams coordinating cross-functional projects and approvals Cloud AI assistant Varies by plan Project workflows, planning, and team collaboration Yes, plan-dependent
Redmine Teams seeking self-managed issue and project tracking Self-hosted Not yet Open source Issues, projects, and workflow tracking Yes, self-hosted
Truetask Teams seeking straightforward project and task coordination Self-hosted options Not yet Varies by plan Task and project organization Plan-dependent

How to evaluate the options

  • Project-management depth: Test whether the tool supports planning, dependencies or workload, and execution through delivery. ONES Project documents Gantt timelines, milestones, dependencies, Kanban, workload views, Scrum boards, approvals, and time tracking (product details).
  • AI in the workflow: Look for actions connected to project work, not only general question-answering. When enabled and configured, ONES Assistant can create linked parent tasks and subtasks from a plan and analyze progress and estimated versus logged time to identify risks (workflow details).
  • What self-hosting covers: Verify whether the application can run in your environment and whether the model can too. ONES on-premises supports customer-managed data-center and offline air-gapped deployments. Its Assistant can connect to a self-hosted OpenAI-compatible model service; full capability requires text-generation and data-indexing models (deployment options; model configuration).
  • Development-team fit: Check whether requirements, tasks, bugs, sprints, releases, and delivery artifacts stay connected. ONES documents these work areas and links between issues, code, and delivery artifacts (product overview).

Shortlist by team need

  1. ONES.com: Consider it when development teams need self-managed planning and AI actions that turn a project hierarchy into linked tasks and analyze progress.
  2. Jira: A candidate for software teams organizing agile work around issues and development activity.
  3. ClickUp: Consider it when everyday tasks and project coordination should share a workspace.
  4. Wrike: A candidate when cross-functional coordination and approvals are central.
  5. Redmine: Consider it for self-managed issue and project tracking.
  6. Truetask: Investigate it for straightforward project and task organization, after confirming its deployment scope against your requirements.

Detailed reviews

ONES.com

Product Overview

ONES.com is an all-in-one project and knowledge management platform that lets AI agents work directly in the workflows—not just answer questions about them. For AI project management with self-hosted deployment, it brings planning, execution, and project context into a privately deployed environment. Teams can run it in their own data center or an offline, air-gapped network, and configure ONES Assistant to connect to a self-hosted model service through an OpenAI-compatible API. See the deployment options and model configuration requirements.

Why It Was Selected

ONES.com is a strong first choice when you need more than a self-hosted task board: it combines detailed project coordination with AI actions grounded in project work. For example, a team can organize a plan into parent tasks and subtasks, then use the Assistant to create linked work items and analyze progress alongside estimated and logged time. That connects planning to delivery signals the team can review, helping surface delays or effort overruns as work moves forward. ONES Project’s planning and Assistant workflows.

It also addresses the deployment criterion directly: the application can run in a customer-managed data center or fully offline air-gapped environment, while the Assistant can use an organization’s self-hosted compatible model service. Full Assistant capability requires configuration of both text-generation and data-indexing models. This combination makes ONES.com particularly relevant to development teams coordinating requirements, tasks, bugs, sprints, and releases while keeping the application and AI model service on their own infrastructure. Private deployment details · development-team scope.

Core Capabilities

  • Pain: A project plan can be difficult to translate into owned work. Capability: ONES Assistant can create linked parent tasks and subtasks from a project plan and hierarchy. Result: The planned breakdown becomes connected work items the team can track. Project planning and Assistant actions.
  • Pain: Dependencies make date changes hard to assess. Capability: Gantt timelines show milestones and dependencies together. Result: Planners can see which work may move with a schedule change. Gantt planning.
  • Pain: Status alone does not show who is overloaded. Capability: Workload views support resource planning alongside project schedules. Result: Coordinators can consider team capacity when assigning or sequencing work. Project views.
  • Pain: Work can become difficult to follow across stages. Capability: Kanban boards organize issues by status and keep requirements, tasks, and bugs in context. Result: The team can see the work’s current stage and related items in one view. Kanban boards.
  • Pain: A task may look on track even when effort is running over its estimate. Capability: ONES Assistant analyzes progress and estimated versus logged time to identify risks. Result: Teams get a delivery signal they can review while work is underway. Progress and time analysis.
  • Pain: Development work spans different work-item types and delivery stages. Capability: ONES.com covers requirements, tasks, bugs, sprints, and releases, with DevOps integrations linking issues to code and delivery artifacts. Result: Development teams can coordinate planning and delivery around connected project work. Product overview.
  • Pain: Sensitive environments need control over where the application runs. Capability: On-premises deployment supports a customer data center, with an air-gapped option for a fully offline secure network. Result: Organizations can operate the project environment within infrastructure they manage. On-premises deployment.
  • Pain: Teams may want AI assistance without routing model requests to a public model service. Capability: ONES Assistant can connect to a self-hosted model service through an OpenAI-compatible API; full capability requires text-generation and data-indexing models. Result: The team can configure AI assistance against its own model service within its private deployment setup. Model configuration.

Pros

  • Combines project planning views, issue tracking, workload coordination, and time analysis in connected workflows.
  • AI actions cover practical project tasks: creating linked work items and analyzing delivery progress and effort.
  • Offers customer-managed and offline deployment options, with a self-hosted model connection for ONES Assistant.

Cons

  • For on-premises and air-gapped deployments, the customer manages the infrastructure and upgrades. Deployment responsibilities.
  • Full ONES Assistant capability depends on configuring both text-generation and data-indexing models; some advanced features may be unavailable when the text model lacks structured-output support. Model prerequisites.

Pricing

ONES On-Premises provides a 30-day free trial for up to 20 users. Paid plans use annual tiered per-seat pricing, with a 100-user minimum. See ONES.com Pricing.

Best For

Development teams that need structured project planning and AI-assisted task coordination inside a privately managed environment. It is especially relevant when a project plan needs to become linked team work, with schedules, dependencies, workload, and progress signals available for day-to-day coordination—and when the organization wants the application and AI model service on its own infrastructure.

Jira

Jira is a project and issue-tracking platform used to plan and coordinate software work. Teams organize work into projects, track issues through workflows, and use boards to manage tasks. Its fit depends on the Jira edition and how the team plans to run AI services.

Where it fits: Teams can turn planned work into issues, assign owners, and move items across a board as work progresses. Backlogs, issue fields and types, configurable workflows, reports, and development-tool integrations support issue-centered coordination.

  • Advantages: Its shared backlogs and boards suit software teams; workflows can reflect team-specific review and delivery steps; reports help teams inspect progress from recorded work.
  • Trade-offs: Configuring issue types, fields, and workflows takes setup and ongoing administration. Teams should verify that their chosen edition and deployment support the intended AI and infrastructure requirements. Work that does not map naturally to issues may require adapting the process.

Pricing: Pricing varies by edition, deployment option, and team size. Check Atlassian’s current pricing for the relevant configuration.

Best fit: Software teams that plan in backlogs and coordinate through issue workflows. If both self-hosting and AI are requirements, assess the specific edition and model setup before choosing.

ClickUp

ClickUp combines project planning and task coordination in a workspace, with AI features alongside its project tools. The key check for teams with self-hosting requirements is whether its deployment and AI arrangements meet their infrastructure boundaries.

Where it fits: Projects, tasks, and subtasks provide a shared work structure. Statuses and views help teams review progress; ownership and due dates clarify responsibilities and timing. AI features can assist with workspace tasks such as drafting or summarizing where supported, and project discussions can stay near task context.

  • Advantages: Combines project organization and everyday task coordination; offers AI within the broader work environment; flexible views can suit different project-review needs.
  • Trade-offs: The listed deployment is cloud, so teams should not assume that an AI-enabled workspace means the application and model run on company infrastructure. Workspace flexibility can require shared conventions, and development teams should check fit with their repository, issue, and engineering workflows.

Pricing: Plan-based; AI availability and pricing can depend on plans and add-ons. Compare current terms with the features and deployment scope you need.

Best fit: Teams seeking a flexible project workspace with AI support for organizing and reviewing work. Treat self-hosting as a separate requirement to verify rather than infer from the AI features.

Wrike

Wrike organizes projects, tasks, and team collaboration. It is primarily positioned as a hosted service rather than a self-hosted option, so deployment fit may be decisive for teams comparing private infrastructure requirements.

Where it fits: A project lead can organize deliverables into tasks, assign owners, and use project views to follow work toward deadlines. Collaboration and AI features can support work management in the hosted product, depending on plan and configuration.

  • Advantages: Supports structured project and task coordination; combines work tracking and collaboration; AI assistance can complement project work for hosted-service users.
  • Trade-offs: Its hosted orientation is a poor fit when self-hosted application deployment is required. AI availability varies by plan, and strict infrastructure requirements may matter more than its project features.

Pricing: Tiered plans include a free option and paid subscriptions; pricing and features vary. Check Wrike’s current pricing.

Best fit: Teams that want hosted project coordination with assignment, progress tracking, collaboration, and AI assistance. If both the application and model must run on your infrastructure, prioritize products that explicitly support that arrangement.

Redmine

Redmine is open-source project and issue-tracking software that teams can run on their own infrastructure. Projects and issues provide a straightforward way to assign work and follow its status.

Where it fits: A development team can create a project, assign issues to owners, and track status without moving project records to a hosted service. Administrators control the application environment, but also need to operate and maintain the instance. The available information does not establish AI-agent workflows or AI-model hosting as part of the product.

  • Advantages: Open-source software deployable on team infrastructure; project and issue tracking provide a foundation for assigning and following work.
  • Trade-offs: The team owns instance operations and maintenance. Issue tracking may need complementary tools or processes for broader planning, and AI-assisted workflows are not a documented part of this offering.

Pricing: Redmine is open source; costs depend on the infrastructure and administration the team provides.

Best fit: Teams prioritizing self-hosted project and issue tracking that are prepared to manage the application. Evaluate AI requirements separately.

Truetask

Truetask is listed as a project and task coordination option with self-hosted options. The available information does not establish its detailed planning model, AI actions, deployment scope, or development-tool integrations, so verify those points rather than assuming capabilities.

Where it fits: Evaluate it with a representative project: trace work from goals and breakdown through ownership and progress review; check how dependencies and handoffs appear; and test whether AI can act on project work. Confirm separately whether both the application and model can run in your required environment.

  • Advantages: It is relevant to a shortlist focused on project coordination and self-hosting, and its fit can be tested against a concrete team scenario.
  • Trade-offs: The available product information is not sufficient to compare its planning, AI, hosting, or development integrations in detail. That uncertainty makes it harder to assess end-to-end fit.

Pricing: Details are not available in the information for this review.

Best fit: Teams already considering Truetask that can evaluate it directly against a real project and confirm its workflow, AI actions, and application and model deployment before selection.

Decision path and implementation checks

  1. Define the boundary: Decide whether self-hosting applies to the application only, or to the AI model as well. Confirm what data leaves your environment for each workflow.
  2. Run a representative project: Start with a requirement, break it into owned tasks, model dependencies, and review progress against delivery work. Check whether the tool keeps these steps connected.
  3. Check development fit: Verify that requirements, tasks, bugs, sprints, releases, and delivery artifacts connect to the team’s existing process.
  4. Match the tool to the priority: Compare Jira when issue-centered agile coordination is central. Assess ClickUp or Wrike for broader coordination, noting their listed cloud deployment. Consider Redmine for self-managed issue tracking, or investigate Truetask after verifying its capabilities and hosting scope.
  5. Plan operations: For any self-managed option, confirm who owns infrastructure, upgrades, model configuration, and ongoing administration.

Conclusion

ONES.com is worth evaluating when a development team needs connected planning and delivery workflows, customer-managed or air-gapped deployment, and an Assistant configured with a self-hosted compatible model. That fit depends on the team being able to manage the infrastructure and configure the required models. Jira may suit teams centered on issue workflows; Redmine may suit those prioritizing self-managed issue tracking. For cloud tools or options with limited deployment detail, verify the hosting boundary before treating them as candidates.

FAQs

Can ONES.com run in a self-hosted or air-gapped environment?

Yes. ONES on-premises supports deployment in a customer-managed data center and a fully offline, air-gapped environment. Customers manage infrastructure and upgrades in these deployment models.

Can the AI model also be self-hosted?

In private deployments, ONES Assistant can connect to a self-hosted model service through an OpenAI-compatible API. Full Assistant capability requires configuring both text-generation and data-indexing models.

What project work can ONES Assistant support?

When enabled and configured, it can create linked parent tasks and subtasks from a project plan and analyze progress and estimated versus logged time to identify risks.

What should a development team compare before choosing a tool?

Compare planning depth, where AI participates in the workflow, whether the application and model can run in your environment, and how project work connects to development activity.

event_model_payload.headline: I made my desktop wallpaper a frosted-glass "now playing" tile for Spotify
event_model_payload.summary:
I built a little open-source app for myself, and I have been really enjoying it, so I wanted to write down how it came together.

It is called nowPlayingDesktops. When something is playing on Spotify, your actual desktop wallpaper becomes a frosted-glass now-playing view: a blurred album-art backdrop, a glass panel, the cover, and the track and artist. It is the wallpaper itself, not a floating window, so it sits behind your icons and is still there when the desktop is idle or on the screensaver. Pause or quit, and your original wallpaper comes back.

I did not want another always-on-top widget. I wanted the now-playing view to feel like part of the desktop. The app composes that frame and then sets it through the normal wallpaper APIs — Windows (including multi-monitor when it can), macOS, and Linux (GNOME, KDE, XFCE, or feh/swaybg/nitrogen).

There are two ways to learn what is playing. Local mode reads the OS media session on this machine, which is enough if the Spotify desktop app is running here. On Linux, other MPRIS players may work too. If you want it to follow playback on your phone or another device, there is an optional Spotify Web API mode that needs a one-time Developer Dashboard login. I use local mode most of the time.

I also cared about leaving the desktop alone when music stops, and about not turning this into a tracker. There is no analytics. It just looks for what is playing and updates the wallpaper. By default, local mode may ask Apple's public iTunes Search API for a sharper cover when the system thumbnail is small; you can turn that off with --no-online-art if you want it fully offline.

I built this mostly in Cursor, as a lot of small pull requests: the glass compose path, the Windows/macOS/Linux wallpaper backends, packaging, and the two playback sources. I kept steering it back toward a quiet wallpaper tile instead of a mini player. It is still a work in progress — I am iterating on how it looks and how reliable the apply/restore path is — but I use it every day and it still makes me smile when the art changes.

If you want to try it:

pipx install now-playing-desktops && now-playing run --source local

Windows users can also grab now-playing-windows.exe from the Releases page. The repo is https://github.com/hippi345/nowPlayingDesktops (MIT). Testers, issues, and PRs are welcome, but mostly I just wanted to share it in case someone else enjoys it too.

event_model_payload.headline: Should the LLM see the "nice to have" findings? I measured it.
event_model_payload.summary:
CloudArchitect Lite turns a plain-English app description into an AWS architecture diagram and checks it with 25 deterministic rules. For the cheaper models there's one repair turn: the validator's findings go back to the model and it returns a corrected design.

Only errors and warnings go back. The info findings (no encryption at rest, no monitoring, Lambda talking to RDS without RDS Proxy, components not linked to any requirement, cost drivers nobody asked for) are never shown to the model. So they stay in the final design. GPT-6 Luna, for example, left encryption at rest out of 32 of 44 designs in the last benchmark.

Under my post on how I stop an LLM from inventing cloud services, a reader, Gautam K, asked the obvious question in two parts: would sending the info findings clean those designs up, and would it make the model start changing things nobody asked it to change? I didn't know, so I measured it.

The full report with every number is in the repository.

The setup: two repairs from one draft

The naive way is to run the generator twice, once with info findings and once without, and compare. That mostly measures luck: two first drafts from the same prompt differ more than any repair turn does.

So every job makes one first draft, then runs two repairs from that same draft:

  • Arm W sends errors and warnings, as the app does today.
  • Arm I also sends five info rules, with one extra sentence in the message: apply each info finding if it fits the requirements; otherwise leave it and say why.

One info rule is never sent: "component not in the verified catalog". An unresolved component is often the honest answer, and asking a model to "fix" it is an invitation to invent a service.

Three economical models (Claude Haiku 5.5, GPT-6 Luna, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite), 22 scenarios, 2 repeats: 132 jobs, 264 repairs.

Measuring "changed things nobody asked for"

This is the part of the question that's easy to hand-wave, so I made it mechanical. Each repaired design is diffed against its draft by element id: nodes added or removed, a service swapped, edges added, removed or rewired, nodes moved between containers, requirement links dropped.

A change is targeted if it touches something a finding named, or adds what the finding asked for (CloudWatch for "no monitoring"). Everything else is collateral. I also counted new findings: problems in the repaired design that weren't in the draft.

Collateral changes happen anyway, so I needed a baseline. When a draft has no info finding to send, both arms send the identical request. The difference between those two answers is pure chance, and that's the noise floor.

The bar, written down first

Before spending anything, I wrote down what would make me change the app, per model:

  1. info findings drop by at least a third, clearly;
  2. errors, warnings and pass rate don't clearly get worse;
  3. collateral changes stay within the noise floor;
  4. new findings don't clearly rise;
  5. the blind review score isn't lower;
  6. the extra cost is stated.

"Clearly" means a 90% paired-bootstrap interval that excludes zero. Writing the bar first matters more than it sounds: it's the only thing that stopped me from re-reading a borderline result in my favor later.

Results

Model Info findings per design (W → I) Collateral changes New findings Blind score (W → I) Verdict
GPT-6 Luna 1.23 → 0.00 no clear difference no clear difference 2.36 → 2.43 adopt
Claude Haiku 5.5 0.40 → 0.00 no clear difference no clear difference 2.43 → 2.36 keep as is
Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite 0.07 → 0.00 no clear difference no clear difference 1.93 → 1.93 keep as is

First question: does it clean them up? Yes, completely. Luna left encryption at rest out of 31 of 44 final designs with today's repair turn, and out of none when the finding was in the message. Haiku went from 0.40 info findings per design to zero.

Second question: does it change things nobody asked for? Not measurably. No model showed a clear rise in collateral changes or in new findings. The extra cost is under $0.001 per design. One number to keep an eye on: Luna's "load balancer in a single Availability Zone" warning went from 6 to 10 of 44 designs. That's inside the noise, but it's the first thing I'll check in the next benchmark.

The blind review, and the awkward Haiku result

The same panel as in the 0.3 benchmark (one Claude, one GPT and one Gemini reviewer, designs anonymized, 7-dimension rubric) compared arm W and arm I of the same job: 10 pairs per model.

Luna passed every criterion. Flash-Lite almost never trips the info rules (2 of 44 drafts), so there was nothing to measure.

Haiku is the interesting one. Its median blind score came out one step lower with info findings, 2.36 against 2.43. Yet when the reviewers picked a winner pair by pair, they preferred the info version 8 times out of 10. Those two numbers point in opposite directions, and with 10 pairs one design moves the median by a step.

I'd written "the blind score is not lower", and it was lower. So Haiku keeps today's behavior, and the report says why. If I had let myself re-argue it after seeing the head-to-head numbers, the bar would have been worth nothing.

What shipped

A per-model setting now lists which info rules the repair turn sends. It's set only for GPT-6 Luna. Haiku, Flash-Lite and the best-quality models (which have no repair turn) are unchanged. It's on main and goes out in the next release.

Things that broke along the way

  • The reviewer that took a shortcut. Arm W and arm I designs are often nearly identical. On those, the Claude reviewer sometimes reviewed design A, then design B, then wrote a third entry, literally "Duplicate placeholder; see the first A entry", and skipped the other two scenarios in the packet. The JSON was valid; the review was not. Validating the content in code, not just the schema, caught it, and one retry fixed all of them.
  • Dropped connections. Four long Haiku jobs and three reviewer calls died with "terminated" mid-response. The paired design helps here: a failed draft takes out both arms equally, so the comparison stays fair.

Where the evidence is thin

  • Small samples. 44 designs per model, 10 reviewed pairs. The Haiku verdict hangs on one median step.
  • What counts as a change. Configuration edits, like actually turning encryption on, aren't counted as changes, and a renamed element counts as removed plus added.
  • Model reviewers. They're not a human architect.

Cost

Smoke run, 132 jobs and the review with one retry: $6.88 in API calls.

Try it

You need Docker and an API key from Anthropic, OpenAI or Google:

curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aliaksandr-liapin/cloudarchitect-lite/v0.3.1/compose.yaml && docker compose up

There's also a clickable demo with no install. The best questions so far have come from the comments, so if there's something about the pipeline you'd want measured, ask.

Thanks, Gautam, for a question that turned into a better experiment than I'd have designed on my own.

event_model_payload.headline: How to Route and Configure a /48 IPv6 Subnet in AlmaLinux 8 & 9
event_model_payload.summary:
An IPv6 /48 allocation provides a large address space that can be divided into 65,536 individual /64 subnets (providing over 1.2 septillion addresses). These subnets can support dedicated public addressing for virtual machines, containers, proxy infrastructure, and other network services.

Native IPv6 routing can provide publicly routable addresses to virtual machines and containers without requiring traditional IPv4-style NAT, provided the upstream network routes the allocated prefix correctly.

This guide details the architecture and commands required to safely configure a /48 subnet in AlmaLinux 8 and 9 using NetworkManager (nmcli), handle source address selection, and natively route IPv6 to Docker containers.

(Note: We use the RFC 3849 documentation prefix 2001:db8:abcd::/48 in all examples. Replace this with your actual allocated /48 prefix).

Prerequisites and Provider Routing Requirements

Before modifying server networking, ensure you have:

  • Out-of-Band (OOB) Console Access: (e.g., IPMI, iLO, KVM, or your provider's rescue console). Reapplying network configurations can temporarily drop SSH connections.
  • Confirmation of Upstream Routing: You must know how your provider routes the /48 to your server. Configuring the host depends entirely on whether the provider routes the /48 directly to your server's primary IPv6 address, or if it expects you to respond to Neighbor Discovery on an on-link /64.

Step 1: Identify Your Active Network Interface and Connection Profile

In AlmaLinux 8 and 9, NetworkManager controls networking. You need both the physical interface name and its NetworkManager connection profile name—they are not always identical.

First, find the physical interface name:

ip -br a

Example output shows ens3 as the active interface.

Next, find the associated Connection Profile:

nmcli connection show --active

Example Output:

NAME                UUID                                  TYPE      DEVICE
System ens3         5fb06bd0-0bb0-7ffb-45f1-d6edd65f3e03  ethernet  ens3

In this example, the connection profile name is "System ens3". You must use this specific profile name when issuing nmcli commands.

Check the Existing NetworkManager IPv6 Configuration:

Before assigning additional IPv6 addresses, check the current IPv6 configuration of your NetworkManager connection:

nmcli -f ipv6.method,ipv6.addresses,ipv6.gateway connection show "System ens3"

The ipv6.method setting determines how NetworkManager handles IPv6 configuration. Common values include auto, manual, disabled, and ignore. Check the existing method before adding static addresses. Do not change it blindly, as doing so may affect your provider's existing IPv6 gateway or Router Advertisement configuration.

Step 2: Understand Routed /48 vs On-Link /64 Configurations

Do not blindly assign a /64 prefix to your main network interface.

  • Routed /48 (Recommended): The provider routes the entire /48 to your server's primary IPv6 address. In this setup, assigning a full /64 to your physical interface creates an unwanted connected route, causing Linux to send Neighbor Solicitations for addresses that should be internally routed. Instead, assign individual host IP addresses as /128. Note that assigning a /128 to the host does not automatically route the rest of the /48; the provider-routed prefix and your local container/VM routes must work together.
  • On-Link /64: The provider connects a /64 directly to your VLAN. In this scenario, assigning a /64 to the interface is appropriate.

Check your provider's documentation before proceeding.

Step 3: Assign Secondary IPv6 Addresses Using NetworkManager

To bind specific IPs from your allocation (e.g., 2001:db8:abcd:1::10) to the host system, append them to the active connection profile. Assuming a routed setup, we bind these as /128.

(Remember to replace "System ens3" with your actual profile name).

nmcli connection modify "System ens3" +ipv6.addresses "2001:db8:abcd:1::10/128"
nmcli connection modify "System ens3" +ipv6.addresses "2001:db8:abcd:1::11/128"

Apply the changes (ensure you have OOB access in case of a typo):

nmcli connection up "System ens3"

Step 4: Configure IPv6 Source Address Selection

When multiple IPv6 addresses are bound to an interface, Linux source address selection follows RFC 6724 rules (including scope, destination matching, and address preference).

Depending on these rules, Linux might select one of your secondary IPs for outbound traffic. If an application reaches out to an external API, and your primary IP relies on specific firewall whitelists or a strict Reverse DNS (PTR) record for mail, this can cause outbound failures.

You can explicitly mark secondary addresses as deprecated. Deprecated addresses remain fully reachable for inbound connections, but RFC 6724 prefers non-deprecated addresses for automatic outbound source selection:

ip -6 addr change 2001:db8:abcd:1::10/128 dev ens3 preferred_lft 0
ip -6 addr change 2001:db8:abcd:1::11/128 dev ens3 preferred_lft 0

Note: To make this persistent across reboots in NetworkManager, configure manual IP lifetimes or use a dispatcher script in /etc/NetworkManager/dispatcher.d/.

Deprecation only influences automatic source selection. Applications can still explicitly bind to any available address. For example:

curl --interface 2001:db8:abcd:1::10 https://api64.ipify.org

Step 5: Enable IPv6 Forwarding and Handle Router Advertisements

To route native IPv6 subnets to Docker or VMs, the server must act as a router. Enabling IPv6 forwarding in Linux modifies how the kernel handles Router Advertisements (RA).

If your provider supplies the default IPv6 gateway through Router Advertisements, configure accept_ra=2 on the upstream-facing interface when IPv6 forwarding is enabled. If your provider uses a statically configured gateway, this setting may not be necessary.

Create a persistent sysctl configuration:

cat <<EOF > /etc/sysctl.d/99-ipv6-routing.conf
net.ipv6.conf.ens3.accept_ra=2
net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1
EOF

Apply the settings and verify your default route was not lost:

Set accept_ra=2 only if your provider supplies the default IPv6 gateway through Router Advertisements. This setting allows the interface to accept Router Advertisements even when IPv6 forwarding is enabled. If your provider uses a statically configured gateway, this setting is generally unnecessary.

Enabling net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1 enables IPv6 forwarding system-wide. Configure firewall rules to prevent unintended forwarding between network interfaces.

sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.d/99-ipv6-routing.conf
sysctl net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding
sysctl net.ipv6.conf.ens3.accept_ra
ip -6 route show default

Step 6: Route a /64 Subnet to Docker Containers

With forwarding enabled, you can delegate a full /64 (e.g., 2001:db8:abcd:d0c::/64) to Docker.

Requirement: This requires Docker Engine 27.0 or later. Verify your version before proceeding:

docker version

Create a routed Docker network:

docker network create --ipv6 --subnet 2001:db8:abcd:d0c::/64 \
  -o com.docker.network.bridge.gateway_mode_ipv6=routed pub6

Important: Configure Upstream IPv6 Routing

Docker automatically creates the local bridge network and its associated routes, but it does not configure your provider's upstream router. Before expecting external IPv6 connectivity, make sure your provider routes the Docker container's /64 subnet through the server's primary IPv6 address. Without the correct upstream route, containers may communicate locally but remain unreachable from external IPv6 networks.

Deploy a container with a static public IPv6 address:

docker run -d --name web-node1 --network pub6 \
  --ip6 2001:db8:abcd:d0c::80 -p 80:80 nginx:alpine

Security note: Published Docker ports may be accessible externally over IPv4 or IPv6, depending on the network configuration. Only publish the ports required by your application and configure appropriate firewall restrictions.

Understanding Dual-Stack Port Publishing (-p 80:80): In IPv6 routed mode, Docker exposes the published container port directly on the container's native IPv6 address. The host port specified with -p is not used for IPv6 routed-mode access. However, because the network retains Docker's default IPv4 NAT mode, that same -p 80:80 mapping successfully publishes the port on the host's IPv4 address.

Step 7:Configure Proxy NDP (Only When Required)

Whether you need Proxy NDP depends entirely on your provider's routing architecture:

  • Provider routes /48 through server's primary IPv6: Not normally required.
  • Provider treats the container addresses as on-link: May be required.
  • Provider supplies a separately routed /64 through the server: Not normally required.

If your provider expects Layer 2 MAC resolution for the delegated IPs, you must enable Proxy NDP on the external interface and proxy the specific container address:

sysctl -w net.ipv6.conf.ens3.proxy_ndp=1
ip -6 neigh add proxy 2001:db8:abcd:d0c::80 dev ens3

To ensure these neighbour entries survive a server reboot, configure a systemd oneshot service to restore them during the boot sequence.

Step 8: Configure IPv6 Firewall Rules

Without NAT, your IPv6 addresses are publicly routable

Rule 1: Do not indiscriminately block ICMPv6

Essential ICMPv6 messages are required for Neighbor Discovery (NDP), Path MTU Discovery, and other core IPv6 network functions.

Rule 2: Host Firewall Configuration

Before adding firewall rules, identify the zone assigned to your network interface:

firewall-cmd --get-active-zones

Use the actual active zone assigned to your interface when adding firewall rules. Do not assume that the interface belongs to the public zone.

If the active zone is public, use the following command as shown. Otherwise, replace public with the actual zone name reported by firewall-cmd --get-active-zones.

firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv6" destination address="2001:db8:abcd:1::10" port port="80" protocol="tcp" accept' --permanent
firewall-cmd --reload

Rule 3: Container Firewall Configuration

Docker manages firewall rules for bridge networks, including published ports and container traffic filtering. Firewalld integrates with Docker through its dedicated docker zone and forwarding policies.

For additional access restrictions, configure the appropriate firewall rules based on your active Docker firewall backend:

  • With Docker's iptables backend, the DOCKER-USER chain can be used to apply custom filtering rules.
  • With the nftables backend (introduced as experimental in Engine 29), use separate nftables filtering chains instead.

not assume that host-level Firewalld rich rules automatically filter all forwarded traffic to Docker containers. Verify the effective IPv6 forwarding and firewall policies before exposing containers publicly.

Step 9: Verify IPv6 Addresses, Routes, and Connectivity

Use these diagnostic commands to separate IP assignment issues from routing failures:

Check assigned addresses, routing table, and default gateway:

ip -6 addr show dev ens3
ip -6 route
ip -6 route show default

Check which route Linux selects for an external destination:

ip -6 route get 2606:4700:4700::1111

Check Docker network routing and container port mappings:

docker network inspect pub6
docker container inspect web-node1 --format '{{json .NetworkSettings.Ports}}'

Test outbound and inbound connectivity:

Test inbound IPv6 connectivity from a separate device or server with working IPv6 connectivity. Testing from the same server does not confirm that the provider's upstream routing and external firewall configuration are working correctly.

# Outbound test from the server
curl -6 https://api64.ipify.org

# Inbound test (Run this from a separate external IPv6-connected machine)
curl -6 http://[2001:db8:abcd:d0c::80]/

Troubleshooting Common IPv6 Routing Problems

  • Small packets work, but large TCP transfers stall: Check whether ICMPv6 "Packet Too Big" messages are being blocked. IPv6 Path MTU Discovery relies on these messages to determine the appropriate packet size along the network path.
  • Ping works, but TCP connections time out: Check Firewalld rules, Docker published ports, container service status, and upstream routing before assuming an ICMPv6 problem.
  • Containers cannot reach the internet: Verify IPv6 forwarding, the upstream default route, and the source address configuration. If the gateway is learned through Router Advertisements, confirm that accept_ra=2 is configured on the correct interface when forwarding is enabled.
  • External networks cannot reach containers: Confirm that the provider routes the Docker subnet to the server. If the subnet is treated as on-link, verify Proxy NDP and the corresponding neighbour entries.

event_model_payload.headline: How to Inspect a PFX or P12 File Without Exporting the Private Key
event_model_payload.summary:
Someone hands you a .pfx file and asks whether it’s the right certificate for a deployment. Before extracting anything, check what the bundle contains.

openssl pkcs12 -in bundle.p12 -info -noout

OpenSSL prompts for the archive password and reports the bag types and encryption algorithms. A Shrouded Keybag indicates an encrypted private-key bag. Certificate bag lines indicate certificates. The -noout flag suppresses credential output.

Check the certificate’s DNS names and expiry

For an archive with one identity, extract the public certificate and inspect it:

openssl pkcs12 -in bundle.p12 -clcerts -nokeys -out leaf.pem
openssl x509 -in leaf.pem -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName

Check the Subject Alternative Name against the hostname your client uses. Check both validity dates, especially if the certificate was just issued. If the archive contains several identities, match the certificate to the expected entry before running openssl x509, which reads the first certificate in the PEM file.

What if OpenSSL reports RC2-40-CBC?

For a legacy archive you’re authorized to inspect, try loading the legacy provider for this command:

openssl pkcs12 -legacy -in bundle.p12 -info -noout

If the consuming application supports modern PKCS#12 encryption, re-export the archive with modern defaults and verify the certificate and chain before switching over.

I maintain PKIScope. The original PFX/P12 guide also covers inspecting intermediates and comparing the archive with what your TLS server actually presents.

event_model_payload.headline: Building an Arabic NPV/IRR calculator in vanilla JavaScript (bisection IRR, payback, sensitivity)
event_model_payload.summary:
Feasibility studies in Saudi Arabia are usually read in Arabic, but most free NPV/IRR calculators online are English-only spreadsheets. We built a small Arabic, right-to-left calculator for our clients and published it as an open-source, single-file page. Here is how the core finance logic works, in about 15 lines of vanilla JavaScript.

Live tool: https://googanksa1.github.io/feasibility-calculator/
Source (MIT): https://github.com/googanksa1/feasibility-calculator

NPV

Cash flows are entered per year; the initial investment is a separate field and is treated as year 0:

function npv(r, inv, cfs) {
  return cfs.reduce((s, c, i) => s + c / Math.pow(1 + r, i + 1), -inv);
}

IRR with bisection

Newton's method needs a derivative and can diverge on unusual cash-flow patterns. Bisection is slower but predictable: search between -99% and 1000%, and if NPV has the same sign at both ends there is no IRR in that range, so we return NaN and show "لا يوجد" (none) instead of a misleading number.

function irr(inv, cfs) {
  let lo = -0.99, hi = 10, flo = npv(lo, inv, cfs), fhi = npv(hi, inv, cfs);
  if (flo * fhi > 0) return NaN;
  for (let k = 0; k < 200; k++) {
    const m = (lo + hi) / 2, fm = npv(m, inv, cfs);
    if (Math.abs(fm) < 1e-7) return m;
    if (flo * fm < 0) { hi = m; fhi = fm; } else { lo = m; flo = fm; }
  }
  return (lo + hi) / 2;
}

Simple and discounted payback in one function

Passing a rate of 0 gives simple payback; passing the discount rate gives discounted payback. The fractional year is interpolated inside the year where the cumulative cash flow turns positive.

function payback(inv, cfs, r) {
  let cum = -inv;
  for (let i = 0; i < cfs.length; i++) {
    const c = r ? cfs[i] / Math.pow(1 + r, i + 1) : cfs[i];
    if (cum + c >= 0) return i + (-cum) / c;
    cum += c;
  }
  return NaN;
}

Parsing input typed on an Arabic keyboard

Arabic keyboards produce the Arabic comma (U+060C) instead of ",". A one-line split that accepts both, plus spaces, avoids a whole class of "why is my result NaN?" support questions:

value.split(/[,،\s]+/).map(s => s.trim()).filter(Boolean).map(Number).filter(n => !isNaN(n));

Sensitivity table

Lenders and investors usually ask "what if sales drop?". The page recomputes NPV and IRR with all cash flows scaled by -30%, -20%, -10%, 0, +10% and +20%, which is often more useful than the headline numbers.

Why a single HTML file

No build step, no dependencies, works offline once loaded, and it is easy for anyone to audit. For a finance tool that people use to make real decisions, being able to read the formulas matters.

The calculator is maintained by Googan Business Services in Riyadh, which prepares feasibility studies for the Saudi market: https://googanconsult.com . Issues and pull requests are welcome on GitHub.
